sections.methods:
We collected clinical, epidemiological, and etiological data from all infants aged 0–18 months, capturing those susceptible during their first and second RSV seasons, who were diagnosed with ALRTI and admitted to three public tertiary-level hospitals (Hospital de Niños Pedro Elizalde, Hospital Nacional Alejandro Posadas, and Hospital de Niños Sup Sor María Ludovica) in the MABA region between January 1, 2018, and November 30, 2024 (a). All the hospitals' Institutional Review Boards approved the study accordingly (Hospital de Niños Pedro Elizalde approval date May 7, 2024; Hospital Nacional Alejandro Posadas approval number 654EMP1S0/24(22)ren; Hospital de Niños Sup Sor María Ludovica approval date May 23, 2024). Informed consent was waived as the study was observational, retrospective, and only anonymized data were used. The study gathered information on hospitalization ALRTI episodes and specific diagnoses coded according to International Classification of Diseases (ICD)-10 standards (). Data was collected on the following characteristics: sex, age, gestational age, comorbidities, health insurance status, and home location. Inclusion criteria were a clinical diagnosis of ALRTI () during hospitalization and having at least one virological test done. Patients were excluded if they did not undergo a molecular diagnosis test, received Palivizumab, or resided outside the catchment area. Maternal vaccination status was obtained from vaccination certificates or the Nominalized Federal Vaccination Registry platform. , ,

A nested test-negative case–control study was conducted to estimate the effectiveness of the RSVpreF MI in preventing RSV-related ALRTI hospitalizations in their infants, compared to infants of unvaccinated pregnant individuals. The eligible population for vaccine effectiveness (VE) analysis included all ALRTI-hospitalized infants younger than 6 months old who were born between March 1st and November 9th 2024. We excluded babies born before 32 weeks gestational age or those whose gestational age had not reached at least 32 weeks during the vaccination campaign, as outlined in the table of dates and gestational weeks (). Cases were defined as infants 6 months old or younger who were hospitalized with ALRTI and laboratory-confirmed RSV infection, and whose mothers were eligible for prenatal vaccination. Controls were defined as infants 6 months old or younger who were hospitalized with ALRTI and laboratory-confirmed lack of RSV infection, and whose mothers were eligible for prenatal vaccination. The exclusion criteria for the VE analysis were as follows: 1) only the first infant RSV-related ALRTI hospitalization or the earliest non-RSV hospitalization was included in the analysis, with subsequent episodes excluded; 2) infants whose mothers were not immunized within the recommended timeframe (at least 14 days before birth) for the vaccine to be effective; and 3) patients with nosocomial RSV infections were excluded (b).

Nasal swabs or aspirates were obtained from all hospitalized infants with ALTRI and were tested for RSV, human rhinovirus (hRV), influenza A (Flu-A) and B (Flu-B) viruses, human metapneumovirus (hMPV), Parainfluenza virus type 3 (PIV3), human adenovirus (HAdV), and since 2020 for coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2), using standardized multiplex real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) in each hospital (Allplex™ RV Essential Assay by Seegene). Results were reported by certified laboratory staff. ,

For comparisons of variables between groups and the univariable analysis, Pearson's χ2 test was applied to categorical variables, and Student's t-test or Wilcoxon's rank-sum test to continuous variables, with a p-value <0·05 considered statistically significant. All variables were analysed for missing data, and none exhibited more than 10% missing values.

The impact of RSVpreF MI on RSV cases among ALTRI-related hospitalizations was assessed using a model with Poisson regression. To estimate the weekly hospitalization rates among infants aged ≤6 months during their first RSV season (Group 1), we used the weekly hospitalization rates of infants within their second RSV season (aged 12–18 months, Group 2) as a reference (Suppl. material, Poisson model specification ). , We used data between epidemiological weeks 15 and 40 from the 2018, 2019, and 2023 RSV seasons, ensuring that Group 1 participants in 2024 were already within the period when vaccinated individuals were recorded ( and ). In Argentina, lockdown measures were enforced for much of 2020 and throughout the 2021 winter season. Due to pandemic-related disruptions, RSV hospitalization patterns varied significantly in 2020, 2021, and 2022, leading to the exclusion of these years from the impact analysis (). , To estimate the number of RSV cases among ALRTI hospitalizations that were directly prevented by the immunization campaign, cumulative hospitalization rates were calculated using a corrected week approach based on deciles of cumulative incidence within the specified epidemiological weeks. This adjustment allowed for better comparability of epidemic timing across seasons. Thus, for 2024, we assumed that Group 2 hospitalization rates reflected the natural dynamics of RSV in the absence of vaccination. , This assumption was based on Group 2 experiencing its second RSV season during both the vaccination campaign and the RSV season, making it a suitable reference for the unvaccinated scenario. To estimate the expected number of RSV cases among ALRTI hospitalizations in 2024 in the absence of vaccination, we used predicted values from the Poisson model for Group 1 based on historical trends (Suppl. Material, Parametric bootstrap for CI and Estimated impact and results ).

To assess the VE of RSVpreF MI in preventing RSV-ALRTI hospitalizations in infants 6 months of age or younger, a test-negative case–control study required a sample of 270 participants to achieve 90% power and a significance level of 0·05, assuming an expected VE of 60%. This calculation assumes an estimated 35% overall vaccine coverage during the vaccination season in the catchment region. Multiple logistic regression analyses were applied to estimate the adjusted Odds Ratio (aOR) and 95% Confidence Interval (CI). The models were adjusted by age in months, sex, and comorbidities. Univariate analysis was performed to evaluate the effect of potential confounding variables such as prematurity, epidemiological week of hospital admission, and health insurance. Variables with p-values <0·20 were included in the multivariate analysis, and if they had at least 10% confounding effect, they were included in the final models. , The RSVpreF adjusted VE was estimated by the following calculation aVE = (1-aOR)∗100. A natural cubic spline with 1 knot was applied to capture non-linear relationships between the epidemiological week and vaccine effectiveness. Our supplemental materials detail the methods used to determine the optimal cut-off points evaluating VE in the context of the interval between vaccination and birth (), the onset of RSV season (, and ), and prolonged hospital stays (). , All statistical analyses were performed using R Studio software (R version 4 2 2). Data curation was done using STATA (version 17) and Python (version 3 13 0) software.
sections.results:
Throughout seven years of surveillance, 8407 infants aged ≤18 months were enrolled after being hospitalized with ALRTI (a). Of these, 2498 were excluded as they were born during the COVID-19 pandemic years (2020–2022), which affected RSV circulation ( and ). Between epidemiological weeks 15 and 40, 4807 ALTRI hospitalizations were recorded. After excluding infants aged 6–12 months and rehospitalization cases (n = 1434), 3373 cases were included for impact analysis (). Descriptive comparisons between the years of surveillance are shown in and

In the absence of RSVpreF MI, an estimated 397 RSV hospitalizations (95% CI 374–420) would be expected among infants aged 0–6 months during epidemiological weeks 15–40 of 2024 (). The implementation of the vaccination strategy prevented an estimated 133 cases of RSV (95% CI 110–156), equivalent to 215·71 (178·44–252·56) per 1000 infants with ALRTI-related hospitalizations (). The estimated reduction of RSV cases in 2024 was 33·6% (95% CI 29·5–37·2) relative to the expected number (). The NNI to prevent one RSV-ALRTI hospitalization was calculated at 83·9 (95% CI 65·9–185·4). Interestingly, the predicted cumulative incidence for past RSV seasons closely aligned with observed cases, whereas during the vaccination period, it significantly declined compared to predictions (a–b, and ).

From January 1st to November 30th, 2024, 647 infants aged 6 months or younger were hospitalized, 399 were born between March 1 and November 9, 2024, to pregnant individuals who were candidates for vaccination (b). Twenty-three excluded cases were born within the first 14 days after vaccination, not ensuring a significant transplacental transfer of antibodies. After excluding 53 rehospitalizations, 323 infants were incorporated in the VE analysis (b), with no recorded cases of palivizumab administration found in the study.

Among the 323 infants, sex and age were evenly distributed between the vaccinated and unvaccinated groups (p = 0·442 and p = 0·095, respectively). Overall, 58·2% were male, the median age was 2·7 months (IQR 1·7 to 3·8 months), 57·6% were younger than 3 months, and 42·4% were between 3 and 6 months old (). Prematurity was significantly more common in the unvaccinated group (p = 0·007), with 18·1% of infants born preterm, compared to 7·1% in the vaccinated group (). Comorbidities (such as cardiological diseases, Down Syndrome, congenital respiratory diseases, neurological diseases, and others) were present in 8·7% of infants, with no significant differences found according to RSV vaccination status (p = 0·610) (). The study was conducted with an underinsured population, with only 8·4% of patients having private health insurance. There was no significant difference observed based on insurance status (p = 0·537). Regional differences were observed in the infants' origins, highlighting disparities in vaccination coverage (p = 0·013). Across the RSV season, 69·5% of the unvaccinated group were hospitalized due to ALRTI compared to 43·4% in the vaccinated group, with a statistically significant difference (p < 0·001).

Viral pathogens were tested in all participants between March and November (cold season), resulting in an overall positive rate of 74·5% between these months. The most detected pathogen was RSV (40·6%), followed by hMPV (17·3%), PIV3 (10·2%), hRV (4·3%), SARS-CoV-2 (2·5%), Influenza A or B (2·5%), and HAdV (0·9%). Other viral pathogens were detected in 4·3% of cases. RSV detection showed a statistically significant difference between the two groups, with a positive rate of 17·7% in the vaccinated group compared to 52·9% in the unvaccinated group (p < 0·001) ( and ). Parainfluenza virus was more frequently found in the vaccinated group compared with the unvaccinated group. Coinfections were identified in 3·5% of the vaccinated group and 12·9% of the unvaccinated group, also showing a statistically significant difference (p = 0·007). Overall, 20·7% of hospitalized infants were admitted to PICU, without a significant difference between vaccinated or unvaccinated groups (p = 0·066) (). However, PICU admission rates differed significantly between cases (n = 45, 34·3%) and controls (n = 22, 11·4%) ().

The aVE estimate of RSVpreF MI against RSV-related ALTRI hospitalizations in infants 6 months old or younger was 66·1% (95% CI 30·1–83·8%) when adjusted for age, sex, comorbidities, and epidemiological week of hospital admission (). In infants 3 months old or younger, the effectiveness estimate was 80·8% (95% CI: 62·8–90·5%), when adjusted by age, sex, and comorbidities. RSVpreF MI showed protection against RSV-related PICU admissions with an effectiveness estimate of 87·2 (95% CI 52·6–97·0) and against RSV related-prolonged hospital stays (≥11 days) with an effectiveness estimate of 88·6% (95% CI: 62·3–97·1%), both estimations adjusted for age, sex, and comorbidities. No deaths were recorded among these infants ().

No significant differences were found (p = 0·594) in aVE when comparing vaccination occurring 15–27 days before delivery (62·2%, 95% CI 2·0–85·8) with vaccination occurring at least 27 days before delivery (73·1%, 95% CI 29·4–90·4), after adjusting for age, sex, comorbidities, and epidemiological week ().
sections.discussion:
Argentina's pioneering free universal vaccination for pregnant individuals in 2024 enabled real-world evaluation of RSVpreF across an entire RSV season in 2024. Our findings reveal a significant protective effect of RSVpreF MI against RSV-ALRTI hospitalizations, PICU admissions, and prolonged hospital stays. Maternal vaccination with RSVpreF reduced hospitalizations due to RSV-ALRTI by one-third and was associated with reduced odds of RSV-related ALRTI hospitalizations in infants younger than 6 months of age. The effectiveness was greatest among infants younger than 3 months old and for those admitted to the PICU or with prolonged hospital stays.

The results are consistent with the MATISSE phase 3 RCT, where the RSVpreF vaccine showed protective efficacy—82·4% within 90 days and 70·0% within 180 days—against severe RSV-associated medically attended ALRTI. The study VE results are similar with findings from two published studies in the country. Pérez Marc et al. reported a 71·3% VE (95% CI: 53·3–82·3) in preventing hospitalizations due to RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infection (RSV-ALRTI), while Gentile et al. found a 68·2% VE (95% CI: 33·1–84·9%). , Additionally, these findings align with earlier modelling estimates that projected a 20–40% reduction in RSV-related hospitalizations, underscoring the transformative potential of maternal vaccination in public health. , This evidence strongly reinforces the WHO SAGE recommendation and position paper for countries to implement MI strategies to protect young infants from severe RSV disease.

Our research revealed a 48% vaccination coverage among control individuals—slightly below the regional average and significantly lower than the national benchmark. , This disparity likely highlights unequal access to vaccination across various population sectors. To address this gap, targeted efforts to raise awareness and improve access are critical. Enhancing community outreach programs and engaging local healthcare providers can play a pivotal role in boosting vaccination rates within underserved groups. Furthermore, with recent RCTs and surveillance reports confirming the vaccine's safety, re-evaluating the optimal vaccination window during pregnancy is essential. , , , Identifying the most cost-effective timing will maximize the intervention's benefits and ensure maternal and infant safety while optimizing healthcare resources. ,

Our study has some limitations. To assess the impact of RSV vaccination on ALRTI hospitalizations, we used a Poisson model with individual-level data, adjusting for RSV rates in the second group as a proxy for intergroup ratios. , The model's predictions are closely aligned with observed case counts in previous seasons, however, there is a possibility that this model does not exactly align with population-level data of the 2024 RSV season in Buenos Aires. Another challenge we faced was estimating the exposed population to calculate important metrics such as the number of averted cases per 1000 infants and NNI. To tackle this, we estimated the incidence of RSV-ALRTI hospitalizations in both exposed and non-exposed populations using available population data. , Our cohort's high RSV prevalence and low vaccination coverage likely influenced these estimations. , Future studies should focus on narrower geographic areas with robust population data to improve accuracy and address these limitations. A higher sample size may provide an adequate power to explore protective role of RSVpreF MI in protecting of PICU admissions in those RSV negative individuals. Finally, confounding variables impacting vaccine effectiveness estimates, such as seasonality, narrow vaccination window, the concentration of cases in infants under 3 months old during the RSV season, and limited case numbers restricted further subgroup analyses. Future research should refine the timing of maternal vaccination, considering RSV seasonality post-COVID-19, infant age during the RSV season, and gestational age at vaccination to optimize outcomes. ,

While Argentina introduced RSVpreF MI during the full RSV season in 2024, Spain adopted nirsevimab in 2023. Since then, nirsevimab has demonstrated over 80% effectiveness against RSV-ALRTI hospitalizations in Spain, Chile, the United States, among other countries, aligning with findings from the MELODY and HARMONIE studies. , , , , Despite both strategies relying on passive immunization, differences in implementation may influence their effectiveness and impact. , , The success of the NIRSE-GAL or NIRSE-CL programs, with over 90% coverage, highlights the importance of timely immunization and rapid uptake. , The comprehensive approach includes infants born during the campaign, catch-up vaccination for those under six months, and high-risk groups aged 6–24 months with high-risk factors. , , This strategy achieved a median reduction of 89·2% in RSV-ALRTI hospitalizations overall and 95·2% in the seasonal cohort in Galicia. Given MI's potentially lower impact and nirsevimab's higher cost, combining both strategies or adopting a future infant vaccination approach, similar to that for pertussis or influenza, may offer greater benefits in Argentina. However, assessing the cost-effectiveness of such combined strategies and compared with different scenarios is essential for a sustainable implementation.

This study provides strong real-world evidence that RSVpreF MI is highly effective in reducing RSV-related hospitalizations, PICU admissions, and hospital stays for infants under six months of age. Furthermore, the vaccination strategy has led to a measurable decline in hospital admissions compared to previous years, reinforcing its public health benefits. These findings present a compelling case for policymakers and health authorities to accelerate the global adoption of RSV maternal immunization, driving meaningful progress in protecting vulnerable infant populations.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Anti-Respiratory Syncytial Virus Monoclonal Antibody Nirsevimab in Neonates: A Real-World Monocentric Study.
abstract: Background RSV remains a leading cause of infant hospitalization worldwide, and the recently approved nirsevimab could represent an effective and safe prophylactic strategy to prevent severe infections in the general neonatal population. Objectives We conducted a retrospective observational monocentric pilot study in a mixed preterm/term birth cohort to add real-world evidence of the efficacy and safety of nirsevimab in preventing severe RSV infection. Methods We included a total of 2035 consecutive infants admitted to the Neonatal Unit, University Hospital "San Giovanni di Dio e Ruggi d'Aragona", Salerno, Italy, from November 2024 to April 2025. We evaluated 30-day safety profiles and season-wide RSV infection rates, and the outcomes were also compared to newborns' birth rate in the two previous seasons (2022-2023 and 2023-2024). Results After the introduction of nirsevimab, a lower RSV infection rate was reported compared to previous seasons, and no adverse effects were observed. Compared to previous seasons, the clinical outcomes were more favorable, as only one unvaccinated neonate with RSV infection required invasive ventilation. Conclusions In this real-world analysis, we demonstrated a good short-term safety profile of nirsevimab, as well as a potentially high efficacy in the general neonatal population with lower RSV infection incidence. However, future studies are needed to better assess its long-term safety and season-wide efficacy.

sections.results:
Among recent advances in RSV infection prevention, nirsevimab is a long-acting MoAb with a half-life of 5 months, offering seasonal protection with a single shot [,,,]. Indeed, RSV prophylaxis with nirsevimab reduces hospitalizations in both healthy and preterm infants [,]. RSV infection affects newborns worldwide, accounting for ~3.6 million hospitalizations and >100,000 deaths per year, 95% of which occur in low- and middle-income regions [,]. RSV mostly affects healthy newborns and infants, as 80–90% of hospitalized children are full-term infants without known risk factors, and primary infection often requires corticosteroids, ventilatory support, and/or enteral nutrition [,,,]. The presence of just one risk factor, such as preterm birth, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, congenital heart disease, chronic respiratory conditions, or immunocompromised status, leads to longer hospitalizations and worse outcomes.

Several countries, including France, Spain, the United States, and Luxembourg, have implemented prevention plans to reduce RSV incidence, showing a significant reduction in hospitalizations and intensive care unit admissions for RSV bronchiolitis [,]. In Italy, RSV circulates seasonally, emerging in October, peaking between December and February, and declining by March–April [,,]. In Italy, the RSV prophylaxis campaign has been initiated in 2023–2024 in the Valle d’Aosta region, which reported zero hospitalizations for RSV-caused lower respiratory tract diseases in newborns who received it []. Based on this pilot program, starting from November 2024, nirsevimab has been introduced in routine clinical practice, but real-life data on its efficacy and safety are still limited, and robust pharmacoeconomic evidence to include nirsevimab in the Italian National Vaccination Plan is needed. Moreover, vaccination hesitancy is another significant barrier to effective infectious disease prevention [,,], and clear evidence of its efficacy and safety can help alleviate parental concerns and highlight economic benefits.

In this retrospective, observational, monocentric, real-world pilot study, we investigated the efficacy and safety of nirsevimab in a cohort of term and preterm newborns during the 2024–2025 RSV season, and the results were compared to the data obtained from the two preceding epidemic seasons.

In this retrospective, monocentric, real-world pilot study, we enrolled a total of 2035 consecutive newborns admitted to the Neonatal Unit, University Hospital “San Giovanni di Dio e Ruggi d’Aragona,” Salerno, Italy, from November 2022 to April 2025. In detail, we defined the RSV outbreak season, in accordance with the World Health Organization, as the period in temperate climates in which RSV highly circulates, typically in late fall and winter, with the peak lasting for about five months []. In Italy, this period is comprised between November and April. For this reason, three consecutive RSV seasons were included in our study: 2024–2025 (nirsevimab introduction); 2023–2024 (pre-nirsevimab); and 2022–2023 (pre-nirsevimab during the COVID-19 pandemic). All infants acquired RSV infection after discharge from the hospital, and only a few cases required NICU admission for severe RSV infection. The inclusion criteria were neonates born or admitted during the study periods, complete clinical records, and parental or guardian consent. The exclusion criteria included missing or incomplete medical records, treatment received outside the study center, and/or lack of consent.

This study adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines []. In accordance with Italian regulations [] and the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Article 89 [], formal ethical approval was waived for this retrospective analysis of irreversibly anonymized data collected during routine clinical practice, as no additional interventions or data collection occurred. Written informed consent for nirsevimab administration was obtained from parents or guardians as part of the standard clinical practice. The anonymized data were retrospectively extracted from the medical records using a structured CRF, ensuring the absence of personally identifiable information.

The collected data included demographic information (gestational age, weight at birth, sex), medical history (comorbidities, prior respiratory infections), and short-term AEFIs, classified by severity and the time of onset. The newborns were classified as preterm when GA was <37 weeks. Birth weight was categorized as follows: LBW, <2500 g; NBW, 2500–3999 g; and HBW, >4000 g. AEFIs and SAEFIs were classified in accordance with the Italian and European pharmacovigilance guidelines [,,].

The primary endpoints were a season-wide RSV infection rate—defined as laboratory-confirmed cases divided by total newborns in that season—and short-term safety, expressed as the cumulative frequency of any AEFI within 30 days after nirsevimab administration.

Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS 23.0 and cross-validated using R version 4.4.0. One infant in the 2024–2025 season developed RSV before nirsevimab administration. For the primary season-wide analysis, this infant was included in the numerator and denominator, while the infant was reclassified into the unvaccinated group for all other analyses. The descriptive statistics were expressed as mean ± SD or median (IQR), as appropriate. Season-level RSV infection rates and within-season comparisons between vaccinated and unvaccinated were analyzed using two-sided Fisher exact tests with mid-P correction (Exact 2 × 2 package, R) due to the low number of patients (<20). RR with 95% CI were calculated using the Katz log method. RSV incidence comparisons between seasons were first performed between 2024 and 2025 (nirsevimab), 2023 and 2024 (pre-nirsevimab), 2024 and 2025 and 2022 and 2023 (pre-nirsevimab during the COVID-19 pandemic), or between 2024 and 2025 and pooled pre-nirsevimab seasons, to account for the broader seasonal variation and increase statistical power (exploratory). A within-season 2024–2025 comparison between vaccinated ( n = 490) and unvaccinated ( n = 92) infants was also performed. For safety analysis, the exact 95% Clopper–Pearson upper bound was calculated for the AEFI rate. For Bayesian sensitivity analysis, a neutral Beta (1, 1) prior was applied to each season’s infection probability. A total of 100,000 posterior draws were simulated to estimate the probability that the 2024–2025 season had a lower infection rate than either 2023–2024 or the pooled 2022–2024 rate. The results were considered statistically significant if the two-sided p -value was <0.05 or the Bayesian posterior probability of benefit was >0.95.

In the nirsevimab-exposed cohort ( n = 491), 53% were male; newborns had a mean GA of 38 ± 2.5 weeks (range, 23–43) and a mean birth weight of 3078 ± 598 g. Preterm neonates (15%) had a mean GA of 34 ± 3.0 weeks (range, 23–36) and a mean birth weight of 2158 ± 651 g (). First, safety analysis was performed, and no AEFIs occurred among the 491 nirsevimab recipients during the 2024–2025 season (95% upper bound, 0.73%), including term/preterm neonates (). One infant in the vaccinated cohort received nirsevimab after RSV infection and was included in the overall vaccinated population for demographic and safety descriptions. However, for all efficacy analyses (including infection rates and statistical comparisons), this infant was classified as unvaccinated at the time of infection and counted accordingly.

During the 2024–2025 season, in which nirsevimab was introduced into clinical practice, the incidence of RSV infection among the total neonatal population was 0.52%, lower than that observed in the 2023–2024 (1.61%) and 2022–2023 seasons (0.71%) (). This reduction was slightly significant when compared to the 2023–2024 season (Mid-P exact test, p = 0.051), with a corresponding risk ratio of 0.31 for 2024–2025 vs. 2023–2024 (95%CI, 0.09–1.13) and a 69% reduction ().

Bayesian analysis estimated a 97% probability that RSV infections were lower in the 2024–2025 nirsevimab season compared to 2023–2024. This probability increased to 99% when excluding the infant infected before receiving nirsevimab, while decreased to 89% when compared to pre-nirsevimab seasons (2022–2024), likely due to lower RSV circulation for pandemic-related restrictions ().

Within the 2024–2025 cohort, three RSV infections were recorded among a total of 582 newborns. Of these, two occurred in infants who received nirsevimab, resulting in an incidence rate of 0.41% in vaccinated subjects (2/490), while the remaining case occurred in an infant who did not have prophylaxis at the time of infection, corresponding to an incidence of 1.09% among unvaccinated neonates (1/92) (). Due to the very low number of events, our statistical comparison lacked power and did not reach significance (Mid-P exact test, p = 0.40). Nonetheless, the trend suggests a numerically lower infection rate among immunized newborns. One infant who developed RSV prior to nirsevimab administration was classified as unvaccinated for this analysis.

The clinical severity patterns differed across seasons, although small case numbers precluded statistical comparisons. During nirsevimab implementation (2024–2025), all three hospitalized RSV cases occurred in term infants with distinct outcomes stratified by vaccination status. The single unvaccinated infant developed severe disease requiring 2 days of invasive ventilation, with moderate clinical severity, and bilateral opacities on chest X-ray. In contrast, both nirsevimab recipients experienced markedly milder illness: one required only brief non-invasive respiratory support, while the other one needed no ventilatory assistance, with both showing minimal radiological perihilar changes. Notably, no concurrent infections or NICU admissions occurred in this season’s cohort.

Pre-implementation seasons revealed divergent profiles. In the 2023–2024 season (pre-nirsevimab), complications were more frequent among the reported 12 hospitalizations: two infants required invasive ventilation (mean duration, 3.5 ± 0.7 days), three had documented viral co-infections, two required NICU admission, and four (33%) showed significant radiological involvement including bilateral opacities or diffuse bronchovascular thickening. During the 2022–2023 COVID-19 period, the five hospitalized cases displayed intermediate severity with no invasive ventilation; however, they included one NICU admission, two co-infections (40%), and exclusively mild-to-moderate radiological findings characterized by perihilar or diaphragmatic enhancement. Aggregate clinical metrics showed relative consistency across seasons (), with a similar mean hospitalization duration (9.7 ± 0.6 days vs. 8.3 ± 2.6 days vs. 9.6 ± 5.4 days) and a mean treatment duration (5.7 ± 1.2 days vs. 6.0 ± 1.7 days vs. 6.4 ± 2.1 days).

Conversely, the proportion of neonates requiring invasive ventilation was higher in 2024–2025 (33%, 1/3) compared to 2023–2024 (17%, 2/12), although the absolute case numbers were minimal and only involved the unvaccinated infant during the immunization season. Vaccination coverage analysis showed that 84.4% (491/582) of eligible neonates received nirsevimab, while 15.6% (91) did not, due to parental reservations.

RSV infection remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in newborns and infants, particularly in preterm and those with underlying respiratory conditions. Despite advances in supportive care, effective RSV prevention is still challenging. Nirsevimab, a long-acting MoAb, has shown high efficacy in RSV prophylaxis in newborns. In Italy, its use has been included in routine clinical practice starting from November 2024, thus real-life data on the efficacy and safety of nirsevimab are still poor. In this retrospective, observational, monocentric, real-life pilot study, the efficacy and safety of nirsevimab were investigated in a cohort of term and preterm newborns during the 2024–2025 RSV season. Our findings showed a trend toward lower RSV incidence with nirsevimab introduction compared to the preceding post-COVID-19 2023–2024 season (1.61%). The 2023–2024 reduction is encouraging, as it occurred despite the absence of COVID-19 containment measures that had suppressed RSV circulation during the 2022–2023 season. While this trend aligns with a potential population-level impact of passive immunization strategies, our study design precluded direct causal attribution to nirsevimab administration, and confounding factors could not be excluded.

In our pilot study, we enrolled all newborns admitted to routine care, both term and preterm, during the first season of widespread nirsevimab implementation, unlike controlled trials [,,], which less frequently include preterm infants. Therefore, our results provide a real-world safety assessment in an unselected population of all admitted newborns. Despite this cohort’s heterogeneity, no AEFIs were reported, according to the literature and trials that describe a favorable tolerability profile in neonates [,,,]. The absence of AEFIs in a real-life setting of unselected newborns, also comprising frail neonates, supports the broader use of this agent, also in near-term infants.

The clinical course of our few RSV cases observed in the 2024–2025 season warrants mention, although the small sample sizes preclude definitive conclusions. All three RSV-positive infants were term neonates, and the single unvaccinated infant developed severe disease requiring invasive ventilation and showed moderate radiological changes. In contrast, the other two infants who developed RSV after nirsevimab experienced milder symptoms, requiring minimal or no ventilatory support, with only mild radiological findings. No co-infections or NICU admissions occurred in this season. While intriguing, this pattern must be interpreted with extreme caution, given the very low event count. Comparatively, RSV cases in the pre-nirsevimab 2023–2024 season were associated with more frequent complications, including invasive ventilation, co-infections, NICU admissions, and more pronounced radiological involvement. Differences in virulence, circulating strains, or clinical management between seasons could contribute to this observed variation in severity, independently from immunization status.

Achieving high coverage remains a challenge, also in our pilot study, as parental reservations accounted for 15.6%, highlighting a significant real-world barrier to maximize the potential population-level benefit of this preventive strategy. In the 2022–2023 season, RSV incidence was low (0.71%) due to the residual effects of the COVID-19 pandemic’s protective measures, such as mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and reduced social mixing. Considering this background is essential when interpreting trends across seasons, as shifting public health behaviors substantially influence infection rates independently of pharmaceutical interventions. Palivizumab was not administered in any infant in the 2024–2025 cohort, thus the safety and incidence reported in our study only reflect the effects of nirsevimab. For the two historical seasons, palivizumab use was undocumented; however, since its indication is limited to very preterm and high-risk infants, its use was likely minimal. Any such use would have biased the earlier-season incidence downward, potentially rendering the apparent benefit of nirsevimab in 2024–2025 a conservative estimate.

This study has several limitations: (i) its single-center, single-arm retrospective design relied on historical rather than contemporaneous controls; (ii) RSV circulation patterns changed during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, and diagnostic intensity likely evolved over time, introducing secular-trend and detection biases; (iii) the exploratory tests were not adjusted for multiplicity, and residual confounding (e.g., GA, comorbidities) could not be excluded; finally, (iv) the very low number of RSV events in our 2024–2025 cohort prevented statistically significant subgroup analyses, even with optimized techniques like mid-P Fisher tests, resulting in underpowered analyses (e.g., 28% power for RR = 0.3). For this reason, we performed a Bayesian sensitivity analysis to contextualize the biological plausibility of a protective effect despite the low absolute case count, revealing a 97% posterior probability of benefit compared to 2023–2024.

A strength of this pilot study is its transparency regarding statistical uncertainty. By applying mid-P adjusted Fisher tests and Bayesian contextualization, we highlighted how near-significant p -values still suggest meaningful trends while avoiding overstatement. Furthermore, our power calculations provide essential insights for future research. Using the within-season effect size, we estimate that a future randomized trial would require ≈2300 neonates per group to detect a significant difference with 80% power and α = 0.05. For ecological comparisons across seasons, larger samples or multi-season monitoring are needed to account for secular trends, underscoring the necessity of multicenter cohorts.

In conclusion, this real-world snapshot of neonatal nirsevimab use during its first full season in Italy suggests a favorable safety profile and a potential role in reducing the RSV infection rate. Our findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and provide a foundation for larger, controlled studies of passive immunization in broader newborn populations. Indeed, our results indicate that nirsevimab could be an effective tool for preventing RSV infection in newborns by reducing hospital admissions and severe respiratory syndrome. However, larger, adequately powered randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm its efficacy and safety across diverse clinical settings. In addition, long-term multicenter surveillance is essential to assess the sustained impact of passive immunization and to optimize vaccination strategies.

title: Estimating the Public Health and Economic Impact of Immunisation with Nirsevimab or Maternal Immunisation for the Prevention of RSV-Related Outcomes Over Infants' First RSV Season in the UK.
abstract: Introduction Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) poses a significant health burden on infants, particularly during their first RSV season. Immunoprophylactic strategies, such as the administration of nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody, have been developed to prevent RSV lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD). This study evaluated the public health and economic impact of nirsevimab or maternal immunisation (MI) compared with standard of practice (SoP) in the United Kingdom (UK). Methods A static decision-analytic model was employed to track the UK birth cohort during their first RSV season. The model incorporated UK-specific data on costs, epidemiology and healthcare resource utilisation. Three strategies were compared: historical SoP (pre-September 2024), universal immunisation with nirsevimab and MI. Outcomes measured included RSV-related primary care (PC) visits, accident and emergency (AE) visits, hospitalisations, intensive care unit (ICU) admissions and deaths. The model also considered the impact of recurrent wheezing episodes, all-cause LRTD hospitalisations and non-medically attended RSV-LRTDs. Results Under the current SoP, RSV was estimated to cause 375,154 total health events and 24,360 RSV-LRTD hospitalisations (including ICU admissions) annually, resulting in an economic burden of £252 million. Universal immunisation with nirsevimab could prevent 208,691 total health events and 16,664 hospitalisations (including ICU admissions) and reduce costs by £105.7 million. MI showed a reduction in RSV-related outcomes but was less effective than nirsevimab, especially in preventing hospitalisations and ICU admissions or protecting infants born outside the RSV season. Conclusions Universal immunisation with nirsevimab for all infants during their first RSV season could significantly reduce both the health and economic burden of RSV in the UK. This strategy is more effective than MI, particularly in reducing severe RSV outcomes and protecting infants born outside the RSV season, thus offering substantial benefits across the infant population.

sections.other:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major contributor to lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD), particularly in infants and young children. In the UK, RSV leads to significant clinical burden, resulting in considerable numbers of hospitalisations and deaths annually. RSV is the leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, resulting in approximately 20,539 hospital admissions in infants under 1 year of age and 33,561 in children under 5 years of age annually [, ]. The impact of RSV is particularly severe in infants under 6 months, with hospitalisation rates peaking during this period []. Despite advances in medical care, RSV remains a major public health concern, underscoring the need for effective preventative measures and treatments [].

RSV infections are seasonal, peaking in autumn and winter (i.e. October through February in the northern hemisphere, including the UK) []. Infants born preterm or with underlying health conditions such as congenital heart disease (CHD) or chronic lung disease (CLD) are at higher risk for severe RSV infection []. However, most severe RSV cases occur in otherwise healthy infants born at or near full term []. The seasonal surge of RSV infections places a considerable strain on the National Health Service (NHS), often leading to overcrowded wards and extended waiting times for care [, ], underscoring the importance of developing strategies to manage RSV outbreaks and mitigate their impact on healthcare systems.

As of the end of 2023, two products have recently received approval by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) for protecting infants against RSV infection. Beyfortus (nirsevimab), a long-acting anti-RSV monoclonal antibody, was approved in November 2022 for preventing RSV-LRTD in newborns and infants during their first RSV season []. In November 2023, Abrysvo (RSVpreF), a maternal RSV vaccine, received UK MHRA approval for vaccinating pregnant women to protect newborns against RSV-LRTD []. Given both products protect newborns during their first RSV season, agencies, such as the UK Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI), must evaluate the relative reduction in the burden of infant RSV-LRTD for each product while establishing national guidelines.

Previous modelling studies have examined the impact of prophylactic measures on RSV burden, including a comparison of nirsevimab and maternal immunisation (MI) leveraging a dynamic transmission model from the UK perspective [–]. However, none have used the most current clinical data to inform protection against RSV-LRTDs offered by nirsevimab in an indirect comparison against MI []. This study also applied the latest costing data, presenting cost-related results in 2024 Great British Pounds (GBP) [–].

The objective of this study was to compare the expected clinical and economic burden of immunisation strategies with nirsevimab or MI compared with a palivizumab-only strategy in preventing RSV-associated LRTDs in UK infants based on the latest clinical evidence for nirsevimab and MI.

sections.methods:
An existing static, decision-analytic model [], developed in Microsoft Excel ® to track the UK birth cohort over the first RSV season and evaluate the impact of various immunisation strategies for the prevention of RSV-related health events was updated to include MI. The model stratified infants into subpopulations corresponding to the three groups assessed in the nirsevimab clinical trials [–]: (1) late-preterm and term infants (born at or after 35 weeks gestational age [wGA]); (2) preterm infants born between 29 wGA and < 35 wGA not eligible for palivizumab); and (3) palivizumab-eligible infants (born before 29 wGA or those with CLD or CHD, in line with the population recommended by the JCVI[]).

Infants entered the model in monthly birth cohorts stratified by subpopulation and were tracked separately across their first RSV season. The model assumed that the UK RSV season extended from October through February with peak infection rates occurring in December based on data collected between 2012 and 2016 (Figure ) [].

Three immunisation strategies were compared in the analysis. Strategy 1, historical standard of practice (pre-September 2024; referred to as standard of practice [SoP]), involved monthly administration of palivizumab to eligible infants during the RSV season only. Strategy 2 involved administration of nirsevimab to term infants before the RSV season aligned with the UK National Immunisation Program (NIP). Infants born before the RSV season received a single dose at their regular NIP immunisation visit (8-, 12-, or 16-weeks post-birth), while those born during the season received one dose at birth. Preterm and palivizumab-eligible infants followed a seasonal “catch-up” approach where infants born before the RSV season received a single dose in October and those born during the season received a single dose at birth. Strategy 3 constituted SoP for palivizumab-eligible infants, with preterm and late-preterm/term infants protected through year-round MI administration to pregnant mothers between 28 and 36 wGA (to reflect the current UK national programme[]). An overview of the model structure is presented in Fig. S2, and detailed depiction of dosing strategies is presented in Fig. S3.

Palivizumab-eligible infants were not considered protected by MI owing to being born before mothers are eligible for vaccination, being born too shortly after vaccination for the maternal antibodies to transfer and the lack of evidence that MI offers protection for infants with CHD or CLD. As the model only tracked infants, assumptions were required related to what circumstances vaccine-induced maternal protection was transferred to infants (e.g. coverage) and at what efficacy level protection was transferred (e.g. antibody transfer). To estimate the coverage of infants with MI, the model first calculated the percentage of infants eligible for MI by analysing the distribution of births by gestational age, separately categorising them into early preterm and late-preterm/full term at birth. Subsequently, the model evaluated the distribution of infants born to vaccinated mothers and the distribution of vaccinations (by wGA).

The proportion of antibodies successfully transferred from pregnant mothers was estimated by using the relationship between the percentage of vaccinated pregnant mothers by wGA and the distribution of eligible infants who received any level of protection at birth within each subgroup. Infants born within 2 weeks of MI administration received no antibody transfer, those born between 3 and 4 weeks post-immunisation received 50% of full antibody transfer, and those born at 5 weeks or later received full transfer based on a previous study [] and the UK Green Book on Immunisation []. Maternal antibodies were assumed to not wane before birth. A tabular summary of the data leverage and structure of these calculations is presented in Table .

Model inputs (Table ) were obtained from literature, publicly available data sources and Sanofi-internal data where relevant. Details related to demographic input, RSV seasonality and risk of RSV-LRTD-related health events have been previously described for the UK setting [].

The efficacy of nirsevimab in preventing RSV-LRTDs in the outpatient setting for preterm infants was obtained from a post-hoc analysis of a phase 2b trial for infants who weighed less than 5 kg at baseline and received the recommended dose []. In preterm infants, the efficacy against medically attended (MA) RSV-LRTD showed a relative risk reduction of 86.2% (95% confidence intervals [CI] 68.0%, 94.0%) compared with placebo []. For late-preterm and term infants not eligible for palivizumab, the efficacy against medically attended (MA) RSV-LRTD was 74.5% (95% CI 49.6%, 87.1%), based on data from the primary cohort in the phase 3 MELODY trial []. The efficacy against MA RSV-LRTD hospitalisations in both the preterm and term infant populations was 83.2% (95% CI 67.8%, 92.0%) from the open-label HARMONIE trial in infants under 12 months of age not eligible for palivizumab []. Nirsevimab also demonstrated a significant reduction in all-cause LRTD hospitalisation of 58.0% (95% CI 34.3%, 97.6%) in the HARMONIE study []. Finally, on the basis of pharmacokinetic data indicating comparable efficacy when extrapolated to infants born extremely preterm or with CLD/CHD, the analyses assumed that nirsevimab was noninferior to palivizumab for this subpopulation (owing to lack of specific efficacy data for this group in the phase 2–3 MEDLEY study) []. As inputs used for this population were defined before the introduction of palivizumab, the efficacy of palivizumab was informed by an updated network meta-analysis of three randomised control trials assessing the prevention of hospitalisation associated with palivizumab versus placebo []. Given lack of data on the efficacy of palivizumab in the outpatient setting, the analysis assumed the same efficacy as in the inpatient setting. However, by using a non-inferiority assumption with respect to nirsevimab, no incremental effect was expected on the basis of the level of protection alone (although the model also assumed additional coverage related to nirsevimab given the need for only one dose per season compared with palivizumab). In the base case, the model assumed that the protective effect for nirsevimab lasted 150 days, with no remaining efficacy after 5 months [, , ], while protection from palivizumab lasted only 1 month [].

The efficacy of MI was based on the results of the phase 3 MATISSE trial [], efficacy data over time in the Abrysvo European Medicines Agency (EMA) label [] and analyses performed by the United States Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee (US VRBPAC) of the MATISSE trial data which were presented to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) []. A polynomial equation was derived on the basis of the overall efficacy trend observed in the MATISSE trial at days 90 and 180 for severe RSV events, RSV hospitalisations and MA RSV-LRTD. The duration of efficacy was assumed from birth to 180 days (6 months), with efficacy waning between 30 and 180 days (Fig. S4). Considering the distribution of gestational ages at birth and MI administration, it was calculated that 29.2% of preterm infants and 92.5% of late-preterm and term infants would benefit from successful antibody transfer. The efficacy was therefore adjusted in the two subgroups by 0.292 and 0.925, respectively. The model assumed that protection from MI immediately dropped to 0% at 6 months (Fig. S4). Owing to data availability, the same efficacy levels for nirsevimab and MI against outpatient managed RSV-related events were assumed to represent protection against non-MA RSV-LRTDs.

The coverage rate for palivizumab under Strategies 1 and 3 (70%) was based on annual sales data for the UK [Data on File]. As the administration schedule for nirsevimab was modelled after the UK NIP, uptake across all three infant subpopulations was presumed to be 91%, comparable to the primary vaccination series for infants under 5 years of age within the UK Cover of Vaccination Evaluated Rapidly (COVER) programme []. MI coverage in pregnant mothers was assumed to be 60%, based on Tdap vaccine coverage in the UK [] as recommended by the UK JCVI []. However, this coverage rate was adjusted in the preterm infant population due to the MI administration schedule as depicted above based on the distribution of maternal vaccinations and the distribution of infants born to vaccinated mothers by wGA (Table ).

The burden of RSV was captured by the risk of RSV events treated as: hospitalisations in a standard ward, intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, accident and emergency (AE) visits, primary care (PC) visits, recurrent wheezing as a complication associated with MA RSV-LRTD hospitalisation, non-MA RSV events and all-cause LRTDs. The source material and transformations to determine the monthly risk rates for MA RSV-LRTDs, RSV case-related fatality and recurrent wheezing were described previously[] (Table ). The risk of a non-MA LRTD event was based on a prospective infant cohort study which showed that one-quarter of infants experienced an RSV-associated acute respiratory infection during their first year of life, of whom half were non-MA (10.7%) []. The incidence of all-cause LRTD including RSV events was estimated at 11.46% []. RSV-specific LRTD hospitalisations were a subset of all-cause LRTD hospitalisations, with a weighted average of RSV hospitalisations across the three subpopulations estimated at 3.65% [, –]. Therefore, the model applied an incidence of all-cause LRTD hospitalisation excluding RSV of 7.81% where palivizumab and MI were assumed to have no impact on infant all-cause LRTD hospitalisations, given evidence supporting a reduction on this outcome was lacking. Owing to data availability, the risk of non-medically attended RSV-LRTD, all-cause LRTD hospitalisation and recurrent wheezing were assumed to be equal across all infant subpopulations and age.

Scenario analysis was conducted for alternative immunisation strategies for nirsevimab: all infants immunised at birth (“year-round” scenario) and a seasonal-based approach with a “catch-up” for all infant populations in which infants born before the RSV season received one dose of nirsevimab in October and those born during the RSV season were immunised at birth (Fig. S3(D); Fig. S3(E)). We also tested assumptions by Hodgson et al. [] around MI coverage and efficacy to highlight the impact of these assumption on results for the impact of MI compared against SoP (Table S2). To assess additional uncertainty in the model results, a deterministic sensitivity analysis (DSA) was conducted by varying key parameters within the model and measuring the impact on total incremental costs. Other than treatment efficacy, in which the lower and upper bound values were informed by the 95% CIs from clinical trial data, variability in the tested parameters was based on an assumed 20% deviation from the base-case value (Table ).

This article is based on previously conducted studies and does not contain any new studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors.
sections.results:
In the SoP scenario, the model projected 23,215 hospitalisations (excluding ICU admissions) and 1145 ICU admissions. Among those hospitalised, there were an estimated 18,270 cases of recurrent wheezing over the first 3 years. RSV infections resulted in 64,558 AE visits, 159,231 PC visits, 62,776 non-MA RSV events and 20 infant RSV-related deaths. Additionally, there were an estimated 45,940 all-cause LRTD hospitalisations (excluding RSV-related hospitalisations). The total RSV-related costs for all subpopulations amounted to £117.7 million, with RSV-LRTD hospitalisations comprising 58% of these costs and ICU costs accounting for approximately 9%. The cost of all-cause LRTD hospitalisations (excluding RSV-related hospitalisations) was £134.2 million (Table ).

In analysis of subpopulations, term infants, considered the lowest risk group, accounted for 92% of total hospitalisation (excluding ICU admissions) and 83% of ICU admissions, whereas palivizumab-eligible infants, the highest-risk group, accounted for only 2% and 3%, respectively (Table S3). Analysis by month of birth indicated that 68% of health events were attributable to infants born between March and September (Table S4, Fig. S5(B)). RSV hospitalisation distribution showed that 58% of cases were infants born out of season, whereas 42% were in those born in-season (Fig. A, B).

Immunisation with nirsevimab was projected to prevent 149,940 MA RSV-LRTDs (including RSV-related deaths) and 36,516 cases of non-MA RSV-LRTDs, compared with SoP. Furthermore, nirsevimab was estimated to reduce RSV hospital and ICU admissions by 68% (16,664) and significantly decrease the number of AE and PC visits. Additionally, it was anticipated to prevent 9736 all-cause LRTD hospitalisations (excluding RSV hospitalisations) and 12,498 cases of recurrent wheezing over 3 years (Table ).

The implementation of nirsevimab was expected to lower the total costs associated with MA RSV-LRTDs and long-term recurrent wheezing by £77.2 million (66%). The largest cost savings came from reduced hospital admissions (including ICU admission) amounting to £53.7 million (68% reduction). Furthermore, reduced all-cause LRTD hospitalisations contributed an additional £28 million in savings (Table ).

As most RSV-LRTDs occurred among term infants, 93% of the events avoided by an immunisation strategy targeting all infants with nirsevimab were observed in this population (Table S3). The high-risk, palivizumab-eligible infant population represented only 0.4% of the avoided RSV-LRTDs and 0.5% of the averted costs estimated for immunisation with nirsevimab compared with SoP. The modelled impact of universal immunisation with nirsevimab on infants born during versus before the RSV season was significant, regardless of age at the start of the RSV season (Table S4). An estimated 64.4% of the total avoided health burden (134,371 total health events) was attributed to infants born before the RSV season, whereas infants born during the season accounted for the remaining 35.6% (74,320 total health events) (Fig. C, D).

Immunisation through year-round administration of MI for pregnant mothers, coupled with monthly palivizumab administration for the palivizumab-eligible population, was estimated to prevent 41,341 cases of MA RSV-LRTDs (including RSV-related deaths), 10,201 cases of non-MA LRTDs and 4292 cases of recurrent wheezing over 3 years compared with SoP. Additionally, this year-round MI approach was projected to reduce RSV hospital and ICU admissions by 23% (5722) and decrease AE and PC visits by 17% (10,684) and 16% (24,931), respectively (Table ). Owing to the lack of data on the impact of MI on the prevention of all-cause LRTD hospitalisations, no reduction in all-cause LRTD hospitalisations was estimated when comparing year-round MI to SoP alone. From a cost perspective, year-round MI was expected to decrease total costs associated with MA RSV-LRTDs by £25.1 million (21%). Like nirsevimab, the largest cost savings were derived from reduced hospital admissions (including ICU admissions) which accounted for £18.3 million (23% reduction) (Table ).

The model assumed equal administration of palivizumab within the palivizumab-eligible population between the SoP and year-round MI strategies, which resulted in no incremental costs for this population. As the majority of RSV-LRTDs occurred among term infants, 98.6% of the events avoided by a year-round immunisation strategy with MI were observed in this group (Table S3). The modelled impact of year-round immunisation with MI in pregnant mothers on infants born during versus before the RSV season was lower than the impact observed for universal immunisation with nirsevimab (Table S4). In terms of seasonality, 42.1% of the total avoided health burden (23,523 total health events) was attributable to infants born before the RSV season, whereas infants born during the season accounted for the remaining 57.9% (32,310 total health events).

The number of avoided RSV events under the base-case strategy (NIP-aligned for late-preterm/term infants), the year-round strategy for nirsevimab in all infant populations and the seasonal-based approach with a “catch-up” for all infant populations were similar for term infants born during the season (Fig. ). For term infants born before the start of the RSV season, year-round immunisation prevents over 50,000 cases. Compared with the base-case strategy in which immunisation with nirsevimab in the term infant population aligns with the NIP schedule, the implementation strategy that included in-season immunisation with a “catch-up” for all infants showed a minor incremental impact on protecting term infants born outside the RSV season associated with aligning administration of nirsevimab in October to maximize protection. The impact on high-risk infants (preterm and palivizumab-eligible) and the prevention of all-cause LRTD hospitalisations across the nirsevimab-based immunisation strategies followed a similar pattern but on a smaller scale (Table ). Immunisation strategies involving nirsevimab consistently resulted in higher levels of avoided RSV-related health events compared with SoP, as opposed to year-round immunisation with MI compared with SoP.

The results of scenarios testing the assumptions related to coverage and efficacy of MI applied by Hodgson et al. [] are presented in Table S5. These scenario analyses revealed that the number of prevented hospitalisations and ICU admissions for the year-round MI strategy versus the palivizumab-only strategy was comparable between the respective base-case analyses. However, when the static model was adjusted to reflect the coverage and efficacy of MI alone (excluding the antibody transfer and coverage adjustments applied in the static model base case for MI), the number of prevented hospitalisations and ICU admissions compared with SoP increased significantly. This increase was attributable to the markedly higher level and duration of protection transferred to infants from their mothers, compared with the static model base case. When adjustments for coverage and antibody transfer to infants were included, the impact on prevented hospitalisations and ICU admissions was reduced relative to the scenario without these adjustments. The analyses also considered AE visits and general practitioner/PC visits. The impact of sequentially applying the coverage and efficacy estimates from the dynamic model (initially without the adjustments applied in the static model, and subsequently with these adjustments) followed a similar pattern to that observed for prevented hospitalisations and ICU admissions.

The results of the DSA are presented as a tornado diagram in Fig. . The analysis indicated that parameters related to the term infant population had the largest impact on model results. Specifically, apart from the distribution of births and RSV circulation throughout the year, the risk of RSV by age, coverage rate for nirsevimab/MI and RSV treatment costs within the term infant population were the most significant drivers of healthcare costs. These results were consistent with observations from the scenario and base-case analysis, highlighting a significant burden and unmet need by infants in this subgroup.
sections.discussion:
Although no head-to-head trials compare nirsevimab and MI, this study adds to recent literature by indirectly comparing the current UK national programme[] (palivizumab and MI) with all-infant protection using nirsevimab. Our model suggests that, in the UK, immunisation strategies with nirsevimab or year-round MI in line with the current UK national programme[] reduce infant RSV-LRTD hospitalisations and events more effectively than the palivizumab-only strategy. This was expected since palivizumab is limited to very high-risk infants only [], while most RSV-related health events occur in otherwise healthy infants born at or near term [].

Universal immunisation with nirsevimab consistently prevented more RSV-LRTD hospitalisations and events than year-round MI compared with SoP. Further, even a year-round strategy with nirsevimab offers additional health benefits and cost savings compared with SoP and the current UK national programme []. Specifically, nirsevimab can prevent up to four times more RSV-related health events and three times more RSV-related hospitalisations than the current UK national programme[] for palivizumab plus MI.

The impact of avoided inpatient-managed RSV-LRTDs on hospital bed-days and ICU bed-days is significant for the UK NHS, particularly when hospitals are already under severe winter pressures. In the absence of UK published data, data from Ireland show an average length of stay (LOS) of 4 days for hospitalised infants and 13 days for those admitted to the ICU []. The current UK national programme related to palivizumab plus MI were estimated to prevent approximately 21,888 hospital bed-days and 3250 ICU bed-days compared with the palivizumab-only strategy. In contrast, nirsevimab can avoid 63,556 hospital bed-days and 10,075 ICU bed-days compared with SoP, resulting in an indirect reduction of 41,668 hospital bed-days and 6825 ICU bed-days compared with the current UK reimbursed programme-aligned strategy. This difference results from the sustained efficacy of nirsevimab through the RSV season, timely immunisation aligning with the RSV season, broad protection for all infants and substantial protection against all-cause LRTDs.

These analyses also highlighted implications of seasonal versus year-round immunisation strategies more broadly. Infants born before the RSV season constitute approximately 60% of the annual birth cohort [, ]. This study estimated 36% fewer MA RSV-LRTDs and 33% fewer MA RSV-LRTD hospitalisations under the NIP-aligned nirsevimab strategy compared with a year-round nirsevimab strategy, despite administering the same total number of doses to the population. This discrepancy arises from the misalignment between the timing of nirsevimab administration and the period when RSV protection is most critical. Specifically, doses administered between March and September may provide inadequate or no protection that endures throughout the RSV season, which extends through February. Regardless of the product, a year-round approach considering clear seasonality leads to wasted doses or under-protection of the infant during the RSV season. As each administration incurs costs for both payers and the healthcare system at large, these findings underscore the importance of aligning nirsevimab administration with the RSV season, when protection is most needed.

A recent study by Hodgson et al.[] employed a dynamic transmission model to estimate MI’s impact on RSV-related health outcomes in the UK. The findings of that study, under a year-round MI strategy, estimated higher levels of avoided RSV-LRTDs (including hospitalisations, ICU admissions, AE visits and general practitioner/PC visits) compared with our study. These differences stem from key assumptions about MI efficacy, including the initial protection levels, duration of protection, the rate of efficacy waning and the timing between administration to mothers and infant. Additionally, Hodgson et al. applied a significant assumption that MI also provides protection to mothers against MA RSV-related health events. This assumption further biased the overarching value message related to MI in the Hodgson et al. study, to which there are currently no data to support this assumption of protection in mothers from MI.

The Hodgson et al. study used data from the MATISSE trial[] to reflect prevention efficacy against non-severe events for MI (e.g. infection, symptomatic cases and general practitioner consultations) and then back-calculated efficacy against severe events (e.g. hospitalisations, ICU admissions, AE attendances and death) based on model calibration. An Erlang-3 distribution was then applied to determine time-dependent efficacy estimates, with mean efficacy levels of 69.4% and 51.3% at 180 days after birth for severe and non-severe events, respectively. Protection offered by MI was assumed to last up to 365 days post-birth at which point efficacy against severe and non-severe events was estimated to be 14.7% and 10.9%, respectively. In contrast, our study directly applied efficacy estimates from the Abrysvo European Union (EU) summary of product characteristics (SmPC) [] and the detailed analyses presented to the US VRBPAC on the MATISSE trial [], specifically against hospitalisations and RSV-LRTDs. These efficacy estimates presented in the Abrysvo SmPC and the US VRBPAC analyses are lower than those generated by Hodgson et al. and are more appropriate given that they served as the basis for approval in the US and EU which highlight that protection is anticipated only up to 6 months. Consequently, Hodgson et al. likely overestimated the efficacy of MI in infants, particularly regarding the duration of protection, while incorporating strong assumptions based on model calibration related to the comparative efficacy against severe versus non-severe cases of infant RSV.

With respect to the adjustments applied to the level of RSV protection transferred to infants from mothers, our study accounted for this directly via antibody transfer estimates based on the findings of Rainisch et al. [] and the UK Green Book on Immunisation []. In contrast, Hodgson et al. did not consider antibody transfer which may not accurately reflect the relationship between the timing of MI versus birth and the resulting efficacy experienced by the newborn infant. This omission of antibody transfer likely overestimated the protection from MI offered to infants from a cohort level both at birth and throughout the window of protection associated with MI.

In our scenario analyses, we estimated the impact of using the MI efficacy assumptions from Hodgson et al. [], which highlighted that the differences in results were driven by the assumption of MI efficacy extending up to 12 months post-birth which does not align with the Abrysvo label []. Specifically, Hodgson et al. estimated a 19.7% reduction in these RSV-LRTDs, whereas our base-case analysis estimated a 16.7% reduction. Applying the assumptions for MI efficacy without considering the adjustments for coverage and antibody transfer from Hodgson et al., the percent reduction in RSV-LRTDs compared with the palivizumab-only strategy increased to 26.8% compared with a 23.7% reduction when the adjustments to MI coverage and efficacy based on antibody transfer were applied. This underscores the sensitivity of the results to higher levels of MI efficacy and extended duration of protection. It is important to note that the adjustments to coverage applied in the base case of our study align with the UKHSA and JCVI recommendations [] regarding the eligibility window for pregnant mothers in wGA and are consistent with the assumption related to antibody transfer applied in the Rainisch et al. study []. It is also important to acknowledge that the efficacy data for MI were derived from the MATISSE study [], a multicentre trial conducted across different countries. The effectiveness of both nirsevimab and MI may vary across different geographical regions and healthcare systems. This limitation should be considered when interpreting UK-specific results. The protection duration with nirsevimab has recently been updated to 5 to 6 months [], which may result in an underestimation of events avoided in our base case which used a 5-month protection duration. Longer duration of protection could also offer greater flexibility in implementation strategies, which could be valuable for managing large-scale infant immunization programs.

A key strength of our model lies in its granularity in modelling monthly infant birth cohorts, but a notable limitation is the lack of equally granular source data available. For instance, the risk of AE visits was assumed consistent across all subpopulations due to specific data absence, and hospitalisation data by age in months necessitating the use of the distribution from the Reeves et al. study [] to convert point estimate data (although this approach is consistent with that applied in the UKHSA Cromer 2017 study []). Further, data informing AE admissions only present rates for infants who do not go on to be hospitalised [], to which, these health events are treated as mutually exclusive and the model cannot capture the potential impact of reduction in AE visits on hospitalisations. This assumption of uniform rates across subpopulations for both AE visits and wheezing may impact the accuracy of our results, particularly for high-risk groups who might have different healthcare utilisation patterns. High-risk infants, such as those born prematurely or with underlying conditions, may experience different frequencies of AE visits and wheezing episodes compared with healthy term infants. Future research with more granular data on AE visits and wheezing incidence by risk group would help better capture the differential impact of RSV prevention strategies.

Assumptions for wheezing in our model align with those of a recent cost-effectiveness analysis on RSV prevention in the EU []. However, the indirect impact of RSV prophylaxis (palivizumab, nirsevimab and MI) on the incidence of wheezing remains uncertain. While new data [] indicate that nirsevimab provides direct protection against wheezing, irrespective of initial hospitalisation, the extent to which it prevents long-term complications associated with RSV infection remains unclear. Furthermore, our static model does not capture indirect effects on RSV transmission (due to a lack of evidence). Impacts on parents/caregivers were not included as we adopted a payer perspective. Finally, our analysis does not consider the lifetime lost earnings owing to infant RSV deaths or other societal impacts, focusing more narrowly on a direct NHS perspective. Decision-makers should consider broader societal benefits and impacts of RSV prophylaxis strategies, as focusing solely on a payer perspective can overlook overall health and quality-of-life improvements for individuals.

This analysis demonstrates that universal immunisation with nirsevimab offers superior protection against RSV-related health events compared with the current UK national programme, potentially preventing up to four times more RSV-related health events and three times more hospitalisations. A seasonal approach to nirsevimab administration, aligned with the UK’s NIP, proves more effective than year-round nirsevimab administration, maximizing protection during periods of highest RSV transmission. These findings have significant implications for healthcare policy and resource planning, suggesting nirsevimab could provide more comprehensive protection while delivering greater value for the NHS.

title: Use of the Pfizer Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine During Pregnancy for the Prevention of Respiratory Syncytial Virus-Associated Lower Respiratory Tract Disease in Infants: Recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices - United States, 2023.
abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of hospitalization among U.S. infants. Nirsevimab (Bevfortus, Sanofi and AstraZeneca) is recommended to prevent RSV-associated lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) in infants. In August 2023, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved RSVpreF vaccine (Abrysvo, Pfizer Inc.) for pregnant persons as a single dose during 32-36 completed gestational weeks (i.e., 32 weeks and zero days' through 36 weeks and 6 days' gestation) to prevent RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease in infants aged <6 months. Since October 2021, CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) RSV Vaccines Pediatric/Maternal Work Group has reviewed RSV epidemiology and evidence regarding safety, efficacy, and potential economic impact of pediatric and maternal RSV prevention products, including RSVpreF vaccine. In August 2023, the Food and Drug Administration approved Pfizer RSV vaccine for pregnant persons at 32–36 weeks’ gestation to prevent RSV-associated LRTI in infants aged <6 months.
