sections.methods:
This phase 3b, open-label, nonrandomized study ( NCT06389487 ) was conducted in 6 countries across 52 sites: Australia (7), Canada (12), Germany (9), Japan (4), South Africa (4), and the United States (16) (). The study enrolled participants from 29 April 2024 to 16 September 2024 and was completed on 18 March 2025.

The study was conducted in 2 parts. Part A focused on immunogenicity and safety, and included 2 parallel cohorts: adults 18–49 YOA at increased risk (at-risk 18–49 group), and adults ≥60 YOA (≥60 group). Part B included an additional at-risk 18–49 cohort to better characterize the vaccine's safety profile in this population ().

The at-risk 18–49 cohorts included nonimmunocompromised adults 18–49 YOA, diagnosed with at least one of the following medical conditions commonly associated with an increased risk of RSV disease: chronic pulmonary disease (COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis, lung fibrosis, restrictive lung disease, interstitial lung disease, emphysema, and bronchiectasis), chronic cardiovascular disease (chronic heart failure, coronary artery disease, and cardiac arrhythmia), diabetes mellitus types 1/2, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, and active or chronic neurological/neuromuscular conditions. All chronic conditions had to be considered stable by the investigator (ie, no significant changes in therapy or disease severity in the 3 months prior to enrollment). Eligibility criteria were applied to the severity of certain conditions to ensure a strong association with increased RSV risk (eg, activity-restricting symptoms or long-term medication).

The ≥60 group served as a control. The same eligibility criteria as in the AReSVi-006 efficacy study [] were applied (ie, adults ≥60 YOA with or without stable chronic conditions).

Individuals with unstable illness, dementia, or a confirmed/suspected immunosuppressive or immunodeficiency condition due to disease or immunosuppressive/cytotoxic therapy, as well as those who had previously received any RSV vaccine or chronic/long-acting immune-modifying drugs 3–6 months before study vaccination were not eligible. Enrollment rules were applied to ensure representation by sex (all cohorts), disease category (at-risk 18–49 cohorts), and age (≥60 cohort) (). All eligible participants received 1 dose of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 on Day 1 and were followed for 6 months. A protocol summary is available at https://www.gsk-studyregister.com/en/trial-details/?id=222253 . Information regarding ethical conduct is available in the .

The primary objective was to demonstrate noninferiority of the humoral immune response to adjuvanted RSVPreF3 in the at-risk 18–49 group compared with the ≥60 group, both in terms of group RSV-A/RSV-B adjusted geometric mean titer (GMT) ratios (GMRs) and group seroresponse rate (SRR) differences from baseline, at 1 month postvaccination.

Secondary objectives included further characterization of humoral immunogenicity, and evaluation of the vaccine's reactogenicity and safety in both study groups until 6 months postvaccination. Characterization of CMI was a tertiary objective.

Blood samples for humoral immunogenicity analyses were collected from participants in Part A of the study at baseline (Day 1, prevaccination), 1 month (Day 31), and 6 months postvaccination. RSV-A/RSV-B neutralizing titers were assessed using GSK neutralization assays and expressed in estimated dilution 60 [].

For CMI analyses, an additional blood volume was collected from a selected number of participants in Part A at the same time points. Frequencies of RSVPreF3-specific CD4+/CD8+ T cells (per million CD4+/CD8+ T cells), expressing ≥2 activation markers—including ≥1 cytokine—among CD40 ligand, 4-1BB, interleukin-2, tumor necrosis factor-α, interferon-ɣ, interleukin-13, and interleukin-17, were determined by intracellular cytokine staining of peripheral blood mononuclear cells [].

Solicited administration-site and systemic events starting within 4 days postvaccination were recorded by all participants using an electronic diary. Unsolicited adverse events (AEs) within 30 days postvaccination were recorded by the investigator in electronic case report forms. Serious AEs (SAEs), AEs leading to study discontinuation, and AEs of special interest (AESIs), including potential immune-mediated diseases (pIMDs) and atrial fibrillation, were recorded up to study end, or up to Day 30 in case of nonserious atrial fibrillation events. The investigator graded the intensity of AEs from mild (grade 1) to severe (grade 3) () and determined the causal relationship between the vaccine and each AE.

All AEs were followed until resolved, until study end, until the participant was lost to follow-up, or until SAEs and nonserious AESIs were considered stabilized.

Pregnancies were documented until study end and followed until 6–8 weeks after delivery.

Primary and secondary humoral immunogenicity objectives were analyzed on the per-protocol set (PPS, all eligible participants who received the vaccine as per protocol, had immunogenicity results both prevaccination and postvaccination available, complied with blood draw intervals, had no interfering intercurrent conditions, and did not receive prohibited concomitant medications/vaccinations). CMI objectives were analyzed on the PPS for CMI subset.

The primary noninferiority objective was assessed according to a hierarchical testing procedure (first for RSV-A, and, if met, for RSV-B) to control the global 1-sided type I error at 2.5%. Noninferiority was evaluated both in terms of group adjusted GMR (≥60 group over at-risk 18–49 group) and group SRR difference (≥60 group minus at-risk 18–49 group) at 1 month postvaccination. SRR was defined as the proportion of participants with a ≥ 4-fold increase in neutralizing titers from baseline to the postvaccination time point. Group adjusted GMRs with 95% CIs were computed using an ANCOVA model on log 10 -transformed titers, with group and baseline log 10 -transformed titers as covariates; group SRR differences with 95% CIs were computed using the Miettinen and Nurminen method []. Noninferiority was demonstrated if the upper limit of the 2-sided 95% confidence interval (CI) was ≤1.5 for the group GMR and ≤10% for the group SRR difference.

RSV-A and RSV-B neutralizing GMTs and mean geometric increases (MGIs) (ie, geometric mean of the within-participant ratios 1 month or 6 months postvaccination over baseline) were calculated with 95% CIs. Titers below the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) were replaced by half the LLOQ and titers above the upper limit of quantification (ULOQ) by the ULOQ. Missing data were not replaced. RSVPreF3-specific CD4+/CD8+ T-cell frequencies (per million CD4+/CD8+ T cells) were summarized using descriptive statistics.

Demographic characteristics, reactogenicity, and safety were analyzed on all vaccinated participants and summarized using descriptive statistics. For these safety analyses, data from all at-risk participants 18–49 YOA in study Parts A and B were pooled.

Details regarding sample size calculations are provided in .

Statistical analyses were performed using SAS (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, North Carolina, US).
sections.results:
In total, 1459 participants were enrolled, and 1458 (at-risk 18–49 group: 1029; ≥60 group: 429) received adjuvanted RSVPreF3 on Day 1 (). Overall, 1445 participants (99.1%) completed visit 2 (Day 31), and 1422 (97.5%) completed visit 3 (Month 6). Thirty-six participants (2.5%) were withdrawn by study end, mainly due to loss to follow-up (27 participants). None withdrew due to an AE.

Of the 855 participants in Part A, 844 were included in the PPS for humoral immunogenicity at Day 1, 810 at Day 31, and 799 at Month 6. The main reasons for exclusion were immunogenicity assessment outside the protocol window (24 participants at Day 31; 15 at Month 6) or administration of vaccine impacted by a temperature excursion (11 participants at each time point). The PPS for CMI subset consisted of 122 participants at Day 1, 116 at Day 31, and 101 at Month 6.

Overall, the demographic and baseline characteristics (excluding age) of the vaccinated participants were comparable between the at-risk 18–49 and ≥60 groups (). The mean age was 38.4 years in the at-risk 18–49 and 68.6 years in the ≥60 group. In the at-risk 18–49 group, 68.8% of participants had 1 chronic condition and the remainder had ≥2. In the ≥60 group, 34.8% had no condition, 35.4% had 1 condition, and 29.8% had ≥2. The most common conditions were cardiopulmonary diseases (55.0% in the at-risk 18–49 and 31.5% in the ≥60 group) and diabetes mellitus (48.9% and 30.3%, respectively) ().

The demographic and baseline characteristics of the PPS were generally similar to all vaccinated participants; some differences were noted in the PPS for CMI subset ( and ).

One month postvaccination, the primary analysis demonstrated a noninferior humoral immune response in the at-risk 18–49 compared with the ≥60 group. The group GMRs were 0.72 (95% CI: 0.64, .81) for RSV-A and 0.73 (0.65, 0.82) for RSV-B. The group SRR differences were −9.36% (−14.58, −4.14) for RSV-A and −10.06% (−15.29, −4.83) for RSV-B. Hence, the upper limits of the 2-sided 95% CIs for the group GMRs and group SRR differences were below their predefined noninferiority margins of 1.5% and 10%, respectively, for both RSV-A and RSV-B ().

One month postvaccination, RSV-A and RSV-B neutralizing titers increased in both the at-risk 18–49 and ≥60 groups compared with baseline ( and ). For RSV-A, MGIs over baseline were 13.32 in the at-risk 18–49 and 9.45 in the ≥60 group; for RSV-B, MGIs were 12.50 and 8.75, respectively. For RSV-A, SRRs were 87.0% in the at-risk 18–49 and 77.7% in the ≥60 group; for RSV-B, SRRs were 87.2% and 77.2%, respectively ().

Six months postvaccination, RSV-A and RSV-B neutralizing titers declined in both groups compared with 1 month postvaccination but remained above baseline ( and ). For RSV-A, MGIs over baseline were 4.98 in the at-risk 18–49 and 4.40 in the ≥60 group; for RSV-B, MGIs were 4.40 and 4.26, respectively. SRRs were 61.6% and 51.0% for RSV-A, and 52.0% and 49.5% for RSV-B, respectively ().

At baseline, the median frequency of RSVPreF3-specific CD4+ T cells expressing ≥2 activation markers (per million CD4+ T cells) was 366.0 in the at-risk 18–49 and 213.0 in the ≥60 group. One month postvaccination, frequencies increased to 1834.5 in the at-risk 18–49 and to 1288.0 in the ≥60 group, and then declined at Month 6 to 997.0 in the at-risk 18–49 and to 667.0 in the ≥60 group (). No RSVPreF3-specific CD8+ T-cell response was observed.

Within 4 days postvaccination, 84.3% of participants in the at-risk 18–49 group and 69.4% in the ≥60 group reported ≥1 solicited event. Solicited administration-site events were reported by 76.4% of participants in the at-risk 18–49 and 58.2% in the ≥60 group, with injection site pain being the most frequent (76.0% and 57.5%, respectively) (). Grade 3 solicited administration-site events were reported by 1.6% and 0.2% of participants, respectively. Solicited systemic events were reported by 75.0% in the at-risk 18–49 group and 54.9% in the ≥60 group, with myalgia (59.9% and 39.5%) and fatigue (59.6% and 34.6%) being the most frequent. Grade 3 solicited systemic events occurred in 5.8% and 2.3% of participants, respectively. Most solicited events were mild or moderate in intensity and resolved within 3 days in both groups.

Unsolicited AEs within 30 days postvaccination were reported by 18.5% of participants in the at-risk 18–49 and 17.7% in the ≥60 group; 8.7% and 3.0%, respectively, experienced an unsolicited AE that was considered vaccine-related by the investigator (). Grade 3 unsolicited AEs were reported in 0.5% and 1.2% of participants, respectively; none were considered vaccine-related. Up to study end, 1.4% of participants in the at-risk 18–49 and 3.0% in the ≥60 group reported ≥1 SAE; none were considered vaccine-related. No fatal outcomes were reported.

Two pIMDs were reported in the at-risk 18–49 group and 1 in the ≥60 group (; ). One case in the at-risk 18–49 group was considered vaccine-related by the investigator; it involved an exacerbated hematoma (onset 14 days postvaccination; nonserious and mild in intensity), that initially developed at an insulin injection site, with other lesions appearing at other body parts over time. The case was classified as a pIMD by the investigator; clinical and laboratory evidence did not suggest an autoimmune etiology. The case resolved by itself 217 days later. One participant from each group reported atrial fibrillation; both occurred in participants with a medical or family history of atrial fibrillation/arrhythmia and were not considered vaccine-related.

During the study, 3 pregnancies were reported: 1 full-term pregnancy before and 2 after the last study visit, all of which resulted in live infants with no apparent congenital anomalies. None of these participants reported SAEs or pIMDs.
sections.discussion:
Expanding access for adjuvanted RSVPreF3 to adults <50 YOA, particularly those at increased risk of RSV disease, could play a key role in further reducing RSV-related diseases. In this study, adjuvanted RSVPreF3 induced a noninferior humoral immune response in adults 18–49 YOA with chronic conditions that put them at increased risk of RSV disease compared with adults ≥60 YOA, in whom efficacy was previously demonstrated [], supporting the inference of vaccine efficacy in this younger population. This inference is based on immunobridging, a well-established methodology [] that follows World Health Organization guidelines for predicting vaccine efficacy in populations not included in efficacy trials using immunogenicity data in the absence of a correlate of protection []. The inclusion of the ≥60 group as a control group with eligibility criteria aligned with the efficacy study [] enhances the validity of our findings.

The robust immune response observed in both age groups sustained for at least 6 months postvaccination. Both populations exhibited a similar trend over time in their RSV-A and RSV-B neutralizing titers, characterized by a sharp increase at 1 month postvaccination, followed by declining titers that remained above baseline levels until at least 6 months postvaccination; MGIs for the ≥60 group were consistent with previous observations in this population []. Although our study was designed to assess noninferiority rather than to compare responses between groups over time, a trend toward higher humoral immunogenicity was noted in participants 18–49 YOA compared with those ≥60 YOA at 1 month postvaccination, with responses converging at 6 months. In terms of CMI, frequencies of RSVPreF3-specific CD4+ T cells expressing ≥2 activation markers increased at 1 month postvaccination compared with baseline in both age groups, which then decreased but remained above baseline levels at 6 months postvaccination. Overall, the immunogenicity data suggest that adults 18–49 YOA may achieve at least similar levels of protection [] and immune persistence [] by adjuvanted RSVPreF3 compared with those ≥60 YOA.

While reactogenicity events were reported more frequently in the at-risk 18–49 group than in the ≥60 group, their duration and intensity were similar across groups. This difference is not unexpected and may be attributed to the generally lower inflammatory response in adults ≥60 YOA following vaccination [], as also noted with other vaccines (eg, COVID-19 vaccines []).

Unsolicited AE, SAE, and AESI reporting rates were balanced between both populations. There was no pattern or cluster of events in any study group. No fatal outcomes were reported, and no SAEs were considered vaccine-related by the investigator. One pIMD considered vaccine-related in the at-risk 18–49 group and 1 atrial fibrillation event in each group (both not considered vaccine-related) were reported. Overall, the vaccine demonstrated an acceptable safety profile over 6 months in the at-risk 18–49 and ≥60 groups, consistent with previous observations in adults ≥60 YOA [].

A key study strength is the demonstration of immunological noninferiority both in terms of the group GMRs and SRR differences of RSV-A/RSV-B neutralizing titers. While there is no established correlate of protection for RSV, serum neutralizing antibodies specific to the prefusion state of the RSV F protein are considered a key component of the immune response to reduce the risk of reinfection and severe disease in adults []. In adults ≥60 YOA, high serum neutralizing antibody levels have been associated with reduced hospitalization risk [], and in pediatric populations, monoclonal neutralizing antibodies have been proven effective in lowering hospitalization rates and mortality [].

One study limitation is the exclusion of immunocompromised individuals. This population is being studied in another phase 2b trial involving individuals ≥18 YOA who received a lung or kidney transplant.

Overall, the findings of this study indicate a favorable benefit-risk profile for the vaccine in adults 18–49 YOA, highlighting its potential to provide meaningful protection against RSV in younger adults.

title: Health and Economic Impact of Seasonal Maternal Vaccination With Bivalent Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Vaccine in Belgium.
abstract: Background Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of potentially severe lower respiratory tract viral infection in infants. Hospitals may encounter challenges during the RSV season following the increased number of pediatric patients' admissions. Maternal vaccination can help address this healthcare threat. This study aimed to analyze the cost-effectiveness of the bivalent respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F-protein-based (RSVpreF) vaccine versus no immunization. Methods A static model was developed to assess the impact of RSV-lower respiratory tract infections immunization via maternal vaccination on hospitalization, life expectancy and quality of life in an annual newborn population, from the perspective of the public healthcare payer. Key input data were derived from an independent Belgian observational study and the latest available clinical data on the bivalent RSVpreF vaccine. The targeted infants were defined based on the recommendations of the Superior Health Council for maternal vaccination. Results Maternal vaccination against RSV is a cost-saving option compared to no immunization against RSV, up to a cost of €183.67 (including 1 dose of vaccine and administration fee). The protection of 46,542 newborns with maternal vaccination prevented 1 infant death and 2242 pediatric hospital admissions while saving €8.57 million. These hospital savings will more than offset the cost of vaccination, resulting in incremental healthcare savings of €102,873. Moreover, in this target population, 80 QALYs will be gained over the lifetime horizon. Conclusions The bivalent RSVpreF vaccine, administered in line with the recommendations of the Superior Health Council, is a dominant option compared with no immunization.

sections.other:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of viral lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) in children under the age of 2. RSV-associated LRTI commonly present in young children as “bronchiolitis” can progress to potentially life-threatening respiratory failure, apnea and possibly death. Studies have also reported that infants infected with RSV may have an increased risk of developing asthma, wheezing and recurrent respiratory infections later in life. ,

Infants <6 months old who contract RSV are at a higher risk of hospitalization. In absolute numbers, most of these hospitalizations occur in previously healthy, full-term infants. , In Belgium, the risk of hospitalization due to RSV has been estimated at 68.3 per 1000 infants under 1 year of age during the RSV season 2017–2018. At that time, the monoclonal antibody palivizumab was the only available and reimbursed preventive option. Its impact on hospitalization rates was limited as it was reserved for infants at high risk of RSV infection, representing approximately 1.5% of the annual infant cohort. ,

Until recently, RSV infections were associated with a significant economic burden on families and healthcare systems, particularly because of hospitalization. During the RSV season, hospitals may be challenged by an increased number of pediatric patients requiring intensive care, oxygen support or other medical interventions. ,

Since the RSV season 2024–2025, 2 new RSV preventive options for infants have become available and are recommended for broad use by the Superior Health Council (SHC): the bivalent respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F-protein based (RSVpreF) maternal vaccine or the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab for passive immunization of infants. Due to its high cost and demanding administration schedule, palivizumab is to be replaced by nirsevimab.

Maternal vaccination is recommended between 28 and 36 weeks of pregnancy for women planning to give birth between early September to end of March. Infants born during the RSV season (October–March) from unvaccinated mothers, prematurely born infants [before 30 weeks gestational age (wGA)], or within 2 weeks following maternal vaccination are recommended to receive nirsevimab.

SHC currently supports both preventive strategies, leaving the choice to the discretion of healthcare providers and parents, pending further data from cost-effectiveness analysis and access.

This analysis assessed the cost-effectiveness of newborn immunization through seasonal maternal vaccination compared with no immunization.

The authors acknowledge Amy Law and Diana Mendes, employees of Pfizer, as well as Ahuva Averin and Mark Atwood, employees of Avalere, who were involved in the conception of the model.
sections.methods:
A static Markov model was developed to depict the health and economic consequences of the RSV-LRTI in an annual newborn population (Fig. ). This model, programmed in Microsoft Excel 2021 as a macro-enabled workbook, has been presented previously. –

A lifetime horizon (99 years) was considered to capture the impact of premature RSV-related mortality on life expectancy.

The key inputs are presented in Table . Additional details are provided in Text, Supplemental Digital Content 1, https://links.lww.com/INF/G589 .

The impact of severe RSV-LRTI infection has been analyzed in a population of 117,884 newborns (estimated in 2025 based on national demographic forecasts). , In accordance with the SHC’s recommendations for maternal vaccination, infants born at 28 wGA or later, between early September and the end March are eligible for this immunization. They represent 57.15% of the total annual number of newborns. Like the high uptake of pertussis maternal vaccination, it is expected that 70% of eligible pregnant women will opt for RSV vaccination funded by the authorities (should nirsevimab not be considered as an option). A lower vaccination uptake of 35% was tested in the scenario analysis. The uptake percentage was assumed to be evenly distributed over the 8-week vaccination window (28 wGA–36 wGA).

The primary objective of newborn immunization is to prevent hospitalization due to RSV-LRTI. The risk of hospitalization is highest in the early months of life and decreases with age. An annual rate of 68.3 hospital admissions per 1000 infants younger than 1 year was reported in an independent Belgian retrospective study during the RSV season 2017–2018. This hospitalization rate is assumed to exclude admissions among high-risk infants, who were expected to be protected by palivizumab, the only available preventive option at that time. The majority of this group of high-risk infants is not targeted by the maternal vaccination, as they are instead expected to receive nirsevimab. The granularity of this mean RSV-hospitalization rate was estimated using additional information sources. The adjustment of the RSV-hospitalization rate by month of age was based on a study conducted at the European level. In this study, infants 0–2 months had nearly twice (1.84 times) the rate of RSV-hospitalization compared to infants 3–5 months and 4 times (4.3) the rate compared to infants 6–11 months of age. The RSV-hospitalization rate was also adjusted for gestational age, based on a systematic literature review. This review suggests that late preterm infants (32–36 wGA) have twice the rate of hospitalization compared to full-term infants, while early preterm infants (28–31 wGA) have 4 times the rate of hospitalization compared to full-term infants. Finally, it was also considered that the majority (98.8%) of these yearly hospital admissions occur during the RSV season, which aligns with the distribution of the infection rate. These estimates, derived from European sources, have since been supported by data of a Belgian study. Further details on this step-by-step approach can be found in Text, Supplemental Digital Content 1, https://links.lww.com/INF/G589 .

Due to the low number of deaths associated with RSV, the same case-fatality rate of 0.0497% was applied to all hospitalized infants younger than 1 year. The life expectancy observed in Belgium in 2023 was applied in this lifetime horizon analysis.

Consistent with previously published cost-effectiveness analyses, the utility value for newborns was assumed to be 1. , Infant’s disutility due to RSV-LRTI hospitalization was derived from the literature ,, and adjusted on a yearly basis. Owing to the challenges in measuring utility values in infants and the uncertainty surrounding this parameter, a scenario is tested using an alternative source of information. The disutility value used was assumed to be independent of term status and age. For this lifetime horizon analysis, the age-specific utilities of the Belgian general population 15 years old and older were applied. The baseline utilities were estimated linearly for the younger age groups.

The effectiveness of the bivalent RSVpreF vaccine against RSV-LRTI hospitalization was estimated from the efficacy data against severe RSV-positive medically attended LRTI primary endpoints in the MATISSE trial. ,–, The hospitalization secondary endpoint in the MATISSE trial referred to RSV-diagnosis and not specifically to RSV-LRTI diagnosis. The study was also conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic and hospitalization decisions for RSV were subjective and related to bed capacity and benefit-risk criteria. This is less of an issue in a typical nonpandemic year; therefore, the pandemic context may have underestimated hospitalization benefits. Hospitalization decision has also been influenced by regional factors, where some countries may have less easy access to hospitalization than it is the case in Belgium. Most severe RSV cases were associated with hospitalization, and is therefore an appropriate estimate for the effectiveness of RSV-LRTI hospitalization. Incremental vaccine effectiveness (VE) monthly estimates were derived by linear regression (ordinary least squares) over the 6-month trial follow-up based on the cumulative efficacy data at 90, 120, 150, and 180 days from the MATISSE trial. While the effectiveness against severe RSV-LRTI was still 55% at month 6 (down from 84.37% effectiveness in month 1, based on the regression), the cost-effectiveness analysis conservatively excluded any benefits beyond this 6-month period. The analysis also considered that infants born within the 2 weeks of maternal vaccination will not be immunized, as 2 weeks are required for sufficient antibody transfer. Based on the immunogenicity data from the MATISSE trial, it is assumed that VE in late preterm newborns (32–36 wGA) is equal to VE in full-term newborns. , In the reference case of the analysis, the vaccine was assumed to be ineffective in earlier preterm newborns (<32 wGA) because the MATISSE trial was not powered to provide efficacy estimates among these infants and there were limited immunogenicity data in early preterm newborns. The effectiveness assumption in this subgroup was tested in the scenario analysis.

Only direct medical costs are considered, in line with the economic guidelines. The mean RSV-LRTI hospitalization cost in infants younger than 1 year is estimated at €3857 based on the cost reported in the national database in 2020 for the corresponding ICD-10 codes (J12.1, J21, J20.5, and part of B974), inflated to 2024. This hospitalization cost is a weighted average, considering that some infants will stay in the general ward, while others will be admitted to the intensive care unit. The vaccination cost is defined as the acquisition cost of 1 dose of the vaccine (€173.76) and its administration (€9.91). The acquisition cost of the vaccine includes the distribution and storage costs (margin to the distribution), as well as the promotion at the charge of the manufacturer. The cost of vaccine administration corresponds to 50% of the cost of a routine visit to the gynecologist, as it is assumed that 50% of RSV vaccinations will occur during a routine pregnancy visit, while the other 50% will require an additional visit. In the absence of severe adverse events, no additional costs associated with the adverse events were included.

A 1.5% discount rate was applied to the effects, and 3% was applied to the costs.
sections.results:
The results are based on maternal vaccination, as defined by the SHC, specifically during the 28–36 wGA window for pregnant women who delivered between early September and the end March, the RSV period. A 70% vaccination rate was assumed for this population. In a yearly cohort of 116,022 pregnant women, 46,542 infants were protected by maternal vaccination. The death of 1 newborn will be prevented, and the number of hospitalizations will be significantly reduced by 2242, saving €8.57 million (Table ). Compared to no immunization, vaccinating an annual cohort of pregnant women in accordance with the SHC’s recommendations is cost-saving, offering infants 80 additional QALY’s and providing public healthcare payers with savings of €102,873 in the healthcare budget (Table ).

Sensitivity analyses were performed to test the robustness of the results. Effectiveness, cost of the vaccine, hospitalization rate, and cost of hospital admission are the 4 key drivers of the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER). Variations by ±20% of their values kept the ICER below the €25,040/QALY threshold when comparing seasonal maternal vaccination with no immunization (Figure 2, Supplemental Digital Content 2, https://links.lww.com/INF/G590 ). The probabilistic sensitivity analysis reports a mean incremental cost/QALY close to the base case results with 82 QALYs gained and €0 incremental healthcare costs (95% confidence interval: −€44,736 to €17,556). The bivalent RSVpreF vaccine has a 50% probability of being cost-saving (offering savings and additional QALYs) compared to no immunization and a 97.3% probability of being cost-effective at a threshold of €35,000 (Fig. ). Figure 2.4, Supplemental Digital Content 2, https://links.lww.com/INF/G590 reports the cost-effectiveness plane.

Additional scenarios were also tested: a shorter time horizon (10 years), alternative discount rates on effects and costs (0%, 3%, and 5%), inclusion of effectiveness in early preterm infants, absence of or lower disutility associated with RSV-hospitalization in newborns, and lower vaccine uptake (Table 2.1, Supplemental Digital Content 2, https://links.lww.com/INF/G590 ). All these scenarios confirmed the cost-saving outcome of seasonal maternal vaccination compared with no immunization. Because we used a static model, the vaccination uptake level did not influence the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. The perspective of the public and private healthcare payers (including patients’ costs) reported an ICER of €9,477 per QALY.
sections.discussion:
Due to the high burden of RSV in infants younger than 1 year, the Belgian SHC currently recommends a seasonal immunization program, which requires support from the (para) medical profession for implementation and increasing parental awareness about RSV and thereby acceptance of the new preventive tools. This analysis estimated seasonal maternal vaccination to be cost-saving compared with no RSV immunization, from the perspective of the public healthcare payer in Belgium. Extreme preterm newborns (<28 wGA) were excluded from the maternal vaccination and cost-effectiveness analysis. As an alternative to the bivalent RSVpreF vaccine, nirsevimab can be administered to these infants. The complementary approach reported by the SHC and defined as the administration of nirsevimab for infants born from unvaccinated mothers or early prematurely born or within the 2 weeks following the vaccine administration might be subject to further cost-effectiveness research. The seasonal maternal vaccination (September–March) and seasonal infant immunization with nirsevimab (October–March, without catch-up), both compared with no intervention, have recently been studied by KCE researchers. Based on same coverage (70%) and current public acquisition costs, they reported that both seasonal options provide similar incremental benefit compared to no intervention (82 QALYs gained with seasonal maternal vaccination and 77 QALYs gained with seasonal immunization with nirsevimab over lifetime horizon) but that the maternal vaccination is less expensive: €924,700 (95% CI: −€1,691,000 to €3,797,000) incremental costs with seasonal maternal vaccination versus €21,977,400 (95% CI: €21,264,000 to €22,859,000) with seasonal immunization with nirsevimab, making seasonal maternal vaccination more cost-effective than seasonal immunization compared to no intervention. These results are based on the current public list prices of both interventions. While the actual price of maternal vaccine is fixed, nirsevimab is subject to a confidential reimbursement convention, meaning that the actual price is uncertain. The KCE authors also report on the option including nirsevimab catch up with seasonal immunization. This option increases further the number of QALYs gained (up to a total of 168) but also the total incremental costs (to €44,104,300). Compared to no intervention, seasonal maternal vaccination is also more cost-effective than this nirsevimab catch-up with seasonal immunization. The KCE report does not include the option including nirsevimab catch-up with seasonal maternal vaccination, making the full comparison of all possible interventions uncomplete.

A static model has been deemed appropriate for this cost-effectiveness analysis, as it primarily focuses on RSV-LRTI hospitalizations avoided in infants by immunization.

The hospitalization rates used in this analysis were derived from a recent independent Belgian observational study. The significant financial burden of RSV hospitalization in infants younger than 36 months has also recently been further confirmed, not only from the perspective of the public healthcare payer but also from the hospital point of view. This recently published study conducted in a sample of Belgian hospitals reported insights into the burden of RSV in infants (up to 3 years), with 4.4% being admitted to the intensive care unit and 28.6% readmitted within the year due to RSV infection.

In addition to the burden of RSV hospitalization, effectiveness is a key parameter for cost-effectiveness. Previous publications have used hypothetical or general effectiveness data of the vaccine over a shorter follow-up period in the trial. ,,, Most recently published efficacy data of the bivalent RSVpreF vaccine have been applied in this analysis. , The KCE report applied the secondary hospitalization endpoint of the MATISSE trial to define the effectiveness of the vaccine against non-intensive care unit hospitalization, while this endpoint has limitations in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic and national specific access to hospitalization. Recent real-world effectiveness data against RSV-LRTI hospitalizations were much aligned with the efficacy data against severe RSV-positive medically attended LRTI in the MATISSE trial. , Based on the currently available real-world data, no statistically significant safety risk of premature births could be associated with RSVpreF administered to women at 32–36 weeks’ gestation. No severe adverse events were included in this analysis. –

This study has some limitations. Due to a lack of data, the same mortality rate and cost of hospital admission were applied regardless of the newborns’ gestational age. Second, the effectiveness of the bivalent RSVpreF vaccine in the late preterm was based on immunogenicity data from the MATISSE trial. Third, VE against hospitalization was derived from the primary endpoint of efficacy against severe medically attended RSV-LRTI because the hospitalization secondary endpoint in the MATISSE trial was considered less appropriate, referring to all RSV-diagnoses, including both upper and lower respiratory tract infections, and not specifically to severe RSV-LRTI. The MATISSE trial was also conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, where hospitalization decisions for RSV were conditional on bed capacity. Hospitalization decisions can also vary by country, where some countries included in the trial have more restricted access to hospital admissions than Belgium. Fourth, this cost-effectiveness analysis is based on a model that simplifies reality and limits the burden of RSV infections during hospitalization. A recent publication reported the impact of RSV infections on primary care burden, , which was not included in this cost-effectiveness analysis, making it conservative. RSVpreF has shown benefits in preventing nonhospitalized, medically attended RSV-LRTIs and associated healthcare costs. ,,, Other conservative assumptions were the absence of protection in infants born within 2 weeks of maternal vaccination, as well as in early preterm infants, while final immunogenicity data from the MATISSE trial showed transfer of maternal antibodies to these newborns. Finally, this cost-effectiveness analysis considers a narrow perspective of benefits. A broader perspective including possible long-term complications of RSV infection such as asthma and recurrent wheezing at later age, ,,, parents’ disutility due to emotional distress associated with infant hospitalization, , parents’ productivity losses, , the potential direct effect of the mother’s immunization against RSV and potential reduced RSV transmission to other relatives, would have provided a more complete estimation of the impact of maternal vaccination.

title: Trajectories and determinants of respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F-specific IgG in older adults.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes substantial morbidity in older adults. However, population-level longitudinal patterns and variability of naturally acquired antibody responses remain insufficiently quantified. We aimed to quantify population-level trajectories and variance components of RSV prefusion F (preF)-specific IgG in older adults. METHODS: We conducted a prospective cohort study of 132 adults aged ≥60 years using residual serum samples, with repeated measurements over one year (666 observations). RSV preF-specific IgG levels were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Population-level trends were estimated using a linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept, adjusting for key covariates. Exploratory analyses were summarized descriptively to characterize variability. RESULTS: At the population level, antibody levels showed no significant temporal change (β = 0.004, SE = 0.003; p = 0.152). Between- and within-individual variability were comparable (SD ≈ 0.247 vs 0.248). Individual slopes were centered near zero (median ≈ 0) with a wide, approximately symmetric distribution. A subset (~31%) exhibited higher variability. No chronic condition was associated with antibody levels after correction for multiple comparisons. CONCLUSIONS: RSV preF-specific IgG levels in older adults were stable at the population level over one year, with substantial within- and between-individual variability. These findings reflect population-average trends and variance components estimated from a random-intercept model and should not be interpreted as evidence of individual-level trajectories or underlying biological mechanisms. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

sections.other:
Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), a negative-strand RNA virus, is a well-established pathogen responsible for lower respiratory tract infections and associated complications in pediatric populations [, ]. Additionally, susceptible adults—particularly those who are 60 years or older and those with chronic comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease and chronic lung diseases—are also adversely affected [–].

In 2019, an estimated 5.2 million cases and 33,000 in-hospital deaths among older adults (≥ 60 years) in high-income countries were attributed to RSV, including approximately 700,000 cases and more than 4000 in-hospital deaths in Japan []. In the United States of America (USA) alone, 60,000 to 160,000 RSV-related hospitalizations among older adults are reported annually []. A recent systematic review further indicated that nearly 80% of acute or community-acquired pneumonia cases among older adult patients in Japan may be attributable to RSV infection [].

Despite these concerning statistics, interventions such as adult RSV vaccines have only recently become available. Notably, the first two adult RSV vaccines—Arexvy ® (GlaxoSmithKline plc) and Abrysvo ® (Pfizer Inc.)—were approved in 2023 for individuals aged 60 years and older, followed by recommendations from the U.S. Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) [, ]. As many countries prepare to introduce adult RSV vaccination programs, there is a growing need for foundational sero-epidemiological data to inform population-level immunity assessments, guide resource allocation, and support evidence-based immunization strategies [, ].

Age-related immune decline further complicates RSV prevention efforts. Immunosenescence—including reduced functional memory T cell populations—contributes to waning humoral responses [–], and natural RSV infection does not confer durable protection. In one longitudinal study, more than 40% of adults were reinfected within two months of a prior RSV infection []. However, despite increasing recognition of RSV as an important pathogen in older adults, the longitudinal patterns of RSV-specific antibody trajectories and the extent of inter-individual variability remain poorly understood. Such variability is clinically relevant, as it may provide insights into susceptibility to infection and potential variability in vaccine response.

To address these gaps, we aimed to characterize population-level trajectories of RSV prefusion IgG antibodies and describe individual variability over time in older adults.
sections.methods:
This prospective observational cohort study was conducted at Mie National Hospital, Japan, between May 28, 2024, and May 24, 2025. Residual serum samples obtained during routine clinical care were collected irrespective of indication to determine anti-RSV prefusion F (preF) IgG antibody levels.

Participants were adults aged ≥ 60 years who had at least two available serum samples collected at different time points during the study period. A total of 132 participants were included, contributing 666 samples.

Participants were excluded if they opted out of the study. No participants had a documented history of RSV vaccination. Systematic documentation of laboratory-confirmed RSV infection was not available.

Demographic and clinical data, including age, sex, and comorbidities (diabetes mellitus, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, chronic heart disease, chronic liver disease, neuromuscular disease, and obesity), were obtained from electronic medical records. Only underlying diseases of interest in the severity of adult RSV were included.

The primary outcome was the log-transformed concentration of anti-RSV prefusion F(preF) IgG antibodies over time. Time (sampling point) was treated as the primary exposure variable. Baseline antibody level was included as a covariate in adjusted analyses.

Anti-RSV prefusion (preF) IgG antibody levels were measured using an in-house enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) based on recombinant trimerized RSV preF protein (DS-Cav1). Serum samples were analyzed in duplicate, and antibody concentrations were quantified using a standard curve derived from reference human IgG. Results were expressed as mIU/mL.

Detailed protocols for expression and purification of RSV protein [–], and ELISA procedures [–] are provided in the Supplementary Methods and .

The R software version 4.4.3 was used for data analysis and RSV IgG antibody concentrations were log10-transformed prior to analysis.

The primary analysis assessed population-level trajectories of log-transformed antibody concentrations over time using linear mixed-effects models. Both unadjusted and covariate-adjusted models were constructed, with participant-level random effects to account for repeated measurements. Prespecified covariates included age, sex, comorbidities, and baseline antibody level. Primary hypotheses focused on:

The overall population-mean change in log antibody concentration over time. The population-mean change in log antibody concentration adjusted for prespecified covariates.

Primary inferences were based on these models without adjustment for multiple comparisons.

Secondary/exploratory analyses were done to further describe inter- and intra-individual antibody variability. These analyses were not prespecified for confirmatory inference and are presented solely for descriptive and hypothesis-generating purposes.

These included:

i. Assessment of time-by-covariate interaction terms in multivariable mixed-effects models to evaluate effect modification. ii. Individual slope estimation to explore participant’s linear slope patterns. iii. Logistic regression to assess associations between derived metrics and clinical covariables. iv. Visualization of antibody trajectories using locally estimated scatterplot smoothing (LOESS).

To account for multiple testing in exploratory analyses, false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied using the Benjamini–Hochberg method. All exploratory analyses were interpreted descriptively.

Below is the link to the electronic supplementary material.
sections.results:
The study included 132 older adults with a median age (range) of 73 years (60–94); 56.1% were female. The most prevalent comorbidities were diabetes mellitus (85.6%), hypertension (64.4%), and chronic kidney disease (57.6%) (Table ). Participants contributed a median of five samples (IQR: 2, range: 2–11) over the one-year follow-up period, with a median sampling interval of 63 days (IQR: 33, range: 28–196). In total, 666 repeated antibody measurements were obtained.

At the population level, no significant temporal change in log-transformed RSV preF IgG antibody concentrations was observed. In linear mixed-effects models, the effect of time was not statistically significant (β = 0.004, SE = 0.003, p = 0.152), indicating overall stability in antibody levels over the study period.

This finding was consistent with LOESS-based visualization (Fig. A), which showed a relatively stable trajectory over time. The predicted trajectory from the linear mixed-effects model (Fig. B) was consistent with the observed data, further supporting the absence of a meaningful population-level trend. Variance component estimates indicated substantial heterogeneity, with comparable contributions from between-individual and within-individual variability (SD: 0.247 and 0.248, respectively). An interaction between time and chronic kidney disease was initially observed; however, this association was not retained after false discovery rate (FDR) correction(adjusted p = 0.252), and no other covariate demonstrated a robust effect on population-level trajectories.

Because of sparse and limited number of repeated measurements from each participant, a median of 5 samples (IQR: 2), there was instability in estimation of individual-specific random slopes in the mixed-effects model. Additionally, the random slope-added model had relatively larger Akaike Information Criteria [AIC] value (275) compared to the random-intercept-only model. Thus, we decided to use the random-intercept-only model as the primary model (Supplementary material , Supplementary figures ).

Despite the overall population-level stability, individual antibody trajectories exhibited substantial heterogeneity. Individual-level changes over time were centered near zero (median slope: +0.0002 log units/day; range: −0.0072 to + 0.0071), indicating that both increases and decreases occurred across participants. The distribution of slopes is shown in Fig. A, demonstrating a continuous distribution without clear separation into distinct groups. Spaghetti plots of individual trajectories (Fig. B) further illustrate the diversity of temporal patterns across participants.

Exploratory analyses were conducted to examine associations between derived measures of antibody dynamics and clinical characteristics.

Higher baseline antibody levels were associated with greater antibody declines over time, consistent with regression toward the mean (Fig. ).

This relationship was consistent across analytical approaches and was descriptive in nature, without indicating an independent or primary effect.

Alternative parameterizations of antibody trajectories, including threshold-based and intersection-based approaches, provided descriptive representations of variability without identifying distinct subgroups or independent biological patterns. Detailed results of these analyses are provided in the Supplementary Results (Supplementary Figs. –, Tables –).

Demographic factors and comorbidities—including chronic kidney disease—were not associated with antibody dynamics after FDR correction.

Exploratory sensitivity analyses identified substantial within-individual variability over time, defined as more than twice the residual standard deviation of the mixed-effects model. Approximately 31% of participants exhibited high variability between consecutive measurements (Supplementary Fig. ).

These patterns may reflect transient immune surging; however, they did not correspond to a consistent population-level effect. Importantly, exclusion of individuals with higher variability did not alter the overall population-level trajectory, which remained stable over time, indicating that individual-level fluctuations do not obscure the primary finding.
sections.discussion:
In this longitudinal study, we observed that RSV preF–specific IgG levels in older adults are generally stable over one-year, with substantial inter- and intra-individual variability. The population-level stability in IgG levels coexisted with diverse individual trajectories reflecting continuous heterogeneity across individuals rather than discrete patterns.

Exploratory analyses showed that individuals with lower baseline antibody levels generally maintained these lower levels over time. However, this pattern is best interpreted as descriptive of a continuous range of variability rather than as evidence for a distinct subgroup. Additionally, high baseline antibody titres were also associated with subsequent decrease in antibody dynamics over time, consistent with regression towards the mean in a stable population. These findings as well should be understood as describing individual variability within an overall stable population and highlight that interpretation of baseline antibodies depends on analytical framework, thus caution is required. The use of repeated longitudinal measurements, rather than relying on a single baseline value, is therefore recommended for comprehensive serological assessments.

Further exploration showed that the observed population-level antibody stability may coexist with intermittent surge in antibody levels, contributing to the high inter-individual variability. However, direct evidence of RSV exposure or immune stimulation was not available in this study. These findings do not establish immune stimulation and may underscore the importance of accounting for exposure history in longitudinal serological studies to better describe the observed individual variability.

Preceding studies have reported reductions in antibodies following RSV exposure, with antibody reductions within approximately 60 days in recently infected adults [] and increases following re-exposure [–]. The coexistence of these individual variability patterns in our cohort, given the exploratory nature of this analysis, warrants more studies with larger cohorts, well-established uncertainty measures and additional linked epidemiological data to clarify heterogeneous exposure histories, measurement and biological variability.

Alternative parameterizations of antibody trajectories, including slope direction and intersection-based approaches, yielded consistent patterns of overall population stability with individual variability and are best understood as different analytical representations of the same underlying variability rather than distinct biological processes. These derived metrics should be interpreted strictly as descriptive representations of variability and do not provide independent biological evidence.

Patterns of persistently lower antibody levels observed in some individuals are consistent with inter-individual variability and may reflect differences in immune history or host factors. This pattern highlights inter-individual variability rather than a discrete biological phenotype and may, in part, be explained with age-related immune decline (Immunosenescence), which reduces the capacity to maintain durable antibody responses in older adults [–], although this cannot be directly inferred from the present data.

Previous studies have reported the potential influence of comorbidities on immune function and antibody responses [, , , ]. However, none of the included comorbidities were associated with differences in antibody trajectories nor interaction over time in our cohort. Therefore, more studies with larger cohorts and clearly defined comorbidity data are recommended.

Several limitations warrant consideration. This was a single-centre study, and some comorbidity-specific effects with wider generalization require larger cohorts for robust estimation. Linear models may oversimplify non-linear antibody trajectories, although mixed-effects models were used to mitigate this limitation. In addition, RSV exposure could not be directly ascertained because RT-PCR or IgM testing was not performed, and adult RSV infections are often mild or undiagnosed. Functional immune correlates were not assessed. Although RSV preF IgG levels correlate with protection [–], this study measured total binding IgG rather than neutralizing activity, which depends on antibody affinity, epitope specificity, and Fc-mediated functions. Therefore, protective capacity cannot be directly inferred. In addition, cellular immune responses, including B- and T-cell memory, were not evaluated and may further explain inter-individual heterogeneity.

Despite these limitations, this study provides novel insight into the dynamics of RSV humoral immunity in older adults. The findings are best interpreted as a detailed characterization of longitudinal variability underlying a stable population-level trend, rather than evidence for distinct immunological subgroups.

In summary, RSV antibody dynamics in older adults demonstrated substantial longitudinal variability across individuals, with overall stability at the population level. These findings support a framework in which antibody dynamics are best understood as a continuum of variability rather than discrete categories and highlight the importance of longitudinal measurements for interpreting immune responses in aging populations.

title: 574. Early Post-Marketing Safety Surveillance for the Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Protein Vaccine (RSVPreF3 OA)
abstract: RSVPreF3 OA (GSK) received its first approval on 3 May 2023 in the United States (US), for the prevention of lower respiratory tract disease caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in ≥ 60-year-olds. By 15 March 2024 (data lock point [DLP] of this analysis), RSVPreF3 OA was also approved in all European Economic Area countries, and > 10 additional countries across both hemispheres. We summarized the post-marketing safety surveillance data following vaccination with RSVPreF3 OA. Exposure was based on RSVPreF3 OA doses distributed and administered. The spontaneous adverse events (AEs) reported from 3 May 2023 up to DLP were retrieved from GSK’s Global Safety Database. Observed-to-expected (O/E) analyses were performed for reports of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and transverse myelitis. Up to DLP, > 9.1 million RSVPreF3 OA doses were distributed globally, of which > 7.8 million doses were administered to adults in the US. There were 1,301 reports including 3,278 AEs following RSVPreF3 OA administration, of which 91.34% were considered non-serious (Table). Most reported AEs were consistent with the expected reactogenicity profile, as observed in clinical trials and listed in the prescribing information. O/E analysis of GBS (N=9) and transverse myelitis (N=1) found that the reporting rates did not exceed the expected background incidence (16 and 6 expected cases, respectively); no other neuroinflammatory events were reported. Nineteen reports of atrial fibrillation were reported and more plausibly reflect the epidemiology of the older adult population being vaccinated. Of all reports, 539 (41.43%) described medication errors, of which 85.34% were without associated symptoms. Although RSVPreF3 OA is not indicated for pregnant women, 263 cases of exposure during pregnancy (48.79% of the medication errors) were reported. Based on the data from the first 10 months of post-marketing surveillance, the safety profile of RSVPreF3 OA was shown to be consistent with that observed in clinical trials. The available evidence does not suggest a causal association between RSVPreF3 OA and neuroinflammatory events or atrial fibrillation. Along with the vaccine efficacy shown in clinical trials, the data supports a favorable benefit-risk profile. Up to DLP, > 9.1 million RSVPreF3 OA doses were distributed globally, of which > 7.8 million doses were administered to adults in the US. There were 1,301 reports including 3,278 AEs following RSVPreF3 OA administration, of which 91.34% were considered non-serious (Table). Most reported AEs were consistent with the expected reactogenicity profile, as observed in clinical trials and listed in the prescribing information. O/E analysis of GBS (N=9) and transverse myelitis (N=1) found that the reporting rates did not exceed the expected background incidence (16 and 6 expected cases, respectively); no other neuroinflammatory events were reported. Nineteen reports of atrial fibrillation were reported and more plausibly reflect the epidemiology of the older adult population being vaccinated. Of all reports, 539 (41.43%) described medication errors, of which 85.34% were without associated symptoms. Although RSVPreF3 OA is not indicated for pregnant women, 263 cases of exposure during pregnancy (48.79% of the medication errors) were reported. Based on the data from the first 10 months of post-marketing surveillance, the safety profile of RSVPreF3 OA was shown to be consistent with that observed in clinical trials. The available evidence does not suggest a causal association between RSVPreF3 OA and neuroinflammatory events or atrial fibrillation. Along with the vaccine efficacy shown in clinical trials, the data supports a favorable benefit-risk profile. title: Cost-Effectiveness of Bivalent Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Vaccine for Older Adults in the Netherlands.
abstract: Introduction Lower respiratory tract disease caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV-LRTD) is associated with substantial clinical and economic burden among older adults and adults with chronic medical conditions. Bivalent RSV prefusion F protein-based vaccine (RSVpreF) has been authorized for use among all adults aged ≥ 60 years in the Netherlands, and The Health Council of the Netherlands has recommended RSV vaccination for at-risk persons aged 60-74 years and all persons aged ≥ 75 years. We estimated the cost-effectiveness of implementing this strategy. Methods We have developed a static cohort model to demonstrate lifetime clinical and economic outcomes associated with RSV-LRTD among adults in the Netherlands, with (vs. without) RSVpreF use (price: €180; age/risk-specific uptake: 44.6-80.4%). Model inputs include population characteristics, disease rates [hospitalization (RSV-H), general practitioner visit (RSV-GP), non-medically attended (RSV-NMA)], fatality rates, vaccine effectiveness (based on real-world and clinical trial data), utilities/disutilities, medical care costs, indirect costs associated with morbidity- and mortality-related productivity loss, and vaccination costs. Discounting was applied to costs (3%) and benefits (1.5%). Results Among at-risk adults aged 60-74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years (n = 4.8 million) in the Netherlands, single-dose RSVpreF would prevent 84,228 RSV-LRTD cases (RSV-H: 16,642, RSV-GP: 21,788, RSV-NMA: 45,798) and 2304 RSV-LRTD deaths over a lifetime horizon. With 11,006 quality-adjusted life-years (QALY) gained and a €195 million increase in total costs, incremental cost-effectiveness ratio for RSVpreF would be €17,740/QALY gained. RSVpreF would thus prevent 16% of hospitalizations, 15% of deaths, 16% of medical costs, and 20% of indirect costs related to RSV among this population over their remaining lifetime. In probabilistic sensitivity analyses applying variability to key inputs, all 1000 replications yielded cost-effectiveness ratios within the Health Council's willingness-to-pay threshold ( Conclusions Findings suggest that RSVpreF would greatly reduce the clinical and economic burden of RSV among older adults in the Netherlands.
