sections.other:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for a substantial burden of acute illness experienced by older adults and may cause severe respiratory disease []. There is an increased risk of RSV-related complications (e.g., pneumonia) among persons aged ≥ 65 years and older adults with chronic medical conditions such as heart or lung disease []. In the Netherlands and globally, RSV outbreaks are common and burdensome throughout nursing homes and other residential care facilities where elderly persons live in close contact with one another []. A recent burden of disease study found the burden of severe RSV to be considerable among adults in the Netherlands, with in-hospital mortality rates as high as 13.8% []. Evidence on the burden of RSV among these populations is sparse due to limited awareness among health care practitioners, lack of routine testing, unreliability of diagnostic tests in older adults, and differences in the use of diagnostic codes employed within burden of disease studies [, ].

Until recently, there were no preventive measures available to protect adults against RSV. Beginning in 2021, the efficacy and safety of bivalent stabilized prefusion F subunit vaccine (RSVpreF) use among older adults has been evaluated in the “RSV vaccine Efficacy study iN Older adults Immunized against RSV disease” Phase III placebo-controlled clinical trial (“RENOIR”, NCT05035212 ) []. In August of 2023, the European Commission gave marketing authorization to RSVpreF for use in adults aged 60 years and older to prevent RSV-related lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) []. Furthermore, in their 2025 review, the Health Council of the Netherlands recommended that at-risk persons aged 60–74 years and all persons aged ≥ 75 years be vaccinated against RSV; however, introduction of the program has been delayed pending evidence on vaccine duration of protection and cost-effectiveness []. While several recent studies have evaluated the clinical and economic outcomes associated with vaccine use (i.e., not specifically RSVpreF vaccine) to prevent RSV in the Netherlands, only one evaluates outcomes among the age group currently recommended for vaccination [–]. To address this gap as well as concerns from the Health Council of the Netherlands regarding vaccine duration of protection and cost-effectiveness, the current study employs a cost-effectiveness model to evaluate the public health and economic outcomes associated with RSV-LRTD and vaccination with RSVpreF (i.e., compared to no vaccination) among at-risk adults aged 60–74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years in the Netherlands.
sections.methods:
To estimate the burden of RSV-LRTD and impact of RSVpreF vaccination among older adults in the Netherlands over a lifetime, we employed a population-based Markov-type model (Fig. ). The cost-effectiveness model has been recently described in detail in an analysis of RSVpreF use among older adults in Germany []. As described in the paper, the model population is characterized based on age and comorbidity profile (with vs. without chronic or immunocompromising medical conditions [CMC+ vs. CMC–)] []. Adults in the model population were assumed to be either protected against RSV-LRTD by way of RSVpreF or to remain vulnerable against RSV-LRTD. Clinical outcomes in the model include cases of RSV-LRTD, stratified by care setting [i.e., hospital (H), general practitioner’s office (GP), non-medically attended (NMA)], and RSV-related deaths. As detailed in the study by Averin et al., economic costs include direct medical care costs, costs of vaccination (i.e., including the vaccine and its administration), and indirect costs related to productivity loss []. Because persons may be retained in the model population over a lifetime, they are subject to experiencing health outcomes and economic costs on a monthly basis until death or age 99 years (i.e., whichever occurs first) []. Consistent with a standard cost-effectiveness model approach, the model follows a single cohort of adults and does not consider any adults entering the population after the first model year or receiving vaccinations after the first model year (i.e., even among the initial cohort). Discounting is applied to costs and benefits each month, beginning one month after model entry.

Model input values were estimated to vary by age group, comorbidity profile, and care setting, as appropriate, based on data from published sources. Netherlands-specific sources were employed where possible, with data from comparable country settings applied as needed. Parameter values employed in base case, sensitivity, and scenario analyses are detailed in Tables , , Fig. , Supplementary Figure , and Supplementary Table . This study does not require ethical approval as it does not involve any human participants, animals, or sensitive data.

The model population (i.e., CMC+ adults aged 60–74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years in the Netherlands) comprised 2.6 million persons, estimated from Dutch Central Bureau of Statistics 2023 data []. Adults were stratified by age group (i.e., 60–64, 65–74, 75–84, and 85–99 years) and comorbidity profile (CMC+ vs. CMC–). The age-specific distribution of persons aged ≥ 60 years by comorbidity profile was estimated based on data from a recent RSV vaccine cost-effectiveness analysis (Table ) []. The CMC+ subgroup is reflective of the target subgroup eligible for free influenza vaccination in the Netherlands (i.e., included persons with chronic respiratory, cardiac, and kidney diseases, diabetes, immunosuppressive diseases, obesity, and neurological disorders) [, ].

Age-specific incidence of RSV-LRTD-attributable hospitalizations was estimated based on a recent burden of disease modeling study conducted by Johannesen et al. []. Age-specific RSV-H rates were then allocated across comorbidity profiles based on relative risk data from a study conducted by Zeevat et al., which also evaluated the cost-effectiveness of RSV vaccination among older adults in the Netherlands []. Age-specific incidence of RSV-GP was estimated based on a recent study evaluating the burden of RSV treated in primary care settings among adults aged ≥ 50 years in the Netherlands []. RSV-GP incidence was assumed to be invariant by comorbidity profile. Incidence of RSV-NMA was estimated based on the study from Zeevat et al. which reported that 70.44% of RSV episodes would not require medical attention []. All rates of RSV (i.e., invariant by setting of care) were allocated across calendar months based on recent data from the National Institute for Public Health (Table ) [].

Case-fatality rate (CFR) was estimated based on Netherlands-specific data on mortality among patients hospitalized with RSV between 2022 and 2024 []. CFR was then allocated by comorbidity profile based on data from a retrospective cohort study of mortality in United States (US) adults hospitalized for pneumonia []. There was assumed to be no mortality among RSV episodes not requiring hospitalization (i.e., RSV-GP, RSV-NMA).

Age-specific general population mortality (i.e., unrelated to RSV-LRTD) was estimated based on Central Bureau of Statistics data []. Age-specific mortality data was then allocated by comorbidity profile based on the assumption that CMC+ persons are at a 75% increased risk of mortality (i.e., compared to CMC– persons). This aligns with assumptions employed in the recent cost-effectiveness analysis of RSVpreF use in Germany conducted by Averin et al. [].

Vaccine effectiveness (VE) against RSV-H was estimated based on 2023–2025 real-world effectiveness data from the Kaiser Permanente Southern California (KPSC) study evaluating VE against RSV-related LRTD hospitalizations and emergency department (ED) visits (Fig. ) []. Endpoints corresponding to season 1 follow-up (i.e., 1.9 months; 87% VE) and season 2 follow-up (i.e., 12.2 months; 77% VE) were employed, with linear interpolation applied between the two timepoints. Linear extrapolation (i.e., based on the estimated slope between 1.9 and 12.2 months) was applied for month 1 and months 13–90 since administration, after which point the VE curve naturally hits 0%.

VE against RSV-GP was estimated based on RENOIR clinical trial data as employed in Averin et al. []. As detailed by Averin and colleagues, efficacy against medically attended acute respiratory illness due to RSV (RSV-ARI) was used as a proxy for VE against RSV-GP []. Endpoints corresponding to season 1 follow-up (i.e., 7 months) and season 2 follow-up (i.e., 16.4 months) were employed, with linear interpolation applied between the two timepoints and linear extrapolation applied after 16.4 months until VE hits 0% at 41 months after administration [].

VE against RSV-NMA was estimated similarly but was based on efficacy data against non-medically attended RSV-ARI from post hoc analyses []. Season 1 VE was estimated to be 60.0% and season 2 VE was estimated to be 31.4%. Waning of VE against RSV-NMA was estimated the same way as the RSV-GP waning curve. Due to the steep decline in efficacy estimates between season 1 and season 2, VE was estimated to reach 0% in month 27 after administration.

Hospitalization costs associated with RSV-LRTD were estimated based on a Netherlands-specific retrospective claims analysis and are reflective of episodes treated in both the general ward and intensive care unit (i.e., weighted by severity based on data included in the study) []. Because costs from Rozenbaum et al. are based on 2008–2011 data, they were then inflated to 2024 Euros [, ]. Cost per GP visit (€34.88) was estimated based on the Dutch manual for costing studies; cost per RSV-NMA episode (€4.32) was assumed to comprise only over-the-counter medication and estimated based on a recent RSV burden of disease study among older adults in the Netherlands [, ]. Medical costs associated with both GP and NMA episodes were inflated to 2024 Euros and were assumed to be invariant by patient age and comorbidity profile []. List price of RSVpreF was €180 []; administration cost associated with RSVpreF use was estimated to be €14.01 based on influenza vaccination reimbursement [].

Indirect costs included morbidity and mortality related productivity loss among patients with RSV-LRTD and morbidity related productivity loss among caregivers (e.g., spouse/child) of patients. Productivity loss among patients and caregivers was estimated based on labor force participation data (i.e., which was assumed to be 0% among retired persons) [], daily wage data [, ], and estimated number of days of work-loss. Work-loss for patients was assumed to vary based on severity of RSV-LRTD episode [, ]. For caregivers of persons hospitalized with RSV-LRTD, work loss was assumed to be the same as for patients []; there was assumed to be no work loss among caregivers of patients treated in GP or NMA settings. Lastly, work-loss associated with premature RSV-related mortality was estimated based on life expectancy data, with expected lifetime earnings discounted monthly [].

Age- and risk-specific general population utility values were estimated based on EQ-5D data from the United Kingdom (UK) []. Utility values among persons with a history of health conditions were assigned to CMC+ persons in this study, while utility values among persons with no history of health conditions were assigned to CMC– persons []. Care setting-specific disutility associated with RSV (i.e., RSV-H: 0.017, RSV-GP: 0.005, RSV-NMA: 0.002) was estimated using an area under the curve approach and data from two recent studies reporting EQ-5D VAS scores among persons with RSV treated in the hospital setting versus GP/NMA settings, respectively [, ]. Quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) loss was assumed to be invariant by patient age and comorbidity profile.

Base case analyses evaluated the cost-effectiveness of the Hypothetical Strategy (i.e., CMC+ adults aged 60–74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years in the Netherlands are eligible for RSVpreF) versus the Current Strategy (no intervention). Age- and comorbidity-specific vaccine coverage was estimated based on observed influenza vaccination rates []. RSVpreF administration was assumed to occur leading up to and during the months of highest respiratory illness rates. Lacking Netherlands-specific data on respiratory disease vaccination by time of year, the distribution of vaccine administration by calendar month was based on 2018–2019 uptake of influenza vaccine as observed in the UK []. As such, vaccine administration occurs from September through February of the first year of the modeling horizon, with some protection from each vaccination lasting for the following 91 months after administration. Consistent with the Dutch guidelines for economic evaluations in healthcare, future costs were discounted at an annual rate of 3% while future QALYs were discounted at an annual rate of 1.5% []. Cost-effectiveness was reported as an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) defined as cost per QALY gained (i.e., difference in costs divided by difference in QALYs).

A subgroup analysis considering vaccination among all adults aged ≥ 60 years (i.e., regardless of comorbidity profile) was conducted to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of RSVpreF use among all adults authorized for vaccination in the Netherlands. One-way deterministic sensitivity analyses (DSA) considering changes (± 20% of base case values) to selected input values (i.e., RSV-H incidence rates, CFR, vaccine uptake, VE, and medical care costs), each in turn, were also performed to evaluate robustness of results to changes in key model parameters. In addition, to address concerns from the Health Council of the Netherlands, scenario analyses were conducted in which alternative vaccine duration of protection was considered for VE against RSV-related hospitalizations. Specifically, VE was estimated using the same methods as base case but employing data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) (Figure in electronic supplementary material) []. Lastly, probabilistic sensitivity analyses (PSA) accounting for uncertainty surrounding key model parameters were conducted with 1000 simulations (Table ). Results of subgroup, sensitivity, and scenario analyses can be found in Tables S2–S13 of the electronic supplementary materials.

Below is the link to the electronic supplementary material.
sections.results:
With no vaccination to protect CMC+ adults aged 60–74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years ( n = 2.6 M) in the Netherlands against RSV-LRTD, there would be 103,449 cases of RSV-H, 270,828 cases of RSV-GP, 889,002 cases of RSV-NMA, and 15,468 RSV-attributable deaths over the lifetime modeling horizon (Table , Tables , ). Medical care costs would total €489 million with an additional €290 million in indirect costs. Use of RSVpreF among CMC+ adults aged 60–74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years would yield reductions in RSV-LRTD cases of 16,642 (16%), 21,788 (8%), and 45,798 (5%) for RSV-H, RSV-GP, and RSV-NMA episodes, respectively. By preventing cases of RSV-LRTD, RSVpreF would also prevent 2,304 (15%) RSV-related deaths, €97 million in medical care costs, and €66 million in indirect costs. With €358 million in vaccination costs, total costs would increase by €195 million. RSVpreF would yield an increase in QALYs of 11,006 and thus the ICER would be €17,740/QALY.

Over only a 1-year time horizon, there would be 99,346 RSV-LRTD cases (RSV-H: 6,882, RSV-GP: 22,549, RSV-NMA: 69,916) and 919 deaths among CMC+ adults aged 60–74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years (Table S2). Associated medical care and indirect costs would be €44 million and €51 million, respectively. RSVpreF use would prevent 47% of RSV-H, 35% of RSV-GP, 32% of RSV-NMA, 47% of deaths, 46% of medical costs, and 37% of indirect costs.

During the first five years of modeling horizon, cases would total 452,296 (RSV-H: 32,272, RSV-GP: 101,718, RSV-NMA: 318,306) with 4,402 RSV-attributable deaths (Table S3). Associated medical care costs and indirect costs for these first five years would be €194 million and €179 million, respectively. Single-dose RSVpreF use would prevent 45% of RSV-H, 22% of RSV-GP, 15% of RSV-NMA, 45% of deaths, 44% of medical costs, and 34% of indirect costs.

By expanding vaccine eligibility to include all adults aged ≥ 60 years in the Netherlands, RSVpreF prevented an additional 62,173 cases of RSV-LRTD (RSV-H: 8,015, RSV-GP: 19,188; RSV-NMA: 34,970) while remaining cost-effective, with an ICER of €22,902/QALY (Table S4).

All DSAs yielded cost-effectiveness for RSVpreF with ICERs ranging from €12,504 to €25,535 per QALY (Fig. ). DSA indicated that changes to hospitalization rates and vaccine effectiveness had the greatest impact on model results.

In the scenario analysis employing an alternative data source for vaccine effectiveness against RSV-H, RSVpreF prevented 46% fewer hospitalizations and 44% fewer medical care costs than in the base case (Fig. ). Regardless, RSVpreF still prevented 76,910 episodes of RSV-LRTD among older adults in the Netherlands and remained cost-effective, with an ICER of €42,523/QALY.

PSA yielded an average ICER of €17,508/QALY gained, with ICERs ranging from €11,141 to €28,865 per QALY (Fig. ). All 1000 replications yielded cost-effectiveness ratios less than €50,000/QALY, with 788 replications (79%) yielding ICERs less than €20,000/QALY.
sections.discussion:
Our results support existing evidence that RSV is responsible for a substantial clinical and economic burden among persons aged ≥ 65 years and those with chronic medical conditions such as heart or lung disease []. Even though RSVpreF has been authorized since 2023 by the European Commission for use among adults aged ≥ 60 years to prevent RSV-LRTD [], and the Health Council of the Netherlands recommended in 2025 that at-risk persons aged 60–74 years and all persons aged ≥ 75 years be vaccinated against RSV, implementation of the program has been delayed, mainly due to concerns surrounding vaccine duration of protection []. We thus employed a Markov-type model to provide further evidence on the burden of RSV-LRTD and the cost-effectiveness of RSVpreF use (i.e., compared to no vaccination) among at-risk adults aged 60–74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years in the Netherlands.

Results suggest that employing the program recommended by the Health Council (i.e., RSVpreF use among at-risk adults aged 60–74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years) would substantially reduce the clinical and economic burden of RSV-LRTD to the Netherlands’ health care system and society. Assuming uptake comparable to levels for influenza vaccination, RSVpreF would prevent 16% of RSV-H, 15% of RSV-LRTD deaths, 16% of medical care costs, and 20% of indirect costs over a lifetime horizon. In the first year alone, RSVpreF use among the target population would prevent 33,573 cases of RSV-LRTD, 434 deaths, and €39.5 million in associated costs, reducing such outcomes by 34%, 47%, and 41%, respectively. This impact would be enhanced if the Health Council were to extend their recommendation to target all adults aged ≥ 60 years with RSVpreF.

To address concerns from the Health Council regarding duration of vaccine protection and cost-effectiveness of RSVpreF immunization, a scenario analysis was conducted employing real-world data on effectiveness against RSV-related hospitalizations from the US CDC []. As demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. , data from the CDC yielded VE that was lower overall and diminished to 0% at month 58 after administration (vs. month 91, in the base case). Assuming lower VE against RSV-H, RSVpreF still prevented 9% of hospitalizations, 11% of total medical care costs, and 15% of indirect costs; the ICER was €42,523/QALY. This suggests that, even if effectiveness inputs employed here are optimistic, RSVpreF use among the target subgroup would be a cost-effective solution to reducing the burden of RSV-LRTD. Lastly, subgroup analyses demonstrated that expanding the vaccination strategy to include all adults aged ≥ 60 years would prevent 48% more hospitalizations, 88% more GP encounters, and 76% more NMA episodes, compared to the base-case vaccination strategy. This expanded vaccination strategy would protect a larger portion of the population, prevent more RSV-related outcomes, and remain a cost-effective use of resources. Overall, across all base-case, subgroup, deterministic sensitivity, probabilistic sensitivity, and scenario analyses, the ICER ranged from €11,141 to €42,523 per QALY gained, consistently falling within the Health Council’s willingness-to-pay threshold.

To the extent of our knowledge, this is the first study to employ multi-season real-world effectiveness data to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of RSVpreF use among at-risk adults aged 60–74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years in the Netherlands. One recent study, by Zeevat et al. [], considered vaccination among a target population consistent with the base case strategy employed herein; however, Zeevat and colleagues considered the use of a generic RSV vaccine (i.e., not RSVpreF-specific) for which VE data were based on a meta-analysis that mainly considered effectiveness over only the first season following vaccination (i.e., opposed to multi-season data employed herein). Zeevat and colleagues also considered costs and QALY loss associated with adverse events of vaccination, which we are not comfortable employing at this point due to lack of data []. Given differences in study design and estimation, outcomes averted (versus no vaccination) and ICERs were comparable to those reported herein []. Zeevat and colleagues reported vaccination to yield 8196 QALYs (vs. 11,006 herein) and €247 million in total costs (vs. €195 million herein); ICER would therefore be €30,162 (vs. €17,740 here).

Our analyses are subject to several notable limitations related to input parameters and modeling assumptions. Since the full duration of protection via RSVpreF will not be known until several more seasons of real-world data become available, we employed methods of linear extrapolation to estimate the VE waning curves. For all settings, it was assumed that the decline of effectiveness between the first two endpoints would persist until the curve naturally hits 0%. Specifically, VE data against RSV-H, RSV-GP, and RSV-NMA were extrapolated to obtain inputs corresponding to months 13–91, 17–41, and 17–27 after administration, respectively (Fig. ). To evaluate the impact of these assumptions on model results, we conducted a scenario analysis evaluating the impact of employing alternative VE against RSV-H []. VE endpoints from the US CDC were lower than KPSC data and the curve waned to 0% VE nearly three years earlier than in the base case (i.e., 58 months opposed to 91 months after administration; Figure ). The scenario analysis yielded a 46% lower reduction in hospitalizations than in the base case but remained cost-effective (ICER: €42,523/QALY gained; Table S13). We also note that there are many studies currently evaluating the effectiveness of RSV vaccines which were not chosen to inform VE inputs herein [–]. The KPSC study is most applicable to our analyses (i.e., considering use of RSVpreF specifically among adults aged ≥ 60 years, with the majority aged ≥ 75 years, which aligns with our modeled population) given its two seasons of data available and thorough methodology (e.g., includes testing of salvaged nasal swabs collected for influenza/SARS-CoV-2 testing) []. We look forward to the release of additional real-world data to inform the rate of VE waning over several seasons; however, we believe that, for the time being, linear extrapolation is a reasonable approach. It is also notable that the VE endpoints employed in the base case may not be perfectly aligned with model outcomes. For example, VE against RSV-H was estimated based on an endpoint associated with RSV-related hospitalizations or ED encounters []. Because VE is typically more effective against severe disease [], it is likely that employing such values underestimates the impact of RSVpreF against hospitalizations alone.

Hospitalization rates employed were based on data on RSV-attributable infections from the modeling study by Johannesen et al., which were also employed by Zeevat et al. [, ]. We note that Johanessen and colleagues report both “RSV-coded” and “RSV-attributable” (i.e., accommodating for underreporting and underdiagnosis) incidence rates; as recommended by the authors, we employed the RSV-attributable incidence rates in order to evaluate the full burden of RSV []. These data on RSV-attributable infections accommodate for underreporting of severe RSV which has been acknowledged and adjusted for in many countries due to low diagnostic testing rates and limited accuracy in case definitions [, –]. The approach herein therefore follows recent standards employed globally to estimate the true burden of RSV-LRTD; however, to the extent that RSV-H incidence is under- or overestimated, the burden of disease may be over- or underestimated.

We also note that, in the absence of the actual net price, the list price of RSVpreF was employed; therefore, the price employed may be overestimated. Furthermore, due to limited availability of data, some model inputs were estimated based on data from comparable country settings. Specifically, estimates of baseline utility and the distribution of vaccine administration by calendar month were based on UK data due to the close proximity and socio-economic status of the two regions [, ]. Estimates of QALY loss were based on global/European data [, ]. To the extent that model inputs are not reflective of the setting of interest, the cost-effectiveness of RSVpreF may be mis-estimated.

There is also growing evidence that RSV infection causes hospitalizations related to exacerbations of existing cardiovascular and pulmonary conditions, and that other serious events often occur concurrently with RSV infection [–]. Because data related to RSV-attributable cardiovascular or pulmonary hospitalizations and the impact of RSVpreF in preventing such events is limited at this time, and because the cost-effectiveness model is not currently capable of assessing these outcomes, such potential benefits from vaccination were not included in the model. The model also did not consider other potential downstream effects of RSV illness. Especially among older adults and those with chronic medical conditions, evidence suggests that patients may experience an increased rate of other illnesses, all-cause hospitalizations, functional status decline, and/or need for nursing care following an episode of RSV-LRTD [, ]. Because the model did not evaluate these additional outcomes, the clinical and economic benefits of RSVpreF may be further underestimated. Future research should expand on this analysis by quantifying the impact of potential RSV-related exacerbations of chronic conditions, subsequent all-cause hospitalizations, and long-term functional decline, as well as the potential role of RSVpreF vaccination in mitigating these consequences.

Results suggest that single-dose RSVpreF vaccination among at-risk adults aged 60–74 years and all adults aged ≥ 75 years in the Netherlands would considerably reduce the clinical burden of RSV-LRTD and would be a cost-effective use of resources. Findings were consistent across all analyses conducted, including scenario analysis considering alternative vaccine effectiveness inputs.

title: Postmarketing safety surveillance for GSK's AS01E-adjuvanted respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F protein-based vaccine in the USA: protocol for a non-interventional postauthorisation safety study.
abstract: Introduction In May 2023, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) initially approved an AS01 E -adjuvanted respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prefusion F protein-based vaccine (adjuvanted RSVPreF3) for adults aged ≥60 years. The approval was expanded in June 2024 to include adults 50-59 years of age at increased risk for RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease. In this paper, we describe the protocol of a postmarketing safety study evaluating the association between adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and new-onset Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) and atrial fibrillation (AF) among adults ≥50 years of age in the USA and provide our rationale for key methodological decisions. Methods and analysis The potential associations between adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and GBS, ADEM and AF will be evaluated using secondary healthcare data and the self-controlled risk interval (SCRI) design. Data from five research partners in the USA spanning August 2023 through June 2030 will be used for the conduct of yearly monitoring queries and, sample size permitting, SCRI analyses. Claims-based definitions for new-onset outcomes (first diagnosis in 365 days) are: ≥1 inpatient diagnosis for GBS and ADEM; ≥1 inpatient or ≥2 ambulatory/emergency diagnoses for AF. The primary risk and control windows are 1-42 and 43-84 days, respectively, for GBS and ADEM; and 1-8 and 9-16 days for AF. SCRI analyses for GBS and ADEM will include chart-confirmed cases. SCRI analyses for AF will adjust for the positive predictive value obtained from validation against charts. Conditional Poisson regression will be used to calculate incidence rate ratios. Ethics and dissemination This study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards (IRB) of Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute; WIRB-Copernicus Group, Inc and its affiliates (collectively, 'WCG'); WCG IRB, Inc; and Sterling IRB, with Federal Wide Assurance (FWA) numbers FWA00000100, FWA00033319 and FWA00025632, respectively, for all participating research partners. Study results will be shared with the US FDA and publicly disseminated through national or international clinical or scientific conferences and peer-reviewed publications. Registration This protocol has been registered in the Heads of Medicines Agencies-European Medicines Agency Real World Data Catalogues (EUPAS1000000486).

sections.other:
STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY This study will include a large, diverse and nationally representative population of privately insured older adults in the USA. The use of a self-matched design will control for time-invariant known and unknown sources of confounding in the potential associations between adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) and atrial fibrillation (AF). Primary analyses will include cases confirmed by clinicians (for GBS and ADEM) or identified using a case-finding algorithm validated in participating data sources (for AF), thereby mitigating potential bias due to misclassification of outcomes. Medical records for case or algorithm validation may not be retrievable for all cases; however, the reasons for irretrievability are expected to be random and administrative in nature. Depending on the number of observed outcomes, the study may have limited power to evaluate the joint effects of concomitantly administered vaccines.

Respiratory syncytial virus-associated lower respiratory tract disease (RSV-LRTD) in older adults causes significant morbidity and mortality., A recent analysis estimated that RSV accounted for 5.2 million cases of acute respiratory infections, 470 000 hospitalisations and 33 000 in-hospital deaths among adults ≥60 years of age in industrialised countries in 2019. Similar to influenza, adults with certain medical conditions, those in long-term care facilities and those who are frail are at increased risk of RSV-LRTD.,

In May 2023, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the first vaccines for prevention of RSV-LRTD in older adults, including a single dose of adjuvanted (AS01 E ) recombinant stabilised prefusion F protein vaccine (adjuvanted RSVPreF3, Arexvy ). AS01 E is an Adjuvant System containing 3- O -desacyl-4′-monophosphoryl lipid A (MPL), Quillaja saponaria Molina, fraction 21 (QS-21) (licensed by GSK from Antigenics, a wholly owned subsidiary of Agenus Inc., a Delaware, US corporation) and liposome (25 mg MPL and 25 µg QS-21). As of July 2025, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends RSV vaccines in all adults aged ≥75 years and those aged 50–74 years at increased risk of RSV-LRTD.

Efficacy data from phase III trial of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 demonstrated a reduction in RSV-LRTD of 82.6% (96.95% CI 57.9% to 94.1%), severe RSV-LRTD by 94.1% (95% CI 62.4% to 99.9%) and RSV-related acute respiratory infections by 71.7% (95% CI 56.2% to 82.3%) compared with placebo in adults aged ≥60 years. These findings extended to a high-risk population of adults aged ≥60 years with at least one pre-existing condition associated with increased risk for severe RSV disease in whom the vaccine efficacy against RSV-LRTD was 94.6% (95% CI 65.9% to 99.9%).

While the rates of short-term severe adverse events were comparable between adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and placebo in these trials, there were three reports of inflammatory neurological events out of a pooled total of 17 922 participants within 42 days of vaccination. One was a case of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), and the other two were initially diagnosed as acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) but later revised to other non-neurological diagnoses. There was also an imbalance in the number of vaccinated participants with atrial fibrillation (AF) compared with those administered placebo (10 vs 4 events) within 30 days after vaccination. However, clinical trials are not adequately powered to detect a meaningful increase in the risk of very rare events, such as GBS, which has a background rate of approximately 4.5 events per 100 000 person-years among those of age ≥65 years in the USA. The FDA required the sponsor of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 to conduct active surveillance of GBS, ADEM and AF as a postmarketing requirement (GBS, ADEM) and commitment (AF) at the time of its licensing approval in 2023.

This paper describes the protocol of a multiyear active surveillance study evaluating the associations between adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and GBS, ADEM and AF in adults aged ≥50 years in the USA. The primary objective is to assess the risk of new-onset GBS and ADEM, separately, within 42 days of vaccination. The secondary objective is to assess the risk of new-onset AF within 8 days of vaccination. We provide the rationale for study design decisions.

We acknowledge Akkodis Belgium for editorial assistance, manuscript coordination and design support on behalf of GSK. The authors thank Laura Shockro, Nina DiNunzio, Vaibhav Sharma and Victoria Boon for their project management support. The authors also thank Meredith Brisco-Bacik, Armina Omole and Tara DiMino for assistance in defining the GBS, ADEM and AF case-finding algorithms; Heidi Bailly, Terese DeFor and Laura Grangaard Johnson for their project and data support; and Smita Bhatia and Darshana Jaiswal for their analytical support.
sections.methods:
This study will be conducted using administrative claims data and electronic health records provided by three US-based national insurers (Elevance Health/Carelon Research, CVS Health, Humana) and two regional insurers (HealthPartners, Point32Health) participating in the US FDA’s Sentinel System at the time of protocol development. These sites currently contribute longitudinal data from medically attended healthcare encounters for approximately 17 million privately insured adults aged ≥50 years. Available data include demographics; diagnoses and procedures recorded in inpatient, ambulatory or institutional care settings; outpatient pharmacy dispensings; and immunisations via procedures for administration in ambulatory settings, pharmacy dispensations and some state-based registries. Data will be transformed to the Sentinel Common Data Model, enabling the execution of standardised analytical programmes in a distributed research environment where patient data remain behind institutional firewalls., Analytical datasets will be returned to Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute (HPHCI), the study coordinating centre. The study protocol and statistical analysis plan have been reviewed by the FDA. The full protocol is registered in the Heads of Medicines Agencies–European Medicines Agency Real World Data Catalogues (EUPAS1000000486).

This study will use a self-controlled risk interval (SCRI) design, a type of self-controlled case series where only vaccinees with outcomes occurring in prespecified intervals of postvaccination risk and control windows contribute to the analysis. This design is suitable for transient exposures, such as vaccinations, and acute outcomes, such as GBS, ADEM and AF. The SCRI design has two main advantages for vaccine safety research: (1) confounding by known and unknown factors that are stable over time is automatically controlled by the self-matched design, and (2) restriction of the analytical population to vaccinated cases over a predefined short observation period makes the process of chart review for adjudication of outcomes efficient in terms of resources.

The study population will include research-eligible adults aged ≥50 years with evidence of receipt of a single dose of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 between 1 August 2023, when the vaccine was first available in the USA, and 30 June 2030, the planned end date of data collection. Vaccination with adjuvanted RSVPreF3 will be identified by National Drug Codes (58160-848-11, 58160-723-03, 58160-744-03), Current Procedural Terminology code (90679) or vaccine administration code (CVX 303).

The index date will be the date of the vaccination. Vaccinees will be required to have ≥365 days of continuous medical and prescription drug benefits prior to index (enrolment gaps ≤45 days within the 365 days are permitted), no evidence of a second dose of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 throughout the risk and control windows, or other products used for RSV disease prevention, such as Pfizer’s RSVPreF ( Abrysvo ) or Moderna’s modified mRNA RSVPreF ( MRESVIA ) vaccinations, at any time prior to the index date or throughout the risk and control windows. Individuals with evidence of a second dose of adjuvanted RSVPreF3 within 7 days of the index date will not be excluded as this is expected to be an administrative error and not a true second dose. Individuals will be required to have continuous enrolment in the same health plan, without any gaps, for the duration of 91 days (GBS, ADEM) or 106 days (AF) after the index date (, ) for identification of outcomes. The postindex enrolment window for each outcome reflects the outcome identification period that includes risk, control and extra days for GBS and ADEM outcomes. The AF algorithm requires ≥1 inpatient diagnosis or ≥2 outpatient or emergency department diagnoses at least 7 days apart, within 90 days of first AF diagnosis. The postindex enrolment window for the AF analysis reflects the maximum time to the second diagnosis code (106 days). An exception to the postindex continuous enrolment requirement will be made when there is evidence of death during the observation window. In the SCRI design, deaths may only occur after the event of interest (GBS or ADEM or AF), as the analytical cohort comprises vaccinated cases. Artificially extending enrolment for vaccinated cases with deaths in the observation window allows for inclusion of all outcomes in the analysis, including those who may lack postindex enrolment because of death. The number of deaths occurring during the observation window will be described. Potential cases will be deemed new onset if the diagnosis in the observation window is the first within 365 days.

The algorithms to identify the outcomes using International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM) diagnosis codes and the corresponding risk windows, control windows and extra days are summarised in .

GBS and ADEM will be defined either as an inpatient encounter with a principal discharge diagnosis or any ambulatory/emergency care encounter with a subsequent inpatient encounter with a principal discharge diagnosis within 7 days occurring in the 91 days after vaccination (1–42: risk window; 43–84: control window; 85–91: extra days). The claims-based event date for GBS and ADEM will be set to the date of the hospitalisation in the former and to the date of the ambulatory/emergency care encounter in the latter, reflecting the continuity between related encounters. The claims-based algorithm to identify GBS has been previously evaluated in US Medicare beneficiaries, yielding positive predictive values (PPVs) between 68% and 79%., The ADEM algorithm has not been evaluated. Medical records of all potential GBS and ADEM cases identified in claims will be requested and adjudicated. The primary analyses for GBS and ADEM will include chart-confirmed cases with an adjudicated date of symptom onset. The chart-based event date for confirmed cases of GBS and ADEM will be the date of symptom onset. In practice, cases with symptom onset near the end of the control window may present with coded diagnoses identified in claims data up to 7 days after the end of the control window. An administrative buffer period or extra days (ie, days 85–91) allows for the identification of such cases. The primary analysis will only include chart-confirmed cases with event dates in risk (1–42) and control (43–84) windows. The 42-day risk window in the primary analysis of GBS has precedence in the literature. Given that ADEM is also a neurological inflammatory disease, we will use the same windows as for GBS. Shorter risk windows are proposed in sensitivity analyses in response to timing of events in unpublished postmarketing safety reports submitted to the sponsor (1–21 days) and clustering of outcomes in an analysis of RSV vaccine safety using Medicare data (8–28 days).

AF will be defined as ≥1 inpatient diagnosis (any position) or ≥2 diagnoses in the ambulatory or emergency care settings that are 7–90 days apart. The claims-based event date for AF will be set to the date of the hospitalisation or the earliest of the two outpatient encounters. Algorithms for AF have been reported to have PPVs ranging from 67% to 76%. Given the prevalence of AF, we will perform a validation of the algorithm in study data sources against medical records as a reference standard after the first annual monitoring study. The primary analysis for AF will use 8-day risk and control windows. The 8-day risk window for AF was chosen on the basis of timing of new-onset events in unpublished postmarketing safety reports submitted to the sponsor indicating a time to onset of 3–8 days.

We will request medical records for all potential cases of GBS and ADEM identified via claims-based monitoring analyses to validate their case status based on criteria from the Brighton Collaboration (). Records for the hospitalisation with GBS and ADEM as the primary discharge diagnoses and the first encounter with a neurologist or primary care clinician within 30 days of discharge will be requested. Two clinicians, preferably neurologists, will independently review each case to classify them as definite (Brighton levels of diagnostic certainty 1–3), possible (level 4) or not a case (level 5) with any disagreements arbitrated by a third neurologist. All adjudicators will be blinded to the date of vaccination with adjuvanted RSVPreF3. The date of symptom onset will be recorded by the clinicians, and cases will be reattributed to the risk or control window accordingly. Only chart-confirmed cases with symptom onset in either the risk or control windows will be included in the primary analysis.

The claims-based algorithm to identify new-onset AF will be validated using medical records as the reference standard. Medical records from a random sample of claims-based cases from one to two participating sites will be reviewed by cardiologists. We will target a sample of 63 adjudicated cases, assuming a PPV of ≥80% and width of the 95% CI of ±10%. Chart validation results will be used to estimate the algorithm’s PPV. We set an a priori threshold of 80% to mitigate significant outcome misclassification, meaning that the inferential analysis will either be based on all claims-identified cases (PPV≥80%) or chart-confirmed cases alone (PPV<80%). If the PPV is <80%, we will request additional charts to meet the minimum necessary 69 confirmed cases for an inferential analysis (). Claims-based analyses for new-onset AF will use the estimated PPV of the algorithm (≥80%) in a bias analysis to correct for outcome misclassification.

We will describe demographic characteristics on the index date and clinical characteristics in the 365 days prior to the index date overall and among those with evidence of the outcomes. provides a list of the characteristics and their conceptual definitions. Factors that might precipitate the outcomes of interest such as infections or immunocompromising conditions will be described within relevant periods in addition to other vaccines received on the index date. Immunocompromising conditions include haematological malignancy and related conditions, HIV infection, multiple sclerosis, rheumatological/inflammatory conditions, solid malignancy, solid organ or stem cell transplantation, systemic lupus erythematosus and other immune disorders defined on the presence of at least one ICD-10-CM diagnosis code in any care setting. Multiple sclerosis and systemic lupus erythematosus further require evidence of treatment defined as at least one dispensing of a medication used to manage these conditions. These data will offer context for interpretation of findings and help identify potential areas for future investigation. The list of precipitating factors for each outcome was curated with feedback from clinicians and US FDA representatives who participated in the review of the study protocol.

Annual monitoring queries will be cumulative and descriptive, reporting the uptake of adjuvanted RSVPreF3, characterising vaccinees and identifying potential cases of new-onset GBS, ADEM and AF after vaccination via claims data.

Inferential analyses will be triggered on accrual of 69 chart-confirmed GBS cases, 12 chart-confirmed ADEM cases and 63 adjudicated or 69 (if PPV<80%) confirmed AF cases during pertinent primary observation windows. Our sample size calculations () support these minimum necessary numbers of vaccinated cases to detect a twofold increase in risk of GBS or AF, or a sevenfold increase in risk of ADEM, during the risk windows with 80% power using a two-sided alpha of 0.05.

Data will be aggregated across participating sites, and conditional Poisson regression will be used to estimate the incidence rate ratio (IRR) of each outcome during the risk window relative to the control window. Attributable or excess risks of each outcome per 100 000 vaccinees will be estimated by multiplying the difference between incidence rates in risk and control windows with the length of the pertinent risk window, an approach that has been previously used with SCRI design. This approach for approximating the absolute risk in vaccine safety research conducted using self-controlled designs has been criticised for failing to incorporate the risk among those who are unvaccinated in the population. We will interpret our estimate as the excess risk attributable to the vaccine among the vaccinated. Such measures are relevant for public health agencies conducting benefit-risk assessments to inform decisions regarding any potential safety communication.

The duration of potential increased risks for rare outcomes following vaccination cannot be reliably assessed through clinical trials and may only become apparent when a larger population is exposed to the vaccine. Therefore, one set of sensitivity analyses will include varying definitions of risk and control windows for all study outcomes. For GBS and ADEM, we will use risk windows of days 1–21 and days 8–28, both with control windows of days 43–84. For AF, we will evaluate risk and control windows of days 1–28 and 29–56, respectively, as well as days 1–3 and 4–8, respectively.

A second set of sensitivity analyses will control for any potential time-varying confounding by season in analyses of GBS and AF brought about by seasonal administration of the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and variation in the incidence of outcomes such as GBS and AF. A prior analysis showed no evidence of seasonal variation in the incidence of GBS or ADEM and some evidence of seasonality for AF. However, since infections can sometimes trigger GBS, it is hypothesised that the incidence of GBS may also be seasonal. These sensitivity analyses will use person-level offset terms generated using background rates of GBS and AF from participating sites, a method used in prior vaccine safety research.

In practice, requests for medical charts may be denied or go unanswered. We anticipate that our chart retrieval rates will be <100% and will conduct sensitivity analyses including chart-confirmed and unobtainable cases for all study outcomes. Separately, given variation in clinical presentations of cases, sensitivity analyses for all study outcomes will include cases adjudicated as confirmed or possible during medical record review. Additionally, if the PPV of the AF algorithm is ≥80%, we will perform a bias analysis correcting for outcome misclassification bias.

Lastly, individuals with immunocompromising conditions () may have a different baseline risk for GBS and ADEM than those without such conditions regardless of the vaccination status. A sensitivity analysis will exclude these individuals.
sections.discussion:
We summarised the design for a postmarketing safety study evaluating the association between the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and new-onset GBS, ADEM and AF. We provided rationale for our choices of the use of the SCRI design, windows for observing new-onset outcomes and methods to improve confidence in ascertainment of vaccine-related safety outcomes of interest within administrative claims data. Due to the rarity of GBS and ADEM, we anticipate that it will take several years for this safety study to accrue sufficient data to provide conclusive evidence on the association between the vaccine and these outcomes.

The labels for adjuvanted RSVPreF3 and RSVPreF vaccines were recently updated with safety information regarding a potential increase in risk of GBS in the 42 days after vaccination following findings from a separate postmarketing active surveillance study conducted by the FDA’s Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research. This self-controlled case series analysis included >3.2 million Medicare beneficiaries aged ≥65 years who were vaccinated with adjuvanted RSVPreF3 or RSVPreF by the end of the 2023–2024 respiratory virus season. There were 95 new-onset GBS outcomes identified using claims data, of which 75 were adjudicated in a medical record review and 51 were confirmed diagnoses. The study reported an excess risk of 6.5 cases of GBS per 1 million individuals vaccinated with adjuvanted RSVPreF3 in the 42 days after vaccination (IRR 2.46; 95% CI 1.19 to 5.08) and an excess of nine cases of GBS per 1 million individuals vaccinated with RSVPreF (IRR 2.02; 95% CI 0.93 to 4.40). For reference, the excess risk of GBS typically attributed to select seasonal influenza vaccinations is between one and two per million vaccinated individuals. Continued investigation is necessary to form a conclusive base of evidence.

Our study has a number of important strengths. We will include large study samples of nationally representative and diverse populations of privately insured older adults and control for known and unknown confounding factors stable over time by virtue of our self-matched design. We will identify chart-confirmed cases of GBS and ADEM adjudicated by two clinicians, preferably neurologists, and we will develop and validate a case-finding algorithm for AF within our data sources. Finally, sensitivity analyses will assess the robustness of the primary results.

With respect to limitations, we do not expect that medical records will be obtainable for all cases of GBS and ADEM identified in claims data, though we do not anticipate systematic differences in the ability to retrieve charts for cases observed in risk versus control windows. While the primary analysis is restricted to chart-confirmed cases, sensitivity analyses will include those with unobtainable charts. We may be limited in our ability to investigate joint effects of concomitantly administered vaccinations depending on the number of outcomes we observe. Our primary analysis evaluating the risk of new-onset AF uses 8-day risk and control windows. Typically, vaccine safety studies account for potential day-of-the-week effects by using risk and control windows that are multiples of 7; however, we chose 8-day intervals under guidance from various stakeholders based on evidence to date regarding postvaccination AF onset, balancing the risks between potential day-of-the-week effects and misspecification of risk window.

The availability of three licensed vaccines for RSV represents an important scientific discovery that was decades in the making. Randomised controlled clinical trials demonstrated efficacy with an acceptable reactogenicity and safety profile for these vaccines. Given that clinical trials are not statistically powered to detect meaningful increases in the risk of rare events, active postmarketing safety surveillance studies such as the one described in this paper are necessary. This study is expected to generate rigorous evidence with adequate power on the safety of the adjuvanted RSVPreF3 vaccine to inform the benefit-risk assessment and support individual decisions on vaccination.

This non-interventional safety study is a regulatory postmarketing requirement requested by the US FDA. Patients and members of the public were not involved in the conceptualisation or design of this study. There is no primary data collection in this study and, therefore, no patient involvement in defining the research questions, selecting outcomes or plans for dissemination.

This study was approved by the HPHCI Institutional Review Board (IRB), Federal Wide Assurance (FWA) FWA00000100; the WIRB-Copernicus Group, Inc and its affiliates (collectively, ‘WCG’), WCG IRB, Inc, FWA00033319 for Carelon Research; and Sterling IRB, FWA00025632 for CVS Health. HealthPartners Institute, Humana Healthcare Research, Inc and Rutgers University have ceded IRB review to HPHCI.

Study results will be shared with the US FDA and publicly disseminated through national or international clinical or scientific conferences and peer-reviewed publications.

title: Maternal Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F Vaccination and Acute Respiratory Illness in Infants.
abstract: Importance The bivalent respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F (RSVpreF) vaccine was licensed in the US in September 2023 to prevent RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) in infants via maternal immunization. Clinical data on vaccine effectiveness are limited. Objective To estimate the effectiveness of maternal RSVpreF vaccination against hospitalization for RSV-associated acute respiratory illness (ARI) and LRTD among infants 90 days or younger during the first 2 postlicensure RSV seasons. Design, setting, and participants This retrospective case-control study (Effectiveness of ABRYSVO Maternal Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine Against RSV in Infants in Western Pennsylvania study) using a test-negative design was conducted within a single health system in western Pennsylvania during the 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 RSV seasons. The analysis included infants 90 days or younger born between October 1, 2023, and April 15, 2024, or between September 1, 2024, and April 30, 2025, who were hospitalized with ARI and tested for RSV using nucleic acid amplification or rapid antigen testing. Exposure Maternal RSVpreF vaccination administered at gestational age between 32 weeks 0 to 7 days and 36 weeks 6 to 7 days and at least 14 days before delivery. Main outcomes and measures The primary outcome was RSV-associated ARI requiring hospitalization. The secondary outcome was RSV-associated LRTD requiring hospitalization. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated as (1 - Adjusted Odds Ratio) × 100% comparing the odds of maternal RSVpreF vaccination among RSV-positive infants (cases) vs RSV-negative infants (controls) using multivariable logistic regression. Results Among 274 included infants (83 with RSV and 191 controls), the mean (SD) age at admission was 29.5 (21.1) days; 143 infants (52.2%) were male. Among these, 11 of 83 infants with RSV (13.3%) and 71 of 191 controls (37.2%) were born to RSVpreF-vaccinated individuals. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated to be 67.6% (95% CI, 33.2%-85.4%) against RSV-associated ARI hospitalization and 69.0% (95% CI, 25.5%-88.0%) against RSV-associated LRTD hospitalization from 0 through 90 days of age. Among infants aged 0 to 30 days, vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated ARI hospitalization was estimated to be 74.2% (95% CI, 25.4%-93.0%). Conclusions and relevance Maternal RSVpreF vaccination was associated with protection against RSV-associated ARI and LRTD hospitalization among infants 90 days or younger. These findings provide early clinical evidence supporting the effectiveness of maternal RSVpreF vaccination in preventing RSV-associated hospitalization in infants.

sections.other:
Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of lower respiratory tract disease (LRTD) in infants worldwide. , Annually, RSV causes an estimated 33 million LRTD cases globally, including 3.6 million hospitalizations and 100 000 deaths in children younger than 5 years. Nearly half of these hospitalizations occur in children younger than 6 months, of whom the majority were previously healthy. , In the US, 24 per 1000 infants younger than 3 months are hospitalized with an RSV-associated illness.

In August 2023, the US Food and Drug Administration approved a bivalent RSV prefusion F (RSVpreF) protein-based vaccine that protects against both RSV-A and RSV-B for prevention of RSV-associated LRTD and severe LRTD in infants from birth through 6 months of age via immunization of pregnant individuals at gestational age between 32 weeks 0 to 7 days and 36 weeks 6 to 7 days. , Among infants aged 0 to 90 days, the pivotal phase 3 randomized clinical trial of vaccination at gestational age between 24 weeks 0 to 7 days and 36 weeks 6 to 7 days demonstrated efficacy against RSV-associated medically attended LRTD (57.6%; 95% CI, 31.3%-74.6%) and severe LRTD (82.4%; 95% CI, 57.5%-93.9%). Additionally, RSVpreF was efficacious against RSV-associated hospitalization (69.7%; 95% CI, 37.1%-86.7%) for infants aged 0 to 90 days.

Vaccine effectiveness studies evaluating RSVpreF in clinical populations using patient-centered outcomes are needed. The Effectiveness of ABRYSVO Maternal Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine Against RSV in Infants in Western Pennsylvania (CASSATT) study is a 4-year study evaluating the effectiveness of maternal RSVpreF vaccination against hospitalization for RSV-associated acute respiratory illness (primary outcome) and LRTD (secondary outcome) in infants. In this planned interim analysis, we report estimated vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated ARI and LRTD hospitalization of infants from 0 to 90 days of age and RSV-associated ARI hospitalization from 0 to 30 days of age during the first 2 US seasons of RSVpreF implementation. Vaccine effectiveness through 180 days of age will be analyzed once sufficient data for statistical power are available from additional seasons.
sections.methods:
We conducted a retrospective case-control study with a test-negative design (TND), a well-established approach for estimating vaccine effectiveness while minimizing bias related to health care–seeking behavior. The study used routinely collected electronic health record (EHR) data from the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center (UPMC), a semiclosed health system in western Pennsylvania. The source population consisted of infants delivered at 2 UPMC birth hospitals with records linked to the maternal birth parent’s EHR and who were subsequently hospitalized at 1 of 2 urban pediatric hospitals.

The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the University of Pittsburgh Institutional Review Board under a waiver of informed consent, as it was determined to be minimal risk and could not be practicably completed without the waiver. We followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guideline. The study protocol was registered previously.

Infants admitted to the hospital based on clinical criteria meeting the protocol-defined ARI case definition were evaluated for inclusion. Infants had to be born at gestational age 32 weeks or greater from October 1, 2023, to April 15, 2024, or September 1, 2024, to April 30, 2025, to individuals expected (based on their estimated date of delivery) to reach the licensed RSVpreF vaccination window (gestational age 32 weeks 0-7 days to 36 weeks 6-7 days) during the local vaccination season. Infants aged 0 to 90 days at hospitalization from October 1, 2023 to April 15, 2024, or October 15, 2024, to April 30, 2025, and with RSV testing results available from a specimen collected 10 days before through 3 days after hospital admission were eligible for inclusion.

Infants were excluded if they received an RSV monoclonal antibody, were born to an individual who received any RSV vaccine other than RSVpreF (licensed or investigational), or had unverified maternal RSVpreF vaccination status. Additionally, a post hoc exclusion of 1 randomly selected infant from each of 3 hospitalized twin pairs was applied to avoid intrapair correlation.

Structured demographic, clinical, laboratory, diagnostic, and immunization data were obtained from April 1, 2023, through April 30, 2025, through EHR platforms. , Additional clinical variables related to the ARI hospitalization were double abstracted from the EHR and entered into REDCap by trained staff. Maternal vaccination status was verified using EHR data and the Pennsylvania Immunization Electronic Registry System. Structured and unstructured data were reviewed for missingness and outliers and then manually reviewed for data completeness and accuracy. All data quality checks and changes were dated and documented for transparency.

Infants born to individuals with documented RSVpreF vaccination between gestational age 32 weeks 0 to 7 days and 36 weeks 6 to 7 days and at least 14 days prior to delivery were classified as exposed. Infants born to individuals who did not receive RSVpreF during pregnancy and who did not receive nirsevimab or any other RSV preventive agent prior to illness were classified as unexposed.

The primary outcome was RSV-associated ARI hospitalization among infants aged 0 to 90 days, where ARI was defined as 2 or more ARI symptoms (cough, congestion, rhinorrhea, documented fever [≥38.0 °C] or hypothermia [<36.5 °C], apnea, or lethargy) or 1 or more ARI symptoms and any other respiratory symptoms of concern (eg, respiratory rate ≥60 breaths/min, accessory muscle use, oxygen saturation <95%, or respiratory support above baseline) within the first 48 hours of the medical encounter, and onset or worsening of symptoms within 10 days prior to hospitalization. The secondary outcome was RSV-associated LRTD hospitalization among infants aged 0 to 90 days. LRTD was defined as ARI with oxygen saturation less than 95%, oxygen or noninvasive ventilation support, or intubation for 1 hour or more within the first 48 hours of the medical encounter to evaluate vaccine effectiveness against disease of higher clinical severity. RSV-associated ARI hospitalization among infants from 0 to 30 days of age was an exploratory outcome.

In addition, infants were required to have had RSV testing of a respiratory specimen collected from 10 days before through 3 days after hospital admission. Infants positive for RSV by any test were classified as cases; controls had to be negative for RSV on results of nucleic acid amplification testing. In sensitivity analyses, cases were restricted to infants with a positive nucleic acid amplification RSV test result.

For the primary outcome, sample size to achieve 90% power with a lower-bound 95% CI of greater than 20% and with a 2-sided α level of 5% was calculated a priori assuming 70% to 75% vaccine effectiveness and under varying RSVpreF uptake assumptions and case-to-control ratios. Actual RSVpreF uptake among control infants was approximately 40%, and the case-to-control ratio was 1:2.3, which indicated a requirement of 80 to 102 infants with RSV and 160 to 203 controls.

We computed crude odds ratios (ORs) using univariable logistic regression models with infant case-control status as the dependent variable and maternal RSVpreF vaccination as the exposure. Adjusted ORs (AORs) for the primary and secondary outcomes were estimated using multivariable logistic regression, and vaccine effectiveness was calculated as (1 – AOR) × 100%. Covariates were selected a priori based on a directed acyclic graph (DAG) constructed to identify minimal sufficient adjustment sets following recommended criteria (eFigure in ). ,, This approach explicitly delineates potential confounding pathways and informs inclusion of covariates that causally influence both vaccination and infant outcomes.

Maternal age at delivery was considered a continuous variable. Maternal race and ethnicity werebased on recorded race in the EHR at time of delivery; race was categorized as Asian, Black, White, or other (including Other Pacific Islander or other race) and ethnicity was categorized as Hispanic or non-Hispanic. Infant race and ethnicity included the same categories as well as unspecified, unknown, and declined to answer. Maternal area deprivation index (ADI) is a continuous, validated measure (range, 1-100) of neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage based on income, educational level, employment status, and quality of housing. It was categorized into quartiles for descriptive tables (eTable 1 in ), where the higher quartile indicates the highest level of deprivation, but modeled as a continuous variable. Calendar time was included as a continuous variable (conception days) representing days from January 1 of the corresponding year to the estimated date of conception, which was calculated based on date of delivery and documented weeks of gestational age at delivery. Fetal congenital anomalies were defined by maternal codes diagnosed during pregnancy from International Statistical Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision ( ICD-10 ) (eTable 2 in ), as these reflect conditions known during pregnancy that could influence vaccination decisions. Identification of 1 or more siblings was based on maternal parity at delivery. Other DAG covariates included gestational age at birth (in days), type of maternal health insurance at delivery (medical assistance, private, or self-pay), multifetal gestation (singleton vs multiparous), maternal asthma based on ICD-10 codes, and prenatal use of health care services (<4 vs ≥4 encounters) based on documented encounters or clinician assessment at delivery. Baseline characteristics were described for infants with RSV and controls with inclusion of standardized mean differences to summarize the magnitude of between-group differences.

We used the predictive mean matching method to impute missing values for the ADI variable, which was the only variable in our dataset with missingness (5.5%). We constructed an imputed dataset, using the multivariable imputation by chained equation (MICE) package in R, version 4.4.2 (R Project for Statistical Computing) for downstream analyses. All reported estimates were based on analysis conducted on this imputed dataset.

After developing the DAG-informed outcome models, we conducted a backward change-in-estimate variable selection. Maternal age, race, ADI, and conception days were forced into all adjusted models. All other covariates were removed sequentially unless their removal changed the estimated association with maternal RSVpreF vaccination by at least 10%. We evaluated potential effect measure modification using interaction terms (ie, maternal age, race, parity, ADI, conception days, and fetal anomalies); however, no significant interactions were identified. All statistical analyses were conducted in R, version 4.4.2.

Prespecified subgroup analyses of the primary outcome included (1) time from vaccination to birth (14-27 vs ≥28 days); (2) gestational age at vaccination (32-33 vs 34-36 weeks); (3) infant risk status (high vs low) for severe RSV (including preterm birth, chronic lung diseases, congenital heart diseases, and complex medical conditions); and (4) infants born term vs preterm. Prespecified sensitivity analyses of the primary outcome included (1) excluding infants with positive test results for human metapneumovirus or other vaccine-preventable respiratory viruses (eg, influenza, COVID-19) from the control group; (2) including infants who were born to individuals who received the RSVpreF vaccine less than 14 days before delivery in the exposed group; (3) including infants born to individuals who received RSVpreF before gestational age 32 weeks 0 to 7 days or after gestational age 36 weeks 6 to 7 days; and (4) excluding infants with antigen-tested RSV positivity.
sections.results:
Among 13 775 infants in the study, 274 were hospitalized at or before 90 days of age with ARI and met all study inclusion criteria (). The mean (SD) age at admission was 29.5 (21.1) days; 131 (47.8%) were female, 143 (52.2%) were male, and 127 (46.4%) had medical assistance (). In terms of race, 6 infants (2.2%) were Asian, 37 (13.5%) were Black, 171 (62.4%) were White, 4 (1.5%) were of other race, and 56 (20.4%) were of unknown race or declined to answer; in terms of ethnicity, 10 infants (3.6%) were Hispanic, 182 (66.4%) were non-Hispanic, and 82 (29.9%) were of unspecified ethnicity or declined to answer. The mean (SD) gestational age at birth was 38.3 (1.5) weeks (range, 34-41 weeks) across all groups; 44 infants (16.1%) were born between gestational age 34 weeks 0 to 7 days and 36 weeks 6 to 7 days 35 (12.8%) were identified as having a pre-existing complex medical condition at admission, and 14 (5.1%) were from a multifetal gestation ().

Eighty-three of 274 infants (30.3%) had positive test results for RSV (cases) and 191 (69.7%) had negative results (controls) ). Infants with RSV were more frequently born between October and December (61 of 83 [73.5%] vs 80 of 191 [41.9%]), preterm (18 of 83 [21.7%] vs 26 of 191 [13.6%]), male (47 of 83 [56.6%] vs 96 of 191 [50.3%]), had 1 or more siblings (69 of 83 [83.1%] vs 114 of 191 [59.7%]), were Black (16 of 83 [19.3%] vs 21 of 191 [11.0%]), and were in the highest ADI quartile (25 of 83 [30.1%] vs 34 of 191 [17.8%]), indicating higher deprivation. Hospital admission in December and January occurred in 50 of 83 case infants with RSV (60.2%) and 58 of 191 control infants (30.4%).

Among 83 case infants with RSV, 72 (86.7%) had LRTD, 28 (33.7%) required intensive care unit admission, 56 (67.5%) required supplemental oxygen or respiratory support, and no deaths occurred (eTable 3 in ). Among 191 control infants, 87 (45.5%) had LRTD, 33 (17.3%) required intensive care unit admission, 40 (20.9%) required supplemental oxygen or respiratory support, and 2 deaths occurred (1.0%) (eTable 3 in ).

Overall, 82 of 274 infants (29.9%) were born to a parent vaccinated with RSVpreF during pregnancy, including 11 of 83 case infants with RSV (13.3%) and 71 of 191 controls infants (37.2%) (). Characteristics among infants with RSVpreF with vaccinated and unvaccinated parents are summarized in eTable 4 in .

The estimated effectiveness of RSVpreF vaccination during pregnancy against RSV-associated ARI hospitalization among infants aged 0 to 90 days was 67.6% (95% CI, 33.2%-85.4%) (). Sensitivity analysis of the primary outcome, which included infants of parents who received RSVpreF vaccine less than 14 days before delivery (n = 14) showed an estimated effectiveness of 64.3% (95% CI, 30.2%-82.6%) (eTable 5 in ). Conversely, after excluding control infants who tested positive for human metapneumovirus or vaccine-preventable respiratory viruses (n = 20), estimated effectiveness increased to 73.7% (95% CI, 45.4%-88.2%). Other prespecified sensitivity analyses were consistent with results of the main analysis.

Similar estimated effectiveness was observed against RSV-associated LRTD hospitalization for infants aged 0 to 90 days (69.0%; 95% CI, 25.5%-88.0%) (). Among infants aged 0 to 30 days, estimated effectiveness against RSV-associated ARI hospitalization was 74.2% (95% CI, 25.4%-93.0%) ().

The results for subgroup analyses were consistent with those for the primary analysis; however, group sample sizes were small, resulting in wide 95% CIs (). Generally, vaccine effectiveness estimates were lower for infants born to individuals vaccinated between 14 and 28 days prior to delivery (compared with those born to individuals vaccinated ≥28 days prior to delivery), infants born preterm (vs full-term), and infants at lower risk for severe RSV (vs those with clinical risk factors) ().
sections.discussion:
This study provides early clinical evidence from the US demonstrating that RSVpreF vaccination during pregnancy may provide protection against RSV-associated ARI hospitalization in infants 90 days or younger, when most RSV-associated hospitalizations occur. The estimates of vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated ARI hospitalization in this study is consistent with those from a pivotal clinical trial, population-based surveillance studies, and other case-control studies ,, ; however, the 95% CIs were wide, and the findings should be interpreted with appropriate caution. These findings were identified in the context of a rigorous epidemiologic approach including a TND to minimize confounding by health care–seeking behavior, careful EHR validation to reduce misclassification bias, and multivariable modeling with covariate selection guided by a DAG to strengthen causal inference. These methodologic strengths combined with the protection identified in a generalizable population support the clinical effectiveness of maternal RSVpreF vaccination in preventing RSV-associated hospitalization among young infants.

Our results align closely with those from the phase 3 RSVpreF randomized clinical trial, which demonstrated efficacy against RSV-associated hospitalization of 69.7% (95% CI, 37.1%-86.7%) among infants 90 days or younger. In our study, vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated ARI hospitalization in this age-group was 67.6% (95% CI, 33.2%-85.4%), with similar estimates observed for RSV-associated LRTD hospitalization. This indicates alignment in the magnitude of effect during early infancy when maternal antibody-meditated protection is expected to be greatest. Other clinical studies have reported similar point estimates , ; several also report outcomes over broader age ranges. , Two large US surveillance networks , reported RSVpreF vaccine effectiveness estimates between 70% and 79% against RSV-associated hospitalization among infants 6 months or younger. Studies from Argentina and Scotland have estimated vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated LRTD hospitalization to be between 71% and 82%, respectively, in analyses restricted to the first 3 months of age. Differences in study populations and design—including use of multisite active and passive surveillance data vs identification of eligible case and control infants among those receiving care within an integrated health system—may influence comparability across studies. Importantly, our study includes infants born preterm, with comorbidities, or from multiple gestations, highlighting the broad utility of maternal RSV vaccination in protecting infants against severe RSV-associated outcomes. While the relatively smaller sample size included in this first analysis from CASSATT resulted in wider 95% CIs, the consistency of point estimates across randomized and clinical studies supports a similar magnitude of protection during early infancy.

Importantly, the CASSATT study reflects clinical US implementation, where vaccination is recommended from a gestational age of 32 to 36 weeks. This later, narrower window allows less time for transplacental antibody transfer than the 24- to 36-week window used in the clinical trial, yet yielded comparable protection. Data from settings with earlier vaccination and larger sample sizes are needed to determine whether earlier vaccination improves effectiveness or duration of infant protection. For example, in Scotland, where vaccination is recommended from gestational age 28 weeks, vaccine effectiveness against RSV-associated LRTD hospitalization was 82.2% among infants 90 days or younger. Although the analysis was not adequately powered for subgroup analyses, vaccine effectiveness estimates trended lower when delivery occurred closer to vaccination (14-27 days) and among preterm infants. These findings are consistent with the biological plausibility that vaccination earlier in gestation (and therefore increased time between vaccination and delivery) may result in higher transplacental antibody transfer, which could in turn lead to higher vaccine effectiveness or longer duration of protection in infants, as observed with tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccine. ,, As postmarketing safety data continue to accrue, modest expansion of the recommended vaccination window in the US to include earlier vaccination in pregnancy may optimize protection against RSV for infants born to vaccinated mothers.

This study has some limitations. As an observational study, residual confounding and possible vaccination misclassification cannot be fully excluded. Vaccination during pregnancy may reflect access to and use of health care services, with potential differences in care-seeking influencing outcome ascertainment. In our cohort, RSV cases had slightly more markers of limited access (eg, self-pay, fewer prenatal visits). Although our integrated health system mitigates incomplete capture, residual bias may remain. While the sample size was sufficient for the primary analysis, the number of vaccinated cases contributing to the primary outcome and to the subgroup estimates was small, which limits the precision of the vaccine effectiveness estimate and is reflected in the wide 95% CIs.

In this case-control study of infants 90 days or younger using a TND, we found clinical evidence suggesting that maternal RSVpreF vaccination during pregnancy was effective in preventing RSV-associated ARI and LRTD hospitalization in young infants, complementing data from clinical trials and other clinical observational studies from the US and elsewhere. Continued data collection across subsequent RSV seasons and larger and more diverse settings will be critical to refine vaccine effectiveness estimates, evaluate the durability of protection, and inform policy decisions regarding the optimal implementation of maternal RSVpreF vaccination programs.
