sections.results:
To stabilize the metastable pre-F conformation of hMPV F, we performed a structure-guided screen focusing on three design strategies: local sequence replacement in the F1 N-terminal/fusion peptide-proximal region, disulfide-bond engineering in regions undergoing rearrangement during the pre-F-to-post-F transition, and optimization of potential interprotomer electrostatic interactions. All substitutions were introduced into a base construct comprising hMPV F A2 residues 1–489 (A). In total, 15 variants were designed, expressed, and characterized. Preservation of the pre-F antigenic surface was monitored via ELISA using the MPE8 antibody, a cross-reactive antibody targeting RSV-F and hMPV-F that preferentially recognizes the pre-F conformation.

ELISA screening in transiently transfected HEK293T cells revealed increased expression for seven disulfide variants relative to wild-type F (WT-F), including L378C/G432C, A140C/S149C, S65C/D183C, T127C/N153C, D54C/S265C, L66C/V191C, and S293C/S444C (B). To determine whether these improvements were maintained in a scalable expression system, the top-performing variants were further evaluated in suspension-adapted 293F cells. A140C/S149C showed a stronger expression-enhancing effect than the previously reported A140C/A147C pair (), whereas L378C/G432C provided greater thermal stabilization than T365C/V463C (). These results indicate that disulfide bonds introduced into regions involved in the pre-F-to-post-F transition can stabilize hMPV F through distinct effects on expression and thermal stability.

We next examined whether stabilization could be further improved by introducing additional substitutions at other sites. An alanine-to-aspartic acid substitution at position 225 (A225D) was introduced to potentially create a salt bridge with arginine 79 (R79) on a neighboring protomer, an interaction predicted to improve structural stability and expression (). Comparison of the pre-F structures of hMPV F and RSV F revealed substantial divergence in the region corresponding to hMPV F residues 103–113. Because this region is adjacent to the fusion peptide and central cavity of the pre-F trimer, hMPV F residues 103–113 were replaced with the spatially corresponding RSV F sequence to examine whether modifying local interactions in this area could affect pre-F conformational stability. Based on these results, we combined the most beneficial changes into a single construct. This yielded VM-874, which contains A140C/S149C, A225D, L378C/G432C, and the 103–113 sequence replacement (C–F). WT-F and VM-874 exhibited comparable overall conformational stability over the 500 ns simulation, whereas VM-874 showed reduced local flexibility around the replacement region (G, H). Antigenic profiling further showed that A140C/S149C, L378C/G432C, and VM-874 retained reactivity with antibodies targeting pre-F-associated antigenic sites on hMPV F. In contrast, these stabilized constructs showed reduced binding to antibody 34, a rabbit-derived monoclonal antibody specific for the post-F conformation, indicating decreased exposure of the post-F-associated epitope (I).

VM-874 was further constructed, purified, and evaluated for manufacturability (A). Relative to WT-F, VM-874 showed a 9.6-fold increase in expression in 293F cells (). Thermal stability analysis showed that VM-874 had a melting temperature (T m ) of 66 °C, representing a 13 °C increase over WT-F (B), which was consistent with improved thermal stability. Functional integrity was assessed by measuring binding to a panel of pre-F- and post-F-specific antibodies targeting distinct epitopes using biolayer interferometry (BLI). VM-874 showed robust binding to epitope-specific antibodies, including MPE8 (C), MPV414 (), ADI-61026, and 101F (), with low dissociation constants ( K D ) (). Predominance of the pre-F conformation was further supported by negative-stain electron microscopy and cryo-EM 2D classification ( and D). To further evaluate manufacturability, the binding of VM-874, v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C (pre-F comparator) (), and WT-F to pre-F-specific antibodies was compared after heat treatment at 65 °C or 70 °C for 30 min. After heat treatment at 65 °C for 30 min, WT-F and v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C showed changes consistent with degradation or conformational transition, accompanied by substantially reduced binding to the pre-F-specific antibodies MPE8 and ADI-61026 (E and ). In contrast, under the same conditions, VM-874 retained structural integrity and showed no apparent loss of binding to any of the antibodies tested, indicating preservation of key neutralizing epitopes under thermal stress. After storage at 4 °C for 7 or 21 days, the binding of antibodies to VM-874 remained unchanged (F and ), indicating sustained antigenicity during storage. Collectively, these results indicate that VM-874 exhibits improved manufacturability, combining enhanced expression in suspension-adapted 293F cells with increased thermal stability and favorable biophysical properties that are important for chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC) development.

The immunogenicity and protective efficacy of VM-874 were systematically evaluated in 6- to 8-week-old BALB/c mice (A). Mice were intramuscularly immunized with 5 μg of VM-874, post-F, or v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C formulated with 50 μg of aluminum hydroxide adjuvant, while control mice received adjuvant alone. A prime immunization was administered at week 0, followed by a booster immunization 3 weeks later. Serum samples were collected 2 weeks after the booster immunization for antibody analyses, and mice were subsequently challenged intranasally with 10 6 FFU of hMPV A2 to evaluate protective efficacy. Body weight was monitored daily after challenge (B).

Following booster immunization, serum IgG binding titers against both hMPV pre-F and post-F were significantly increased in the antigen-immunized groups relative to the adjuvant-only control group (C, D and ). Antibody functionality was further assessed by measuring serum neutralizing activity using a focus reduction neutralization test (FRNT 50 ). VM-874 elicited robust neutralizing responses against both hMPV A2 and B1 strains. Against hMPV A2, VM-874 induced a neutralizing titer (GMT: 713) that 7-fold higher than post-F (GMT: 99) and 1.9-fold higher than that of the previously reported optimized pre-F comparator v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C (GMT: 369), although no significant difference was observed between VM-874 and v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C (E and ). Against hMPV B1, VM-874 induced significantly higher neutralizing titers than post-F (GMT: 1020 vs. 79) and numerically higher neutralizing titers than v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C (GMT: 572), although no significant difference was observed between VM-874 and v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C (F).

Protective efficacy was then assessed in an hMPV A2 murine challenge model. Two weeks after the booster dose, all mice, including adjuvant-only controls, were challenged intranasally with 10 6 FFU of hMPV A2. Compared with the adjuvant-only group, the VM-874-immunized group showed significantly reduced infectious viral titers and viral RNA levels in lung homogenates (G and H). Consistent with previous reports in BALB/c hMPV challenge models, body weight declined after challenge in both immunized and control mice, with broadly comparable kinetics across groups (B). Histopathological analysis further showed that mice immunized with pre-F antigens, including VM-874 and v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C, exhibited attenuated inflammatory lung injury, as evidenced by reduced inflammatory cell infiltration and less pronounced alveolar septal thickening (I and J). Together, these findings indicate that VM-874 elicits protective immunity that limits viral replication and mitigates infection-associated lung pathology.

Cotton rats are among the most widely used and highly permissive rodent models for hMPV research (; ; ). This model is particularly well suited for simultaneously assessing viral replication in both the upper respiratory tract (nasal turbinates) and lower respiratory tract (lungs), as well as lung inflammation and the in vivo efficacy of preventive or therapeutic interventions. VM-874 was therefore further evaluated in cotton rats using a prime-boost immunization regimen followed by viral challenge, with body weight monitored daily after challenge (A and B). Cotton rats were intramuscularly immunized with 5 μg of post-F, v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C, or VM-874 formulated with 50 μg of aluminum hydroxide adjuvant, while control animals received 50 μg of aluminum hydroxide adjuvant alone. A prime immunization was administered at week 0, followed by serum collection at week 2 and a booster immunization at week 3. Two weeks after the booster immunization, serum samples were collected for antibody analyses, and animals were subsequently challenged intranasally with 10 6 FFU of hMPV A2 to evaluate protective efficacy.

Humoral immunogenicity was first assessed by antigen-binding assays, which showed readily detectable serum IgG responses against both pre-F (VM-874) and post-F following booster immunization (C and D). All antigen-immunized groups showed markedly increased hMPV F-reactive binding antibody responses compared with the adjuvant-only control group. Functional activity was then evaluated by neutralization assays, which showed that VM-874 elicited neutralizing antibodies against both hMPV A2 and B1 strains (E and F). Against hMPV A2, VM-874 elicited neutralizing titers with a GMT of 3,059, comparable to v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C (GMT: 2821) and higher than post-F (GMT: 1377). Against hMPV B1, VM-874 induced significantly higher neutralizing titers than both post-F (GMT: 8462 vs. 3317) and v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C (GMT: 8462 vs. 1971). Overall, under the corresponding immunization regimen, the neutralizing titers elicited by VM-874 in cotton rats were higher than those observed in BALB/c mice, supporting its ability to induce cross-lineage neutralizing responses in this model.

Protective efficacy was subsequently assessed following hMPV challenge. Compared with adjuvant-only controls, antigen-immunized cotton rats showed significantly reduced pulmonary viral RNA copy numbers (G). Infectious viral titers in lung homogenates were readily detected in the adjuvant-only group but were not detectable in the post-F-, v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C-, or VM-874-immunized groups (H), demonstrating effective suppression of viral replication in vivo . Consistent with the relatively mild clinical course of infection in this model, body weight remained broadly stable after challenge in both immunized and control animals (B), indicating the absence of overt systemic illness. To assess viral replication in the upper respiratory tract, viral burden in the nasal turbinates was quantified. Infectious virus was detected in the nasal turbinates of adjuvant-only controls but was undetectable in antigen-immunized animals (I). Concordantly, histopathological analysis showed attenuated inflammatory lung injury and reduced pathological scores in antigen-immunized animals, including VM-874-immunized cotton rats, compared with adjuvant-only controls (J and K). Together, these results indicate that VM-874 induces strong F-directed binding and neutralizing antibody responses and confers protection against hMPV infection in the cotton rat model.

Because RSV F and hMPV F share structurally conserved antigenic features and cross-reactive epitopes, we investigated whether the pre-F-stabilized hMPV F immunogen VM-874 could elicit RSV F-cross-reactive antibody responses and whether these responses mediated heterologous protection against RSV infection. To evaluate this, cotton rats and BALB/c mice were intramuscularly immunized with 5 μg of antigen formulated with 50 μg of aluminum hydroxide adjuvant. The immunization groups included hMPV post-F, the pre-F-stabilized hMPV F variant v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C, VM-874, pXCS847, and an aluminum hydroxide adjuvant-only control (A). pXCS847, a pre-F-stabilized RSV F antigen derived from Pfizer's RSV pre-F antigen-design program and corresponding to the optimized RSV pre-F construct 847, was included as a homologous RSV F positive-control immunogen (; ). Animals received a prime immunization at week 0 and a booster immunization 3 weeks later. Serum samples were collected 2 weeks after the booster immunization to assess binding antibody responses to RSV pre-F and RSV post-F antigens, as well as RSV-A2 neutralizing activity via FRNT 50 assay. BALB/c mice were subsequently challenged intranasally with RSV-A2 to evaluate heterologous protection and potential vaccine-enhanced disease-associated pulmonary pathology.

In cotton rats, immunization with v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C or hMPV post-F induced detectable serum binding antibodies that bound both RSV pre-F and RSV post-F antigens, although the magnitude of these responses was lower than that induced by pXCS847 (B and C). In contrast, VM-874 immunization induced detectable serum antibodies against RSV pre-F, whereas little or no binding to RSV post-F was detected (B and C). As expected, pXCS847 elicited the strongest RSV F-binding responses and robust RSV-A2 neutralizing activity. In contrast, RSV-neutralizing activity remained undetectable in all hMPV F-immunized groups, including the VM-874, v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C, and hMPV post-F groups (D). A similar pattern was observed in BALB/c mice. Immunization with v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C or hMPV post-F induced measurable cross-binding antibodies against both RSV pre-F and RSV post-F, whereas VM-874 predominantly induced antibodies that bound RSV pre-F, with little or no detectable binding to RSV post-F. Nevertheless, only pXCS847 induced detectable RSV-A2-neutralizing antibodies (E–G). These findings indicate that VM-874 elicits antibodies that recognize RSV F; however, these cross-reactive responses are detectable by binding assays but non-neutralizing under the conditions tested.

To determine whether these cross-reactive antibody responses confer heterologous protection, immunized BALB/c mice were challenged intranasally with RSV-A2, and lung viral titers were measured as FFU/g. Consistent with its potent RSV-neutralizing activity, pXCS847 markedly reduced pulmonary RSV titers compared with the adjuvant control and hMPV F-immunized groups (H). In contrast, VM-874 did not significantly reduce lung RSV replication, and viral titers in the VM-874 group were comparable to those in the adjuvant control group (H). Importantly, VM-874 immunization did not increase pulmonary RSV burden relative to the adjuvant control. Histopathological analysis further showed that lung sections from VM-874-immunized mice did not show evident exacerbation relative to adjuvant-treated mice, with no obvious enhancement of inflammatory pathology (I). By contrast, hMPV post-F immunization was associated with more pronounced pulmonary inflammatory cell infiltration after RSV challenge (I), and additional quantitative analysis showed increased eosinophil and neutrophil infiltration in this group (). Together, these results suggest that distinct conformational states of hMPV F may differentially influence the outcome of heterologous RSV exposure. The pre-F-stabilized hMPV F immunogen VM-874 induced RSV F-cross-reactive binding antibodies but did not elicit detectable RSV-neutralizing activity or heterologous protection. Nevertheless, VM-874 did not enhance pulmonary RSV replication or lung pathology following RSV-A2 challenge, whereas hMPV post-F immunization was associated with an unfavorable inflammatory phenotype in this heterologous challenge model.
sections.discussion:
Pre-F stabilization has become a central design principle in the rational development of pneumovirus F-based vaccine antigens. Previous studies have demonstrated that hMPV F can be stabilized through proline substitutions, cleavage-site engineering, disulfide stabilization, cavity-filling mutations, electrostatic optimization, single-chain trimer design, AI-guided prefusion-trimer design, and computational antigen design (; ; ). These studies established important design principles for hMPV pre-F immunogens, but they also showed that improved stability alone may not fully ensure preserved antigenicity, efficient expression, manufacturability, or protective immunogenicity. Therefore, further antigen optimization remains necessary to preserve neutralization-related epitopes while maintaining efficient expression, trimer formation, and stability under stress conditions.

In this study, VM-874 was designed to improve both local conformational stability and trimer stability of hMPV F. Unlike designs that mainly rely on a single class of stabilizing mutations, VM-874 combines two engineered disulfide bonds, A140C/S149C and L378C/G432C, a designed electrostatic interaction through A225D, and replacement of hMPV F residues 103–113 with the corresponding RSV F sequence. The A140C/S149C disulfide bond is positioned in a region involved in conformational rearrangement during the pre-F-to-post-F transition and may restrict local refolding near HRA and the central helix. A225D was introduced to promote a potential interprotomer salt bridge with R79, whereas L378C/G432C and the 103–113 sequence replacement were designed to support trimer integrity. Thus, VM-874 integrates local disulfide stabilization, potential interprotomer electrostatic stabilization, and trimer-interface stabilization within a soluble trimeric antigen.

The antigenic evaluation of VM-874 further highlights its improved ability to maintain pre-F antigenic integrity under stress conditions compared with the v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C pre-F comparator. Because the DSF profile of v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C could not be reliably determined, we did not use T m as the primary basis for direct comparison between the two pre-F antigens. Instead, their conformational quality was compared using conformation-sensitive monoclonal antibody binding and stress-condition antigenicity. VM-874 showed robust binding to multiple epitope-specific antibodies, including MPE8, MPV414, ADI-61026, and 101F, indicating preservation of several neutralization-relevant antigenic surfaces. Notably, after heat treatment, v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C showed markedly reduced binding to pre-F-specific antibodies, whereas VM-874 retained binding to the tested antibodies and maintained pre-F epitope integrity. VM-874 also preserved antibody binding after storage at 4 °C. These results suggest that VM-874 provides a more stress-resistant pre-F antigenic platform than the comparator antigen and has an improved capacity to maintain neutralization-relevant conformational epitopes during antigen handling and storage.

The immunogenicity results demonstrate that the structural stabilization strategy used for VM-874 translates into a functional antibody response in vivo . In BALB/c mice, VM-874 induced strong F-specific binding antibodies and generated a pre-F-biased serum IgG binding profile, as shown by the elevated pre-F/post-F binding IgG ratio (). Moreover, VM-874 elicited neutralizing antibody responses against both hMPV A2 and B1 strains, with titers higher than those induced by post-F and numerically higher than those elicited by the v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C pre-F comparator. In cotton rats, VM-874 similarly induced robust cross-lineage neutralizing responses and reduced viral burden in both the upper and lower respiratory tract. These findings suggest that VM-874 preserves key pre-F antigenic features required for broad hMPV neutralization and in vivo protection.

Because hMPV F and RSV F share conserved structural features, hMPV F immunization may elicit antibodies capable of binding RSV F (; ). In particular, antigenic sites III and IV are conserved regions shared by RSV F and hMPV F, and several antibodies, including MPE8, 101F, 54G10, and 17E10, have been reported to show RSV/hMPV cross-reactivity or cross-neutralization (; ; ; ). However, cross-binding does not necessarily indicate cross-neutralization or heterologous protection. This distinction is important because RSV and hMPV differ in the conformational distribution of protective antibody epitopes. For RSV, a large fraction of serum neutralizing activity is mediated by antibodies specific for the pre-F conformation, whereas hMPV-neutralizing antibodies more frequently recognize epitopes shared between pre-F and post-F conformations (; ). Therefore, hMPV F-induced antibodies that bind RSV F may differ in epitope specificity, binding orientation, avidity, and functional activity from antibodies elicited directly by RSV F immunogens.

The observation that hMPV post-F immune serum bound RSV pre-F more strongly than RSV post-F may reflect conformational and epitope-presentation differences between the two pneumovirus F proteins. Although hMPV post-F may induce antibodies targeting conserved regions such as antigenic sites III and IV, these cross-reactive epitopes may be more accessible or more favorably displayed on RSV pre-F than on RSV post-F in the recombinant antigens used for binding assays. Antigenic site IV is present in both RSV pre-F and post-F, whereas site III includes antibodies with different conformation preferences, including pre-F-biased cross-reactive antibodies such as MPE8 (; ). Thus, stronger binding of hMPV post-F immune serum to RSV pre-F does not necessarily mean that the serum contains RSV pre-F-specific neutralizing antibodies. Rather, it may indicate that some hMPV post-F-induced antibodies recognize conserved surfaces that are better presented on RSV pre-F in the binding assays. This interpretation is consistent with previous findings showing that antibody binding to RSV/hMPV F is influenced not only by sequence conservation, but also by conformational state and binding orientation (; ).

Notably, VM-874 induced RSV F cross-binding antibodies but did not generate detectable RSV-neutralizing activity and did not increase pulmonary RSV burden after heterologous RSV challenge. In contrast, hMPV post-F immunization also induced RSV F cross-binding antibodies but was associated with higher lung viral titers and more pronounced inflammatory pathology after RSV challenge. These results suggest that the conformational state of the hMPV F immunogen may influence not only homologous neutralization, but also the functional quality of cross-reactive antibody responses during heterologous RSV exposure. One possible explanation is that VM-874, as a pre-F-stabilized trimer, may preferentially focus antibody responses toward structurally constrained and neutralization-related F epitopes, whereas post-F may elicit a higher proportion of non-neutralizing or poorly protective cross-binding antibodies. In the context of RSV vaccine-enhanced disease, non-protective or low-avidity antibodies, immune complex formation, complement activation, and Th2-biased pulmonary inflammation have been implicated as contributing factors (; ; ). Therefore, the biological effect of RSV F cross-binding antibodies may depend less on binding titer alone and more on epitope specificity, avidity, IgG subclass distribution, Fc-mediated effector functions, complement activation, and the accompanying T cell response.

This interpretation may also explain why RSV F cross-binding antibodies induced by VM-874, despite lacking detectable RSV-neutralizing activity, were not associated with evident vaccine-associated enhanced viral diseases-like pathology, whereas hMPV post-F immunization was associated with enhanced pulmonary inflammation. VM-874-induced cross-binding antibodies may bind RSV F in a manner that is insufficient for neutralization but also insufficient to promote pathogenic immune complex deposition or pro-inflammatory Fc receptor- and complement-mediated activation. Conversely, hMPV post-F-induced antibodies may preferentially recognize non-neutralizing conserved surfaces that bind RSV F during infection without blocking fusion, thereby allowing viral replication to proceed in the presence of antibody-antigen complexes. Such a scenario could amplify local inflammation through Fc receptor engagement, complement activation, or recruitment of inflammatory leukocytes. Because these mechanisms were not directly tested in the present study, this explanation remains speculative. Future studies should evaluate RSV F cross-binding antibody avidity, epitope specificity, IgG subclasses, complement deposition, Fcγ receptor-dependent effector functions, cytokine profiles, and pulmonary inflammatory cell composition after heterologous RSV challenge.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, although VM-874 was obtained through structure-guided design, molecular dynamics simulation, and experimental screening, it was not derived from exhaustive screening of all possible cysteine-pair, electrostatic, or multi-substitution combinations. Further combinatorial optimization may therefore identify variants with improved expression, thermal stability, antigenic durability, or manufacturability. Second, although VM-874 induced cross-lineage neutralizing antibody responses and reduced viral burden in BALB/c mice and cotton rats, these findings were mainly obtained from short-term preclinical animal experiments. Further studies are needed to evaluate immune durability, dose-sparing potential, adjuvant compatibility, the effects of repeated immunization, and protective efficacy in additional preclinical models. Third, the mechanisms underlying the different outcomes associated with RSV F cross-binding antibodies remain unclear. Future studies should therefore evaluate not only cross-binding and cross-neutralization, but also antibody avidity, epitope specificity, IgG subclass distribution, Fcγ receptor-dependent functions, complement deposition, cytokine profiles, and virological and pathological outcomes after sequential or heterologous virus exposure. These analyses will help define the functional boundaries and safety implications of hMPV/RSV cross-reactive immune responses.

Taken together, our findings support pre-F-focused hMPV F design as an important principle for next-generation hMPV vaccine development and suggest that this principle should also inform RSV/hMPV combination or sequential immunization strategies. This interpretation is consistent with structural-vaccinology studies showing that pre-F stabilization best preserves neutralization-relevant surfaces on pneumovirus F proteins and can improve the immunogenicity and protective performance of hMPV F immunogens. Because RSV and hMPV exhibit overlapping seasonal circulation and share structurally conserved, partly cross-reactive F epitopes, combined or sequential exposure may give rise to immune interactions that are not apparent in single-pathogen settings. Accordingly, preclinical evaluation of combined RSV/hMPV strategies should extend beyond homologous immunogenicity to include cross-binding versus cross-neutralization, the potential for sub-neutralizing or non-neutralizing cross-reactive responses, and virologic as well as pathologic outcomes in heterologous or sequential challenge models. Such benchmarking will be important to determine whether combined approaches can provide additive protection while minimizing unintended immune modulation.
sections.methods:
All hMPV F variants were cloned into a pcDNA3.1 expression vector containing a C-terminal 6 × His tag using homologous recombination, and all constructs were verified by DNA sequencing. Plasmids encoding F variants were transiently transfected into FreeStyle 293F cells using polyethyleneimine (PEI, MKbio, Shanghai, China). At 5 days post-transfection, culture supernatants were clarified by centrifugation at 5000× g (Beckman Coulter Avanti JXN-26, Brea, CA, USA) for 30 min and incubated with Ni-NTA resin (GenScript, L00666-100, Jiangsu, China) at 16 °C for 2 h. Bound proteins were eluted with PBS containing 500 mM imidazole. Protein purity (> 90%) was assessed by SDS-PAGE, and samples were further purified by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) on a Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva, Uppsala, Sweden) equilibrated with PBS to obtain monodisperse fractions. The v3B_Δ12 D454C/V458C antigen was provided by the Beijing Institute of Biological Products.

Plasmids encoding the heavy and light chains of MPE8 (), DS7 (), ADI-61026 (), and MPV414 () were co-transfected into FreeStyle 293F cells at a 1:1 ratio using PEI. To purify IgG, clarified supernatants were applied to Protein A resin, and bound material was eluted with 100 mM glycine (pH 3.0). Eluates were immediately neutralized with 1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and further purified by SEC on a Superdex 200 column (Cytiva, Uppsala, Sweden) in PBS to obtain monodisperse fractions. All protein samples were concentrated using Amicon Ultra centrifugal filter units (Merck Millipore, Ireland) to 2–4 mg/mL, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed using the pre-F hMPV F trimer structure (PDB: 5WB0 ) as the starting model. Simulations were carried out with ACEMD using the AMBER14SB force field, the TIP3P water model, and a Langevin thermostat. The protein was solvated in an explicit water box with a 10 Å solvent buffer under periodic boundary conditions and simulated at 50 °C. After energy minimization, heavy-atom restraints were gradually released over the first 60 ns to allow equilibration. Three independent 500 ns production runs were then performed. Structural dynamics and stability were evaluated by analyzing backbone RMSD and per-residue RMSF using GROMACS ().

Heat-treated and untreated pre-F proteins were individually immobilized on 96-well ELISA plates (NEST, Jiangsu, China) at a concentration of 2 μg/mL (100 μL per well) overnight at 4 °C. Plates were then blocked with 2% (w/v) BSA in PBST for 2 h at 37 °C. A panel of hMPV F-specific monoclonal antibodies (MPE8, MPV414, 101F, and ADI-61026) was serially diluted from an initial concentration of 10 μg/mL, added to the pre-F protein-coated wells, and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. Plates were washed three times with PBST to remove unbound antibodies, and bound antibodies were detected using an appropriate HRP-conjugated secondary antibody for 1 h at 37 °C. Plates were washed three times with PBST, developed with TMB Single-Component Substrate (Solarbio, PR1200, Beijing, China), and absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a Multiskan FC microplate reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA).

hMPV F proteins subjected to different treatments (e.g., accelerated or long-term stability conditions) were immobilized on 96-well ELISA plates at a concentration of 2 μg/mL (100 μL per well) overnight at 4 °C. Plates were washed with PBST, blocked with 2% (w/v) BSA for 2 h at 37 °C in PBST, and washed again. Serial dilutions of antibodies starting from 10 μg/mL (10-fold serial dilutions) were then added and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. After washing, bound antibodies were detected using an HRP-conjugated anti-human IgG secondary antibody (Sino Biological, Beijing, China) at a dilution of 1:5000 for 1 h at 37 °C, followed by development with TMB substrate and measurement of absorbance at 450 nm.

Serum IgG binding to hMPV F proteins was measured by ELISA. hMPV F proteins (2 μg/mL) were immobilized on 96-well ELISA plates overnight at 4 °C. Plates were washed with PBST, blocked with 2% (w/v) BSA in PBST, and washed again. Serial dilutions of sera (starting with an initial 1:80 dilution, followed by 5-fold serial dilutions) were added and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. Bound IgG was detected using an HRP-conjugated anti-mouse IgG (H+L) antibody (Proteintech, SA00001-1, USA) or an HRP-conjugated anti-cotton rat IgG (H+L) antibody (ICL Lab, CCOT-25P, Oregon, USA) at a dilution of 1:5000 for 1 h at 37 °C, followed by TMB development and measurement of absorbance at 450 nm.

SYPRO Orange dye (5000 × ; Invitrogen, Carlsbad MA, USA) was diluted in 1 × PBS to prepare a 50 × working solution. For each reaction, 3 μg of purified protein was diluted in 1 × PBS to a final volume of 27 μL, and 3 μL of 50 × SYPRO Orange was added to give a final reaction volume of 30 μL in a 96-well PCR plate. Wells containing 1 × PBS without protein served as negative controls. Plates were sealed with MicroAmp Optical Adhesive Film (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), and fluorescence was measured on a real-time fluorescent quantitative PCR instrument (Bio-Rad CFX96, Hercules, CA, USA). Samples were held at 25 °C for 3 min, followed by a temperature increment of 0.5 °C per minute within the range of 25 °C–95 °C. The melting temperature (T m ) was determined from the peak of the negative first derivative of the fluorescence signal with respect to temperature (−dF/dT), corresponding to the midpoint of thermal unfolding.

Assays were performed on an Octet R8 system (Sartorius, Germany) at 25 °C using 1 × PBST as the running buffer in black 96-well plates (Greiner Bio-One, Germany). Protein A biosensors (Sartorius, Germany) were pre-soaked in 1 × PBST for 10 min and equilibrated with a 60 s baseline step. Purified antibodies (8 μg/mL) were immobilized until a response of ∼1.2 nm was reached. After a second 60 s baseline in 1 × PBST, sensors were exposed to a 2-fold serial dilution series of antigen (seven concentrations, starting at 100 nM), including a buffer-only reference (0 nM antigen), for 180 s, followed by a 600 s dissociation step in 1 × PBST. Biosensors were regenerated between cycles using 10 mM glycine (pH 1.5). Data were analyzed using Octet Analysis Studio v13.0 with a 1:1 global fit model to determine K a , K d , and K D ( K D = K d / K a ).

Purified VM-874 was diluted to 10 μg/mL in 1 × PBS. A 4 μL aliquot was applied to a glow-discharged, carbon-coated grid (Zhongjingkeyi Technology; 60 s at 15 mA, 38 mbar) and incubated for 1 min to allow adsorption. Excess solution was removed by gentle blotting with filter paper. Uranyl acetate (3%, RXSV CHEM) was centrifuged at 12,000× g for 10 min before use. A 100 μL volume was placed on parafilm and divided into three drops. The grid (carbon side down) was briefly dipped into each drop sequentially, with an incubation time of 30 s per drop. After the final dip, residual uranyl acetate was removed by gentle blotting, and the grid was air-dried at room temperature. TEM imaging was performed on a Talos L120C G2 microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) operated at 120 kV. Representative micrographs were acquired at 120,000 × magnification, and particle morphology was assessed from the resulting images.

Baby hamster kidney (BHK-21-STD) cells were kindly provided by Guangzhou Starda Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Guangzhou, China), whereas human embryonic kidney 293T (HEK293T) cells were purchased from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA; CRL-3216). Both cell lines were maintained in Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium (DMEM; Gibco, MA, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Sigma, MO, USA) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (100 IU/mL penicillin and 100 μg/mL streptomycin; Sigma, MO, USA). BHK-21-STD cells were seeded 1 day before infection and reached ∼80% confluence on the day of infection.

The hMPV A2 strain (HMPV-A2/GZ/1804-183) and hMPV B1 strain (HMPV-B1/GZ/1712-70) were propagated in BHK-21-STD cells. BHK-21-STD cells were infected at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.2. After adsorption for 1 h, the inoculum was removed and replaced with DMEM containing 0.1% BSA and 0.5 μg/mL TPCK-treated trypsin. After 2−3 days of incubation at 35 °C in 5% CO 2 , the culture supernatant was collected, clarified by centrifugation to remove cell debris, and stored at −80 °C.

HEp-2 cells were seeded in T75 flasks at 5 × 10 6 cells per flask and incubated overnight (12−20 h) to reach ∼80% confluence. RSV A2 was used to infect cells at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.1. Prior to infection, the culture medium was removed and the monolayer was rinsed once with 10 mL DMEM. Cells were then inoculated with 2 mL of RSV inoculum diluted in DMEM and incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 for 3 h, with gentle rocking twice during the adsorption period. After adsorption, 8 mL of pre-warmed DMEM-based maintenance medium was added, and cultures were incubated at 33 °C with 5% CO 2 for 2.5 days while monitoring for cytopathic effect (CPE). For virus harvest, infected cultures were subjected to one freeze–thaw cycle at −80 °C. Supernatants were collected, clarified by centrifugation at 2000× g for 10 min at 4 °C, filtered through a 0.45 μm membrane, and stored at −80 °C.

Specific pathogen-free 6- to 8-week-old female BALB/c mice were used for immunization and viral challenge experiments. Animals were group-housed in ventilated racks under a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle at an ambient temperature of 21 °C, with food and water available ad libitum. Groups of five mice were inoculated intramuscularly into both quadriceps muscles (100 μL per site; 5 μg total antigen per dose), formulated in PBS with 50 μg aluminum hydroxide adjuvant. Three weeks after the prime, mice were boosted with the same formulation, and blood was collected two weeks later by retro-orbital sampling. For the post-F construct, the protein was heated at 70 °C for 10 min before inoculation. Two weeks after booster immunization, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and challenged intranasally with 10 6 FFU of hMPV A2 or RSV A2 in a 50 μL volume. At 4 days post-challenge, mice were humanely euthanized, and lungs were collected to determine viral burden. All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Guangzhou National Laboratory (GZLAB-AUCP-2025-10-A06).

Cotton rats ( Sigmodon hispidus ) used in this study were derived from breeding pairs purchased from ENVIGO RMS, LLC (Indianapolis, IN, USA), with authorized breeding rights. The animals were subsequently bred and maintained under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions in the animal facility of Guangzhou Laboratory. Animals were immunized using the same antigen dose and formulation described for mice. Two weeks after booster immunization, cotton rats were anesthetized with isoflurane and challenged intranasally with hMPV A2 (10 6 FFU in 100 μL), as indicated. At 4 days post-challenge, animals were humanely euthanized, and lungs and nasal turbinates were collected for determination of viral burden. All animal experiments were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Guangzhou National Laboratory (GZLAB-AUCP-2025-10-A06).

BHK-21 cells or HEp-2 cells were seeded in 96-well plates 1 day prior to infection. Serum samples were serially diluted in DMEM (starting with an initial 1:20 dilution, followed by 3-fold serial dilutions) and mixed with an equal volume of hMPV A2 or hMPV B1 (MOI = 0.2) or RSV A2 (MOI = 0.2). After incubation at 37 °C for 1 h, the serum-virus mixtures were added to BHK-21 monolayers (for hMPV) or HEp-2 monolayers (for RSV). FRNT 50 was defined as the reciprocal serum dilution that reduced fluorescent focus counts by 50% relative to virus-only controls.

Virus titers were determined using a focus formation assay (FFA). For hMPV, BHK-21-STD cells were seeded in 96-well plates 1 day prior to infection. Undiluted virus stocks or lung homogenates, followed by four-fold serial dilutions, were added to BHK-21-STD cell monolayers and subjected to spinoculation at 1500 × g for 90 min. The inoculum was then removed and replaced with 200 μL DMEM containing 0.1% BSA and 0.5 μg/mL TPCK-treated trypsin. After 24 h, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and blocked with 5% BSA (Macklin, B824162, Shanghai, China) for 30 min. Cells were incubated with the human anti-F monoclonal antibody MPV414 for 2 h, followed by a FITC-labeled goat anti-human secondary antibody (Sino Biological, Beijing, China). Fluorescent foci were imaged and counted, and viral titers were calculated as focus-forming units (FFU) per mL. For RSV, HEp-2 cells were seeded in 96-well plates 1 day prior to infection. Undiluted virus stocks or lung homogenates, followed by four-fold serial dilutions, were added to HEp-2 monolayers. After 24 h, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100, and blocked with 5% BSA (Macklin, B824162, Shanghai, China) for 30 min. Cells were then incubated with an FITC-conjugated anti-RSV antibody (1:100). For tissue homogenates, viral titers were reported as FFU/g tissue.

Total RNA was extracted from lung tissues using TRIzol (Invitrogen, USA). Viral RNA levels were quantified by one-step qRT-PCR using gene-specific primers and the HiScript II One Step qRT-PCR SYBR Green Kit (Vazyme, Q221-01, Jiangsu, China) on an Applied Biosystems QuantStudio 6 Flex instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Primer sequences (forward/reverse; 5′–3′) were as follows: hMPV N gene, ACAGCAGATTCTAAGAAACTCAGGC/TCTTTGTCTATCTCTTCCACC; RSV F gene, CGAGCCAGAAGAGAACTACCA/CCTTCTAGGTGCAGGACCTTA; Relative quantification was performed using β-actin as the internal control.

Excised lungs were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde. Fixed lungs were processed for histological analysis, with the left lung lobe embedded in paraffin, sectioned, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). H&E staining and quantification of eosinophils and neutrophils were performed by Wuhan Baiqiandu Biotechnology Co., Ltd. Lung histopathological changes were evaluated by three independent blinded reviewers using a four-point ordinal scoring scale, with a score of 1 indicating normal tissue and a score of 4 indicating extensive or severe pathological changes. Representative histopathological images were selected from samples with pathology scores close to the median score of each group, in order to minimize subjective selection bias.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 10. Continuous variables, including antibody titers and viral titers, were log10-transformed when appropriate to reduce data skewness and better satisfy the assumptions of parametric tests. Geometric mean titers (GMTs) were calculated by back-transforming the mean values of log10-transformed titers. Comparisons between two groups were performed using a two-tailed Student's t -test; when the assumption of equal variance was not met, Welch's corrected t -test was used. Comparisons among multiple groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (one-way ANOVA), followed by Dunnett's or Tukey's multiple-comparison test as appropriate. Values below the lower limit of detection (LLOD) were assigned the LLOD before statistical analysis. All statistical tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

title: Adverse Events Reported Following RSV Prefusion F Protein Vaccines Administration Among Approved Populations: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Introduction Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is a major cause of lower respiratory tract infections among children and older adults. Two RSV prefusion F protein (RSVpreF) vaccines currently are approved for adults aged 60 years and older. However, little is known about the adverse events reported among individuals in this age group who have received an RSVpreF vaccine. The purpose of this study was to compare adverse events reported by nonpregnant adults (≥60 years old) who received an RSVpreF vaccine. Methods This study included individuals who reported a vaccine-related adverse event to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). Data abstracted from VAERS were recoded into standardized adverse event categories for analysis. Results A total of 2,321 individuals were included. The three most frequently reported adverse event categories were neurologic, musculoskeletal, and constitutional symptoms. Recipients of Arexvy™ (Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine, Adjuvanted) reported more injection site reactions compared with those who received Abrysvo™ (Respiratory Syncytial Virus vaccine). There were no adverse event categories that were more commonly reported among Abrysvo™ recipients compared with Arexvy™ recipients. Conclusions The adverse events observed in this study were consistent with findings from previous Phase II/III trials. The higher frequency of injection site symptoms among Arexvy™ recipients may be attributable to the adjuvant included in Arexvy™ but absent in Abrysvo™. Overall, these findings indicate that both vaccines provide safe protection against RSV for older adults, with minimal side effects, in a population that previously had no vaccination option.

sections.other:
Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is a major cause of lower respiratory infections among children and older adults., In the United States, RSV leads to approximately 1.6 million outpatient pediatric visits each year., Older adults also remain at high risk for severe RSV disease due to waning immunity and comorbid conditions. Among this population, RSV is associated with an estimated 10,000 deaths annually, 267 hospitalizations per 100,000 people, and 1.4 million outpatient visits., The true burden likely is even greater, as RSV is under-detected when clinicians do not routinely test for it, particularly in older adults.

Historically, RSV treatment strategies have centered on secondary and tertiary prevention, including supportive care, ribavirin, monoclonal antibodies, RSV intravenous immunoglobulin (RSVIVIG), glucocorticoids, and bronchodilators. Ribavirin, however, is known to cause teratogenic and other adverse effects and is therefore reserved for select cases. Likewise, monoclonal antibodies and RSV-IVIG generally are limited to “high-risk” individuals such as immunocompromised patients, premature infants, and older adults with significant comorbidities., Most available treatment approaches provide symptomatic relief but do not prevent infection.

A major advance occurred on May 3, 2023, when the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved two RSV prefusion F (RSVpreF) protein vaccines (Arexvy™ [Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine, Adjuvanted] and Abrysvo™ [Respiratory Syncytial Virus vaccine]). for adults aged 60 years and older, offering a new primary prevention tool for at-risk populations.– These vaccines target the RSVpreF protein, which had historically been difficult to isolate and purify.,,

Clinical trials for these vaccines reported common adverse events such as injection site pain, muscle pain, joint pain, headache, fatigue, and nausea. Rare but more serious events, including inflammatory neurological conditions like Guillain-Barré syndrome, also were observed. However, real-world data on adverse events reported by individuals who received an RSVpreF vaccine remain limited. Therefore, authors of this study aimed to compare adverse events among nonpregnant adults aged 60 years or older who received an RSVpreF vaccine.

The authors thank Rosey Zackula for her support with data management and commitment to this research. They also thank Melinda Chenault for her assistance with the data organization.
sections.methods:
This study included individuals who reported a vaccine-related adverse event to the Health and Human Services Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). VAERS is an open reporting system that allows anyone to submit post-vaccination adverse events using free-text entries. Eligible participants were adults aged ≥60 years who received one of the two RSVpreF vaccines and reported at least one adverse event between August 1, 2023, and January 31, 2024. Exclusions included missing age, age <60 years, pregnancy, receiving an inappropriate vaccine based on guidelines, or incomplete required information.

Extracted variables included demographics (e.g., age, sex), vaccine details (e.g., vaccine name and brand), and adverse event information (e.g., symptoms, disability, vaccination problems). Demographics were used to confirm eligibility, while vaccine details and event characteristics allowed comparison of adverse event profiles between the two RSVpreF vaccines.

The study was approved by The University of Kansas Medical Center (KUMC) Institutional Review Board (IRB) and followed STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) guidelines.

De-identified VAERS data were downloaded and stored in REDCap® (CTSA Award # UL1TR002366), electronic data capture tools hosted at The KUMC., Because VAERS relies on unstructured free-text reporting, adverse events were recoded into standardized categories based on the affected system. Coding was completed by one researcher and reviewed by four others, with consensus reached through discussion. Categories included vaccine information (e.g., vaccine name, inappropriate administration) and adverse event types (e.g., constitutional symptoms, cardiovascular issues, injection site reactions).

Data were analyzed using SAS® version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC). Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Continuous variables were described using means and standard deviations (SD) or medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs), depending on distribution. Associations between categorical variables were tested using likelihood-ratio Chi-square tests in 2×2 tables. Statistical significance was set at p <0.0015 after Bonferroni correction.
sections.results:
A total of 2,764 individuals initially met study criteria. After review, 443 were excluded: 198 lacked age information in their VAERS report, 197 received a vaccine outside the recommended age range or received the incorrect vaccine, and 48 were identified as pregnant after data abstraction. The final sample included 2,321 participants. Of these, 28.5% (n = 662) were male, 71.2% (n = 1,654) were female, and 0.2% (n = 5) did not report sex. Ages ranged from 60 to 102 years, with a mean age of 73 years (SD 7.2). Most participants received Arexvy™ (69.8%, n = 1,620), while 30.2% (n = 701) received Abrysvo™.

The most frequently reported adverse event categories were neurologic (31.6%, n = 733), musculoskeletal (29.1%, n = 676), and constitutional symptoms (28.4%, n = 658; ). Vaccine administration problems, such as incorrect dose, reconstitution issues, or administration errors, accounted for 8.9% (n = 206) of reports. Serious neuroinflammatory events, including Guillain-Barré syndrome, were reported in 0.9% (n = 20) of cases. Mortality was 0.7% (n = 15).

Patients who received Arexvy™ reported injection site symptoms more frequently (29.4%, 477/1,620; χ 2 1 =27.7; p <0.0001; ) than those who received Abrysvo™ (18.9%, 133/701; χ 2 1 =27.7; p <0.0001; ). Patients who received Abrysvo™ did not report any specific adverse event more often than those who received Arexvy™.
sections.discussion:
In this study, adverse events were grouped by organ system as well as broader categories, such as constitutional symptoms, injection site symptoms, and vaccine administration problems, that emerged during data abstraction. Because VAERS reports consist of unstructured free-text entries, recoding was necessary to standardize symptom categories and enable meaningful analysis. This approach differs from clinical trials, which tracked a narrower set of predefined adverse events such as headache, injection-site pain, and fever.,

Of all vaccine recipients, about two-thirds reported being female and almost a third reported being male, which aligns with prior research showing that men are less likely to seek medical care or visit their primary care physician., These demographic differences highlight the need for continued counseling of both elderly on the importance of RSV vaccination.

Neurologic adverse events, including headache, dizziness, and paresthesia, were the most reported symptoms. This is consistent with a Phase II trial of adults aged 18–40 years, where headache was the most frequently reported systemic adverse event (42–52%). Similar findings were reported in a Phase III trial of adults aged ≥60 years, in which 27% of participants reported a systemic adverse event, most commonly headache (13%).

In our study, 26.3% of patients reported injection-site symptoms. By comparison, the Phase II trial reported local reactions in 39–71% of participants, and the Phase III trial reported local reactions in 12%. Differences in symptom grouping and sample size may account for variability between this study’s findings and those of the clinical trials.

Recipients of Arexvy™ reported injection-site symptoms more frequently than those who received Abrysvo™. This difference may reflect the presence of an adjuvant in Arexvy™, which is absent in Abrysvo™., Adjuvants enhance immunogenicity by stimulating a stronger inflammatory response, but they also are associated with increased reactogenicity, the physical manifestations of that response.

In our study, vaccine administration problems accounted for 8.9% of reports, including administration errors, expired vaccines, or improper reconstitution. These events are not captured in controlled clinical trials but may arise in routine practice, underscoring the need for quality-control measures as RSV vaccines become more widely used. Serious adverse events were uncommon, representing 2.3% of all reports in our study. Neuroinflammatory conditions such as Guillain-Barré syndrome were reported by 0.9%, with no observed differences between vaccines. Mortality also is rare in our finding. Continued monitoring is warranted as vaccine uptake expands.

Overall, RSVpreF vaccines demonstrated a safety profile consistent with Phase II/III trials and offer important primary prevention for elderly populations who previously had no vaccine option., Future research should aim to better characterize vaccination rates across demographic groups, identify barriers to uptake, and, ideally, benefit from a centralized database that includes all vaccine recipients, not only those who submit VAERS reports.

This study differed from earlier clinical trials in that VAERS includes a much wider range of adverse events, necessitating grouped symptom categories. While this improved data usability, it limited the ability to assess the frequency of individual specific adverse events. As a cross-sectional study, causal relationships between the vaccines and reported adverse events cannot be established. Only individuals who submitted VAERS reports were included; therefore, the overall incidence of adverse events in the vaccinated population cannot be determined. VAERS reports may be incomplete, especially when submitted by individuals without medical training, and severe symptoms may overshadow mild ones, further contributing to incomplete reporting.

The most frequently reported adverse events among RSVpreF vaccine recipients were neurologic symptoms, musculoskeletal symptoms, and constitutional complaints. Recipients of Abrysvo™ were not more likely to report any specific adverse event compared with Arexvy™ recipients, whereas Arexvy™ recipients more commonly reported injection-site symptoms, likely related to the adjuvant. These findings are consistent with Phase II/III clinical trials and indicate that both vaccines provide safe and important protection for elderly adults, a group that previously had no primary prevention option for RSV. Given RSV’s long-standing role as a major cause of lower respiratory infections in the United States, the availability of safe vaccines represents an important advancement in protecting older adults.

title: Effectiveness of bivalent respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F protein-based vaccine in individuals with or without atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease: the DAN-RSV trial.
abstract: Background and aims It is not known whether the bivalent respiratory syncytial virus prefusion F protein-based (RSVpreF) vaccine reduces outcomes in individuals with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). The aim was to evaluate the vaccine effectiveness (VE) of an RSVpreF vaccine vs no vaccine on respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes in persons with or without pre-existing ASCVD. Methods We conducted a prespecified secondary analysis of the DAN-RSV trial. Adults aged ≥60 years were randomized 1:1 to RSVpreF vaccine or no vaccine. Baseline and outcome data were collected through nationwide registries. The primary outcome was respiratory syncytial virus-related respiratory tract disease hospitalization. The principal major adverse cardiovascular event outcome was a composite of hospitalization for myocardial infarction, stroke, or heart failure. Heterogeneity in VE was assessed among participants with and without ASCVD. Results The incidence rate of almost all outcomes was higher in participants with pre-existing ASCVD (n = 14 241) vs those without (n = 117 035). Vaccine effectiveness was generally consistent by ASCVD status (Pinteraction ≥ .05 for all but one interaction). Among persons without and with ASCVD, VE for the primary outcome was 80.0% [95% confidence interval (CI), 29.3-96.3] vs 100.0% (95% CI, -141.3 to 100.0), respectively (Pinteraction > .99). Vaccine effectiveness for major adverse cardiovascular events was 9.3% (95% CI, -15.1 to 28.6) in participants without, and 12.0% (95% CI, -34.6 to 43.3) in participants with, pre-existing ASCVD (Pinteraction = .90). Conclusions The VE of an RSVpreF vaccine vs no vaccine against respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes was similar among individuals ≥ 60 years of age with pre-existing ASCVD as compared with those without.

sections.other:
See the editorial comment for this article ‘Respiratory viruses, vaccines, and the heart: lessons from DANFLU-2, DAN-RSV, and beyond’, by B. Heidecker and T.F. Lüscher, https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf697 .

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events, including stroke and acute coronary syndromes. The risk of symptomatic RSV-related illness, hospitalization, and poor outcomes appears to be particularly high among individuals with pre-existing cardiovascular disease. ,,

A bivalent RSV prefusion F protein-based (RSVpreF) vaccine containing stabilized prefusion F glycoproteins from RSV subgroups A and B demonstrated efficacy against symptomatic RSV infection and viral shedding. The RSVpreF vaccines further prevented RSV-associated lower respiratory tract illness and acute respiratory illness in adults ≥ 60 years of age in both the RENOIR trial (RSV Vaccine Efficacy Study in Older Adults Immunized against RSV Disease) and the AReSVi-006 trial (Adult Respiratory Syncytial Virus). However, these randomized studies did not have a sufficient number of cases for evaluation of hospitalization outcomes. Furthermore, it is conceivable that individuals with high a priori risk, e.g. those with a history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), have a different degree of benefit from vaccination.

The purpose of this prespecified secondary analysis of the DAN-RSV trial (A Pragmatic Randomized Trial to Evaluate Bivalent RSV Prefusion F Protein–based Vaccine Effectiveness for Preventing RSV Hospitalizations in Adults Aged 60 Years or Above) was to evaluate the effectiveness of the RSVpreF vaccine vs no vaccine against respiratory and cardiovascular events, including ASCVD events, in persons ≥ 60 years of age, with or without pre-existing ASCVD.
sections.methods:
The rationale, design, baseline characteristics, and primary results of the DAN-RSV trial are reported separately. In brief, DAN-RSV was an investigator-sponsored, pragmatic, open-label, parallel-group, individually randomized clinical trial conducted during the 2024/2025 Northern Hemisphere winter season. The trial enrolled individuals aged ≥60 years irrespectively of comorbidity status during November and December 2024 at more than 40 sites across Denmark. Participants were mainly recruited using electronic invitation letters sent through the Danish governmental digital mail system, Digital Post. All potentially eligible individuals with access to this mail system were invited to participate. Although there were no formal exclusion criteria, vaccination procedures were required to follow routine clinical guidelines, including assessment for contraindications.

Participants were individually randomized 1:1 to the RSVpreF vaccine or no vaccine. The RSVpreF vaccine contained RSV subgroup A stabilized prefusion F antigen (60 µg) and RSV subgroup B stabilized prefusion F antigen (60 µg) and was administered as a single intramuscular injection. The control group did not receive any vaccine as part of the trial. Participants could provide electronic informed consent prior to their scheduled study visit, or they could consent in-person at the study visit, in case of which randomization was performed on-site. Accordingly, only participants randomized to RSVpreF (and those who had not consented electronically beforehand) were required to attend a study visit.

The trial was approved by the Danish Medical Research Ethics Committees and the Danish Medicines Agency. It was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and the International Council for Harmonization Good Clinical Practice guidelines.

Baseline data were collected via linkage to the nationwide administrative health registries. International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes and/or Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) codes were used to define baseline conditions and vaccination status. Pre-existing ASCVD was defined as a history of ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, or peripheral artery disease, all using ICD-10 codes.

Outcome data were also collected through linkage to the nationwide health registries. Access to electronic medial records was available for clinical outcome confirmation. Participants were followed for clinical outcomes from ≥14 days after the initially booked study visit date through 31 May 2025. The primary outcome was RSV-related respiratory tract disease hospitalization, analysed using the intention-to-treat principle. Key secondary outcomes included various other respiratory, hospitalization, and mortality outcomes. Detailed outcome definitions are presented in , . All specific cardiovascular outcomes (except the secondary endpoints: RSV-related and all-cause cardiorespiratory hospitalization) were considered exploratory. All outcomes required overnight hospital stays. The principal major adverse cardiovascular event outcome for the present analysis was defined as a composite of hospitalization for myocardial infarction, hospitalization for stroke, or hospitalization for heart failure.

Baseline characteristics were displayed stratified for pre-existing ASCVD status and randomization group. Continuous variables were presented as medians and interquartile ranges. Categorical variables were presented as number (%). Comparisons between groups were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test or Pearson’s χ 2 test, respectively.

All analyses were performed according to the intention-to-treat principle. All effectiveness endpoints were examined using vaccine effectiveness (VE) and based on the first outcome event only. Vaccine effectiveness was calculated as [1 − (incidence rate in the vaccine group/incidence rate in the control group)] × 100%, and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were constructed using the exact Clopper–Pearson method for binomial proportions. Vaccine effectiveness is the proportion of disease prevented by the vaccine. For example, a VE of 10% is mathematically equal to a relative risk of 0.90 for the intervention vs control. A VE = 0 signifies a null effect, a VE > 0 favours the intervention regimen, and a VE < 0 favours the control regimen. Of note, VE is capped at 100%, meaning that 100% of the disease is prevented by the vaccine; by contrast, a negative VE may extend to infinity. This also explains why the CIs may be asymmetrical. Event rates and VE were summarized by pre-existing ASCVD status and randomization group.

Treatment heterogeneity among participants with and without ASCVD was assessed using a Poisson model with a subgroup-by-randomized treatment interaction term; however, in case of low cell counts (<3), an exact Poisson model was used. A two-sided P < .05 was considered statistically significant. Although a minimum VE and a formal testing hierarchy were defined for the primary analysis, the results from this prespecified secondary analysis should be interpreted as exploratory in nature. Statistical analysis was performed using SAS Software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA), Stata MP, version 19.5 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA), and R, version 4.3.3 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).
sections.results:
A total of 131 276 participants were randomized to either the RSVpreF vaccine ( n = 65 642) or the control group ( n = 65 634). Overall, 14 241 (10.8%) participants had a history of ASCVD. Of these, 9746 (7.4%) had ischaemic heart disease, 4673 (3.6%) cerebrovascular disease, and 735 (0.6%) peripheral artery disease. A total of 883 (0.7%) individuals had ASCVD affecting more than one vascular bed. Baseline characteristics in participants stratified by pre-existing ASCVD status are shown in ; characteristics stratified by both ASCVD status and randomization group are shown in , . Those with ASCVD were older, more often male, and generally had a more adverse cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular risk profile. Characteristics were well-balanced among participants with and without ASCVD randomized to the RSVpreF vaccine vs no vaccine.

The incidence rate of almost all reported primary, secondary, and exploratory outcomes was higher in participants with pre-existing ASCVD as compared with those without ( ). For example, the incidence rate of the primary outcome was 0.51 per 1000 participant-years (PY) among individuals with ASCVD and 0.37 per 1000 PY in those without. The rates of all-cause cardiorespiratory disease hospitalization were 60.18 and 23.89 per 1000 PY, respectively. The rate of the composite of hospitalization for myocardial infarction, stroke, or heart failure was 15.66 per 1000 PY in participants with ASCVD and 5.87 per 1000 PY in individuals without. Absolute risk reductions are shown in .

Results were generally consistent among participants with and without ASCVD ( ). The incidence rates for the primary outcome were lower in the RSVpreF group than in the control group among individuals without ASCVD [0.12 events/1000 PY vs 0.62 events/1000 PY, VE: 80.0% (95% CI, 29.3–96.3)] and among those with ASCVD [0 events/1000 PY vs 1.02 events/1000 PY, VE: 100.0% (95% CI, −141.3 to 100.0)] ( P interaction > 0.99). For all-cause cardiorespiratory disease hospitalization, the incidence rates among persons without ASCVD were 22.54 events/1000 PY in the RSVpreF group vs 25.23 events/1000 PY in the control group [VE: 10.6% (95% CI, −0.5 to 20.5)]; among those with ASCVD, the incidence rates were 57.86 events/1000 PY vs 62.49 events/1000 PY [VE: 7.4% (95% CI, −14.1 to 25.8)] ( P interaction = .77).

For the principal major adverse cardiovascular events outcome, the incidence rates were 5.58 events/1000 PY vs 6.16 events/1000 PY in the no ASCVD group [VE: 9.3% (95% CI, −15.1 to 28.6)] and 14.66 events/1000 PY vs 16.66 events/1000 PY in the ASCVD group [VE: 12.0% (95% CI, −34.6 to 43.3)] ( P interaction = .90). Vaccine effectiveness estimates for myocardial infarction, hospitalization for heart failure, and hospitalization for atrial fibrillation were also consistent across ASCVD status at baseline ( P interaction ≥ .05 for all). For stroke, ASCVD modified the treatment effect such that the vaccine appeared to prevent strokes more effectively among participants with ASCVD as compared with those without [without ASCVD: 3.04 events/1000 PY vs 3.16 events/1000 PY, VE: 3.9% (95% CI, −34.0 to 31.1); with ASCVD: 3.06 events/1000 PY vs 8.82 events/1000 PY, VE: 65.3% (95% CI, 23.9–85.8), P interaction = .02].
sections.discussion:
In this prespecified, secondary analysis of the DAN-RSV trial, the incidence of both respiratory and cardiovascular events was higher among participants with pre-existing ASCVD than among those without. The VE of the RSVpreF vaccine vs no vaccine was generally consistent across these two subgroups. However, because of their higher a priori risk, the absolute benefits of the RSVpreF vaccine appeared more pronounced among individuals with ASCVD ( ).

A recent clinical consensus statement from the European Society of Cardiology highlighted RSV as a pathogen associated with increased cardiovascular risk, with older individuals and those with coronary artery disease emphasized as susceptible risk groups. However, unlike influenza vaccination, the role of RSV vaccination for cardiovascular event reduction has not been established by high-quality randomized studies. Indeed, the intriguing concept of cardiovascular risk reduction with RSV vaccination has been based largely on extrapolations from observational studies linking RSV infection with cardiovascular events. The strategy is also appealing from a mechanistic standpoint as the pathophysiological consequences of RSV infection may trigger both atherosclerotic plaque rupture and thrombosis, with likely greater consequences among persons with pre-existing ASCVD. ,

In the overall DAN-RSV trial, the primary outcome of RSV-related respiratory tract disease hospitalization occurred at a significantly lower rate in the RSVpreF vaccine group than in the control group. However, the finding was based on a limited number of events due to relatively infrequent RSV testing. While we observed absolute risk reductions that numerically favoured the RSVpreF group, the relative effects did not achieve statistical significance, possibly due to the limited number of cardiovascular events that may otherwise be directly affected by a reduction of the RSV burden. Systematic RSV testing was also not conducted as part of DAN-RSV and is infrequently conducted as part of routine care in older adults, and most individuals with laboratory-confirmed RSV are not admitted to hospital. Patients with ASCVD likely also have other, more important, determinants of adverse risk that are more directly linked to their cardiovascular pathology. Of the specific cardiovascular endpoints, stroke was significantly reduced in persons with ASCVD, with a significant effect modification of the effectiveness of the RSVpreF vaccine. This is supported by both the overall DAN-RSV results and by a prior registry-based, self-controlled case series analysis in which acute RSV infection temporally increased the risk of ischaemic stroke. However, the specific underlying mechanisms and the reasons as to why the beneficial effect of the RSVpreF vaccine did not appear to involve myocardial infarction remain unclear. Nevertheless, based on the numbers of statistical tests conducted, one cannot rule out that the effect on stroke was a chance finding. The burden of cardiorespiratory hospitalization attributable to RSV among high-risk individuals is substantial, and our study results suggest use of RSVpreF vaccination overall, with considerably larger absolute risk reductions among participants with ASCVD, although further evaluation among individuals with ASCVD is warranted. As the protective effects of the RSVpreF vaccine have been demonstrated over at least two full RSV seasons, and additional follow-up of the DAN-RSV trial is already planned, it is possible that more significant differences related to cardiovascular outcomes may emerge over time.

Strengths of this study included the large, well-characterized population and complete follow-up. Data were derived from the largest randomized RSV vaccine trial ever conducted. Use of the nationwide registries and the governmental digital mail system allowed for recruitment of virtually all participants who were willing. Some limitations also require mention, the most notable of which was the overall low RSV-related event rate and lack of systematic RSV testing in the trial, which may obscure interpretation of subgroup analyses. The trial was open label, but the investigators were not involved in vaccine administration, daily clinical management of the participants, or data collection. Well-defined objective outcomes like myocardial infarction, stroke, and death are also less likely to be affected by knowledge of the treatment to which a participant is allocated. The Danish registries are known for very high-quality data ; however, the reliance on administrative, routinely collected data may introduce misclassification bias. Nonetheless, this is not likely to have affected between-treatment group differences. Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease may comprise a heterogeneous group of persons, but stratified analyses were not conducted because of the low event rates. Finally, as this was an older, Danish population, which is predominantly white, generalizability to younger age groups and other ethnicities may be limited.

This prespecified analysis of the DAN-RSV trial found that the VE of an RSVpreF vaccine vs no vaccine against respiratory and cardiovascular outcomes was similar among individuals 60 years of age with pre-existing ASCVD as compared with those without. Moreover, the incidence of stroke was lower in the RSVpreF group than in the control group. As absolute risk reductions were higher for most outcomes among persons with ASCVD as compared with those without, this high-risk group may potentially derive greater absolute benefits with the RSVpreF vaccine.

title: Cost-Effectiveness Analysis of Older Adult Vaccination with the Bivalent Respiratory Syncytial Virus Prefusion F (RSVpreF) Vaccine in Mexico.
abstract: Background/objectives Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) causes substantial morbidity and mortality in older adults, and in Mexico's rapidly growing older-adult population it may place increasing pressure on hospital-based care; however, Mexico-specific evidence to inform adult RSV immunization policy remains limited. This study estimated the long-term clinical and economic burden of medically attended RSV among adults aged 60-99 years in Mexico and evaluated the health impact and cost-effectiveness of a year-round RSVpreF vaccination program. Methods A population-based Markov cohort model compared the RSVpreF vaccination with no vaccination in a hypothetical Mexican cohort aged 60-99 years over a lifetime horizon. Outcomes included RSV-related hospitalizations, emergency department (ED) and physician office (PO) encounters, in-hospital deaths, life-years (LYs), and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs). Analyses were conducted from Mexican healthcare system and societal perspectives in 2025 Mexican pesos (MXN$) and US dollars (US$), with costs and outcomes discounted at 5% annually. One-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses and scenario analyses assessed the robustness of the findings. Results With 58% uptake, RSVpreF reduced hospitalizations by 187,825, ED encounters by 178,278, PO encounters by 465,976, and RSV-related deaths by 15,384. In the first 5 years, hospitalizations, ED encounters, and deaths declined by 31% each, and PO encounters by 14%. Over the lifetime horizon, vaccination generated an additional 96,227 discounted LYs and 71,526 discounted QALYs, while avoiding MXN$ 19,484 million (US$ 1061 million) in direct medical costs and MXN$ 3324 million (US$ 181 million) in indirect costs. Conclusions Year-round RSVpreF vaccination in Mexico among adults aged 60-99 years could substantially reduce medically attended RSV cases and RSV-related mortality and is projected to be cost-effective, thereby supporting the adoption of preventive strategies to address the growing clinical and economic burden of RSV in Mexico's aging population.
